THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with Nellie Lutcher by Patricia Willard
Reel One

January 10, 1979
February 15, 1979

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
rfm
P R O C E E D I N G S
Nellie Lutcher, I was born Nellie Rose Lutcher, and of course I married. From my second marriage my name now is Nellie Lutcher Lewis, but a very few people know about the Lewis, L-e-w-i-s.
And you were born in Lake Charles, Louisiana?
Lake Charles, Louisiana, yes.
And the date?
October 15, 1915.
Okay. So the Encyclopedia of Jazz is correct.
Well, sort of, kind of.
Okay.
It's a little bit -- well, I'm really a 1912 child, but 1915 is my professional birth date.
Okay. All right.
(Laughter)
I'm a 1912 child. But that is not for publication.
Okay, we won't publish that at all. You sure can't tell by looking. You look wonderful.
Well, I feel marvelous, I do. I don't feel any different now than I did, oh, 25 or even 30 years ago.
You don't look any different.
(Laughter)
In fact you look even better. You look great. You were one of how many children?
15. My dear mother was the mother of 15 and my father was the father of 16, because he had a son by a previous marriage, so I was one of 16 children.
And where were you chronologically?

About -- let me see, where was I? I would say about the -- about the 10th child, I was about the 10th, because my mother lost several children before I was born, so I was about the 10th child. I think that's correct.
What are the names of the children who did survive?

Well, next to me is a sister, Florida, her name is Morgan now. And next to her is a brother, Bubba, his name is Isaac, after my dad, and then we have twin brothers, James and Joe, Joe Lutcher, who is pretty well known, was known in the jazz circles at one time. He's gone into another field now, the religious field. And then we had a brother, a young brother to die, in the service, he was a bass player and his name was Charlie. And I think he was about 21 when he died. And we have four -- we had four little sisters, Florence, Eugenia, Vida and Margie. Vida, unfortunately is not with us anymore. She passed -- and incidentally, my older brother's not with us anymore. We lost him this past year. His name was
Bennie, I didn't mention his name. He was the oldest of the family. And Vida was next to the younger girl. She died in 1971.
Did anybody besides you and Joe go into music? Well, Charlie, but --

Charlie, but all of the kids had music, all of them studied music, but they didn't stick with it of course, and they all could sing and dance, and when they were little they used to dance and they were known as the little girls -- four little sisters right together, so they used to call them the Lutcher Sisters. And they all could sing and dance a little, but as they matured, well, you know, they went into something else.

I do have a sister now who has gone into -- she does a little something, a little writing, and she has a little group which they do little shows and things of that nature. But none of them studied music, none of them wanted to go into it, to that extent.
And your father was a professional musician, right?

My father was, yes. He was a marvelous musician. His basic instrument was the bass violin. However, he played all of the string instruments, and we had every type of instrument you could mention in our home in Louisiana. And I was fortunate enough to learn several of those instruments.

My father taught me the guitar and the violin and the mandolin, and I had a chance to do that when I was very young in school, because it gave me a chance to really get the, you know, get the fundamentals about all these instruments, the string instruments.

My mother also studied the piano before of course she got married, and it was her desire to really be a pianist, because she just loved the piano, and she married very young, I think she must have been about 13 when she married, or something like that, and she married. Well, she started having her children so fast, she just didn't have time. You can understand that.
Yeah, with that many children.
She didn't have time for the piano, so I think I fell heir to her talent and the talent of my father, and this was a combination that helped me to get along.
What was your mother's name?

My mother's name was Susie, and her maiden name was Garrett. She was born -- and my dad, were born down around Franklin, Louisiana, around Sheraton, and my mother was born in Sheraton and my father was born in Franklin, Louisiana, I think a little town out from Franklin known as St. Joseph. That's where their roots are.
Did your -- was your father's family and your mother's family also musical?

No, from what I -- I didn't know, really didn't know too much of my mother's family. I knew my -- well, I knew my mother's mother. My mother had three sisters, and my father had two sisters. I only knew one of my father's sisters, but they -- no, neither of them were musical. My dad seems to have been the only one in his family that took to music.
And tell me something about his career.

Well, of course he was well known around Franklin and around Louisiana, Lake Charles, and of course we used to play little towns right around Texas. Incidentally, my home, Lake Charles, is just about 28 miles from the border of Texas, coming west, and we used to play all around that area, Lake Charles and Port Arthur, Texas, Galveston, Texas, and all those different places. And he couldn't play all the time with us because my father also worked at a packing house. He was a truck driver and delivery man for a packing house, the Houston Packing Company. And he couldn't, you know, he couldn't play as much as he would like to, particularly if we would want to go out of town or something for a few days, he had to stay there and keep the store.
And had he -- how old was he when he started playing professionally?
Well, he must have been very young, Pat. I don't -- I don't recall what age, but from every indication

he must have been very, very young when he first started playing, because I think -- I know my mother said she was about 13 when she married, and my father was about -- he was about 12 years her senior. So, really, I've never figured out just how old he must have been. Now you've got me. I'll have to figure that out so I'll have the exact answer.
But he was playing professionally at the time they got married?
Yes. Oh yes, yes.
He had been.

Yes, he had been playing. At that time that's all he was doing, was just playing music, see, when they got married. But when that family started growing, you know, well that's when he had to do something else.
(Laughter)
I understand. And the band that he was playing in was the Imperial Jazz Band?

The Imperial Jazz Band. That was a very popular band in Lake Charles and the gentleman at that time that was leader, when I got into the orchestra, was a Mr. Clarence Hart$, and Mr. Hart$ was a very marvelous saxophone player, he played all of the saxophones, but I think his basic instrument was the tenor saxophone. No, not the tenor, I'm sorry, the alto, he was an alto man. And he and my father and Tony Babbins and Bunk Johnson, the late Bunk Johnson was

a friend of my dad's, incidentally. They knew each other down in that area where my father was born. I think Bunk came from a little town called New Iberia, if I'm not mistaken.* If he wasn't born there he stayed in New Iberia quite awhile, but that's where he and my father knew each other, and of course when Bunk Johnson came up to Lake Charles, then he played in the Imperial Orchestra, and I -- this is the one thing that I really -- I didn't realize naturally at the time, I didn't even think, I don't think anybody ever thought that Bunk Johnson would have gotten to be a very famous man. Because for many years I think Bunk even sort of -- I don't know, I don't remember if he -- he did not stop playing, but he sort of got away from that particular area, you know, and then in later years you began to hear somebody discovered him, and he became quite famous.
Well, did you consider him an outstanding player when you knew him and heard him?

Well, I guess I did, yes, I did, because in his way and whatever he played was perfect, you know. It was strictly what they called, refer to (as) Dixieland. At that time it wasn't even called Dixieland, it wasn't even labelled, frankly. It wasn't, it was not labelled. But whatever he played, nowadays this is Dixieland, this is what they call Dixieland.
Uh-huh.
*correct.

And he was a very articulate musician. I can remember that, every note he played was very distinct, that was his style, you know. So when he suddenly left the Louisiana area, as I said, and I didn't know where he was, then later I think he was discovered, and he came out to California. I think he was around San Francisco. And this was I think where he was when he passed, if I'm not mistaken.
I just opened up the Chilton book* here and it says here that he was born on Laurel Street in New Orleans, the 27th of December 1879, and he died in New Iberia.
Yeah, well New Iberia, you see, he lived in New Iberia. As I said, that was his home for an awfully long time.
What kind of a person was he?

He was a very nice man and very jovial, very, very humorous, very humorous man. I can remember he used to keep everybody laughing all the time with these old jokes. You know, one of the most marvelous things that I can remember about people like Bunk Johnson, Pat, you know, one of the most wonderful things that I can remember is to have worked around people with humor, with a sense of humor. For instance, in our little town we used to have -- the minstrels used to come there. They wouldn't play but one day, they couldn't afford to stay in a little town like Lake Charles but one day. Then we used to have the medicine shows to come there.
John Chilton's Who's Who In Jazz.

Then we used to have the vaudeville shows to come, you know, to Lake Charles. But they would all come there and maybe they would just play one day, it was a one nighter. What I'm saying is the humor, and these people weren't, you know, they weren't making any money, so to speak, just barely existing really, but the marvelous sense of humor and the love of what they did was so marvelous, and this sort of always -- it impressed me and it helped me to know that when I saw these people performing or saw them playing, like for instance Bunk Johnson, I knew that they were real sincere in what they were doing.
Can you describe what the medicine shows and the minstrel shows were like, what you remember, because that's something that's, you know, gone.

Yes. I heard someone not long ago talking about this particular thing. They used to, what they would do, for instance, a minstrel show, well a minstrel show of course would come to town and they would have these -- the minstrel men -- you've seen that, I think that has been shown on television, where they have what you call an interlocutor, whatever they called this particular man, he would be sort of like an M.C. of the thing, you know, and he would egg the rest of them on or lead them on, and each one has a little joke or a little something to tell, you know, a little something, a rhyme or something, and this would go on, and of course they would have the dancing girls and whatever, and singers and

whatever.

The medicine shows, well that was usually limited to they would get on one corner. Well the medicine shows would really stay a little longer than -- they would stay longer than one night. They would maybe sometimes spend a week in a town like Lake Charles, but they'd build a little stage like, a little platform like, and they would have maybe a two or three piece orchestra, you know, loud, very loud, and then this guy would make his -- make his spiel or squeal, whatever you want to call it, spiel I suppose I should say, about this medicine, and this medicine would do everything in the world for you.
(Laughter)

Everything imaginable, you know. He'd tell you, yes, this is the greatest medicine. And they would do this, and my God, the people, they would just buy it like crazy, just because the guy was a good salesman, you know. And --
How much would the medicine cost, about?
Well, I don't --
Can you remember?

I really can't remember. We never bought any, my folks never bought any, you know. But I would say maybe about a dollar. I don't think it would hardly cost more than that. Maybe the same thing today would cost you five or six dollars.
Uh-huh.

But they used to make money selling it like that, you know, and make enough money to pay for the little Spot pills?, which didn't cost them that much, I'm sure, and the musicians, there was no such thing as the unions at the time. And -- but it was a form of entertainment, you know. It was just a form of entertainment that went by the wayside many years ago I'm sure.
Well, so the medicine shows supported themselves selling their medicine. But a minstrel show, did they charge admission, or --
The minstrel shows charged admission, that was the difference, yes, and the minstrel shows of course had a tent, this was a tent show.
Uh-huh.

Yes, it was a tent show, and the medicine show was not, it was just -- you'd stand, you'd stand up and you'd be entertained by the orchestra and by all of these guys could play and sing and entertain, you know, tell jokes and what have you. But it was a very funny thing and the people would crowd around, you know, and just get the biggest kick out of that.
So that was the principal entertainment there.
Yes, particularly in small towns, see.
How many people lived in Lake Charles

Well, oh my Lord, I guess I would say about -- maybe about 20,000, 25,000, maybe. Surprising. I never even thought about that, because I've been away from there so long. It has grown up to be a very lovely, beautiful city, Lake Charles, Louisiana, and it has progressed so and they have gorgeous buildings and gorgeous homes, just built up tremendously.
What is your earliest recollection of music?
Well -- you mean my participating in music?

Just the first music that you can remember as a child that you were interested in and you remember hearing and it meant something to you, and then when your first recollection of your actually playing.

Well, I guess I can say, Pat, really I can hardly remember when I couldn't play music, because as I say, it was a natural thing with me, although I did study music, I have studied. We had instruments around the house. We had an old broken down phonograph, you know, with the horn, the big horn, we had that. And by my dad being a musician, and they used to play. He and, used to be another gentlemen who used to come around the house, he was a guitar player, and he and my father used to just sit and just play, and sometimes one or two

of the other old guys would come by and they would just sit. That was the way they entertained themselves, you know, they would just sit and play, and we always had instruments around the house, and I just took a liking and a love of the piano, and my feet couldn't even reach the pedals, and I could get there and pick out certain things, you know, and my folks, my folks saw to it, naturally, by my mother being home all the time, and of course daddy was at work, but they both knew, you know, they thought I had some talent, some ability, and so my mother started me -- they started me in music, with a marvelous teacher who -- well, my God, she just took a liking to me and I was very fortunate to have had somebody like her. Her name was Eugenia King Raynaud (PHONETIC), and she was a magnificent teacher, just magnificent. She was not a jazz person at all. She was a woman who had studied and she had a degree in music, but I don't know if it was even a degree that you could get today. But anyway she had a certificate or something in music, because she taught and all of the children in that area, and adults for that matter, well, she was the main teacher in Lake Charles. And incidentally, her husband, who was R. C. Reynaud, Ralph Reynaud, was the principal of the school in Lake Charles that I attended.

She egged me on and encouraged me on, and she showed me all the -- whatever she could. I shall never forget one time at a graduation exercise, she had me to play the 'Blue Danube Waltz' behind a choral group. Yes, and I was very young

at the time, very small, and this was so marvelous, because at the time we had a woman in Lake Charles who was -- I can't remember her maiden name, but her name was Mrs. Alton J. Foster, who was also a very magnificent concert pianist. Her husband at one time I think was the President of the rice mill up there, if I'm not mistaken. And she happened to have been at this particular event and she was very inspired by me, and she contacted my teacher and she told her she would like her to bring me down to her home, her studio was at her home. And so I went there, and for a little while I studied under Mrs. Foster, and so she told Mrs. Reynaud, "Well, I don't think I can do much with Nellie, I don't think I can teach her very much, because she's so advanced." Well, I could memorize, whatever she taught me I could memorize it right away, you know. But that was one thing that I don't think I've ever mentioned that before, but it was something that I feel grateful for today, because this lady wasn't a well known person in other sections of the country, but in that area she was very well known and a very highly respected musician.

But anyway, Mrs. Eugenia Reynaud was also the organist and the pianist of the little Baptist Church where we belonged, the Sunlight Baptist Church in Lake Charles. And she trained me to be her assistant at the church, and then I used to play for her at Sunday school. I became the Sunday school pianist. I was getting the big sum of $2.00 a month. And when I would

help her, she would always give me, I think I'd get about four or five dollars for helping her with the music. So you know, after she had trained me I could carry on myself, so many Sundays when she couldn't come to church, if she felt ill, she felt like Nellie could carry on, so she would just let Nellie carry on, and I did. Of course the only thing was they used to have to wake me up at night to play for collection, you know, when it came time, after the minister had preached. Well, of course in those days -- I suppose this still exists, but the ministers, you know, used to preach an awfully long time. Oh, my gracious, and people didn't really think they had gone to church. Now if you go to church and you're in church one hour that's plenty.
(Laughter)

And on Sundays we would go to church in the morning, go to Sunday school first, and then after Sunday school we would stay in church about two hours or two and a half hours, and then you'd come back in the evening, you know, for the B.Y.P.U.--Baptist, Young People's Union. And then the church service. Well, that's what I would play for, and my teacher. And sometimes even when she was there she would let me play, you know. She just wanted me to be trained.
So you were playing organ then?
Piano. No, just piano. We had one of the old fashioned organs, you know, but I didn't do too much with that. One of the old pump organs. But this was piano.
How old were you when you were playing at the church?
Well, I was about eight years old when I first started doing that. Eight or nine.
When you were playing for the services at night you were --

Yeah, that's why I'm saying they had to wake me up. I would go to sleep. I would be sitting up there asleep and they would wake me up and say, 'Wake Sister Lutcher up. Wake little Sister Lutcher up and tell her it's time for collection.'

So they would wake me up and I would start playing, you know, and it was -- that was an awful lot of fun, and that's something that helped me an awful, awful lot. And then of course later on I -- they needed a pianist in the orchestra, because there was a piano player from Columbus, Ohio by the name of Al Freeman, and Al Freeman was a marvelous pianist, just marvelous, and he'd lived in Lake Charles for quite some time, and he decided to go back to his home town in Columbus, and he left, and of course they didn't have a piano player. They needed someone. So they were trying to locate, trying to find a piano player, and so Mr. Harts, who was the leader of the Imperial Orchestra and he said to my father, he said, 'Well, what about Nellie?' He said, 'Nellie plays well enough to play with us.' So my dad says, he says -- my dad was all for

it and he said, "Well, I think she can play well enough to play with us," you know, because sometimes at the house my dad and I would play, you know. He would be playing and I would play along with him. But my mother wasn't too keen on it. She didn't think too much of the idea. Well, of course it was a natural thing at that time, this was a biased thing, in thinking about religion and music, you know. And many people felt -- this was the general, not many, but it was the general feeling, somehow they looked down at jazz music, you know, and as I get older, and as I got older, I realized how stupid it was because you were only expressing a natural gift and a natural talent.
Yeah.

And I shall never forget, there were certain women, like older women at the church, you know, they just thought it was awful. Finally, when my mother did consent to let me play in the orchestra with my dad, you know, and Mr. Hartz, they said, "I think it's awful for that little girl." "That little girl is playing jazz music, and I think it's terrible. She's going to hell."
(Laughter)

"I don't think it's right. I don't think her mother and father should let her do this." So of course my mother felt very bad about it, but my dad didn't, and my dad said, "Listen, she's my daughter and I want her to play. She's got talent, she's got ability and I want her to use it.
I want her to play." And so he just didn't pay any attention to them, and I didn't pay any attention to them either, you know, but my mother, she felt a little funny about it, you know.
Well, did your mother feel funny because it was jazz music or because you were a little girl out there in an orchestra?

I guess it was because I was a little girl, because I was young, you know, and my mother loved me, naturally, like any mother, she was proud of the fact that I could play, because she really -- she used to even wash and iron for my music teacher to be sure that my lessons were paid for, you know. She did that because my dad, as I say, he wasn't making a lot of money. But she did that to help. And she was a beautiful laundress anyway, and as a girl that's what she did, she worked in a Chinese laundry and learned how to do beautiful laundry work. So she would do this sometimes in exchange for my music lessons, for my teacher.

So she was just -- it was just the idea of because I was so very young at the time, and -- but as the time went on, of course, I really didn't leave Louisiana right away. I was still in school. I was still in school, but I didn't leave Louisiana right away. I did marry when I was very young, and I'm not going to even give the name of the gentleman that I married at that time. I was very young and he -- I felt that I was taken advantage of in a way, and I don't even want to
go into that. But nevertheless, that marriage lasted two months and I went back home.
How old were you?

Oh, I was about 16. And I went back home. And when I went back home, this is really when I started travelling. I did not start travelling before that time. What I mean travel, I mean the road, you know, like we went through Louisiana and Texas with this other group, with the Southern This was a bunch of Rhythm Boys, younger musicians, and some of them were from Texas, in fact three or four of them were from Texas. And we did go into Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, you know, travelled around.

But at that time I was into the arranging thing, I was learning to arrange music. Yes, I wanted to study. I wanted to study arranging, and we had a very wonderful saxophone player and arranger in the band by the name of Al Wilson. Al was from New Orleans, and he taught me. I studied under him, he taught me how to arrange. So I was arranging for all of this band, and at that time we had about 15 pieces, I think, or 16 pieces.
Was that the Imperial --
No, the Southern --
Oh, this was the Southern Rhythm Boys.
It was called the Southern Rhythm Boys.
And in one of these groups I think Paul Barnes, the wonderful
Paul Barnes, from New Orleans, was in this group. Also at one time, Collins, Neil Collins -- not Neil Collins.

This is February 15th, 1979, and we're continuing the oral history with Nellie Lutcher, and we're going to do over part of this reel because we unfortunately developed some surface noise in there, and about when it started we were talking about the Southern Rhythm Boys, and you were telling me who was in the band, Nellie. You said Al Wilson? Okay, the personnel of the Southern Rhythm Boys.

The personnel consisted of a -- let's see, there were brothers, there were two brothers from Texas, Leo Williams and Eddie Williams. Leo played trombone. Eddie Williams played bass violin, and then we had Al Wilson, who was a marvelous saxophonist and arranger. And he taught me, I studied arranging under him. Yes, he had me arranging for the big Southern Rhythm Boys Orchestra for a while. And also in that orchestra was Alexis Rochan and Shelly LeMelle from New Orleans, and also a John Collins, I think that's the right name, he was the brother to Lee Collins, who was from the Collins family, very, very popular, well known jazz family in New Orleans, and he was with the orchestra also.
And both John and Lee played trumpet, is that right?
I think so, yes, uh-huh. John was
a younger man than what's his name. And then we had, let's see, from Lake Charles we had Eldridge Joe and we had --
And Eldridge Joe played what?

He played drums. Eldridge Joe. Then we had Snake Griffin. Snake was a saxophone player, a tenor saxophone player. We also had, from Lake Charles we had -- let's see, Eldridge Joe, Snake Griffin -- oh, from Apaloosa, Louisiana we had a marvelous saxophone player by the name of Lawrence Emerson who later sort of got away from the music business and became an educator. He was the principal of a school. I think he just retired a couple of years (ago). Down in the little city of Apaloosa, Louisiana. And then I mentioned Baker Millian. Baker Millian was with the -- no, he wasn't with this orchestra, I'm sorry, he was with the Imperial Orchestra. Shelly LeMelle, I don't know if I mentioned his name before, but he was also from New Orleans.
I think you mentioned on the earlier tape that Eldridge Joe later played with what orchestra, Don Abbott?
Don Albert.
Albert.
I think it was Don Albert's orchestra. Anyway, when he left Lake Charles he went on into Texas and stayed around San Antonio. I think he was with Don Albert's orchestra.
Don Albert was based where?
In San Antonio. San Antonio. And Don Albert was very well known in Louisiana. He is originally from -- was, rather, from New Orleans, a trumpet player.
And I think you also said before that Snake Griffin was a Creole, right?

He was Creole, yes. He was Creole and he was from Lake Charles. In later years he went up -- he came out to California as a matter of fact, and I don't know now if he's still around or not, but he did come out to California. He was a part of this orchestra, part of the Imperial Orchestra, and then he went into the Southern Rhythm Boys.
You mentioned earlier that you had learned from your father how to play guitar, violin and mandolin. Did you ever use any of that knowledge in any of the bands you played in?

No, not really, no. I used it at school, you know. We had a mandolin club, we had a violin club and a guitar, and just enough to know a little about it. Now don't ask me today if I have any knowledge of any of them. No, I don't.
(Laughter)
But it was fun at that time, and the ukelele, of course I played the ukelele, which was a very simple instrument, very easy. I played the ukelele quite well,

but the rest of the instruments, I just wanted to -- I had access to the instruments, which was marvelous you know. We had all sorts of instruments around the house, and since my father did play all of the string instruments very well, but his major instrument was the bass violin. He also played the piano.
Oh, you didn't mention that before.

No, he played the piano, but he didn't -- you know, he didn't really study the piano, but he just used to play. Because at one time, long before I started playing, he used to play little parties and little dances, but he never played in an orchestra. You know, he just played. But his basic instrument was the bass violin, and he was a very fine musician.
Before, we were talking, when we talked about the Southern Rhythm Boys, you mentioned that they were all around the same age, is that right?
In the Southern Rhythm Boys, yes, most of these guys in the Southern Rhythm Boys were younger musicians, much younger.
At the time you were there with them their age range was what, about?
Well, I would say in the 20s, like in the 20s. And one guy that played with us, this comes to mind too, Kermit Scott, who in later years was featured with the

[Earl] Hines band. Kermit was a very young musician, Kermit Scott, when he first came to the Southern Rhythm Boys. He and Eddie Williams and Leo were friends, they were all from Beaumont, Texas. And he came to us and he was just marvelous, just a marvelous musician. I don't know where he is today or what he's doing, but it just came to my mind that he did come to us, and all the girls were so excited over him, you know.
But all the guys were younger musicians, uh-huh.
And the size of the band, there were-- many were in the band?
Well, in this particular orchestra we must have had about 16 or 17 pieces.
So you were arranging for a 17-piece band.

Yes, I -- I thought that was what I wanted to do. You know, I enjoyed doing it at that time. I really never gave any thought to ever really becoming a vocalist. At that time I did maybe -- I would do a couple of songs, something -- you know, I think most people have one or two songs that they particularly like. I would maybe do a couple of songs like that, but I didn't really concentrate on being a singer. But I did concentrate on being an arranger, because I loved chords and I had a good sense of chords, you know, and harmony, naturally so. So this is what I had really planned to do, and then I remember Mary Lou Williams later, you know, went
into arranging, and this is really her forte. She was an excellent arranger, and I don't know at that time -- maybe I was sort of inspired by her and didn't realize it.
(Laughter)
How old would you have been then, when you first started arranging for the big band?
Well, I must have been about -- I would say about, maybe about 18 or 19, or something like that.
That's great. And you played with the Southern Rhythm Boys until you left to go back to Lake Charles when your mother was ill?

Yes. Well, we went -- you know, we travelled around parts of Louisiana and parts of Mississippi, playing the little dances and little clubs. And at that time there was no such thing hardly as you getting a salary. That was unheard of. And at that time we didn't know anything about unions. Can you imagine me being so unionized now?
(Laughter)
Yes.
We used to play these dances, Pat, and we'd play, like we'd say percentage dances, you know, and that meant perhaps you'd get and perhaps you wouldn't get, you know.
(Laughter)
Well, you always made something, didn't you?

Oh, we'd always make some money, yeah, and we travelled by car, you know, and I don't ever remember the orchestras, any of them, having new cars, you know. The cars were old cars and sometimes they'd break down on the road and there we'd be, we'd sit until they could get it fixed, get to the nearest town.
Tell me how the percentage dance worked. Would somebody book you, they would call you to come there and you would work for whatever you could make?

Well, what they would do, no, we'd get a -- they'd get a percentage. Maybe we'd say 30, 40 or something, I can't remember the exact percentage now, but that's how it worked, you know. And it means that the promoter or whoever would -- we would be allowed to have a ticket, you know, our own ticket man with us, and he would, you know, give an account. He would be responsible for the orchestra's -- pardon me, for the tickets, to see that we got our fair share of the money that was taken in, see.
But there was no such thing as you -- maybe once in a while we would get a guarantee, but it would be a small guarantee.
What would small be at that time?
Well, just say maybe you'd be guaranteed about $5.00 a person or something like that, you know. And then of course that would be held until the affair was over, you
see. It was against the guarantee, and of course that would come out of the gross money, you see.
Uh-huh. Did they usually -- were they good for their guarantee? Was there ever a time when they'd say that and then not pay?

Well, no, as a rule they did pay. Well, they didn't have anything to lose, really. You see, you don't hear of anything like this today, Pat. You know, if you're booked someplace, man, I mean they've got to come across with that bread, you know. But at that time, the guy, what he had to do was promote, he had to promote the affair, you see, and he would promote it and if he would promote it well, if he was a good promoter, well he would make money and we would make money, you see. Because I think what happened, all of the expenses would come off the top thing, and then after the expenses were all taken off, well that's how they used to do it. That's how it used to be done.
Do you remember what admission would be to a dance?
I don't remember, but it wouldn't be that much, maybe 50 cents, a dollar or a dollar and a half, I imagine, at the top, you know.
Uh-huh.
But you see, at that time people had no other source hardly of entertainment, you know, and they

looked forward to the dances. I know how it was in our little town, Lake Charles. My God, when they had a dance there and if they had a good orchestra, you know, they would just -- the people would just turn out like crazy. They were crazy about this type of thing. They loved to dance, they just loved to dance.
But you also mentioned before that a lot of the people in your church didn't approve of dancing.
No, they did not.
That was the Baptist attitude, right?
That's very well -- the Protestants, all the Protestant churches, the Baptists, the Methodists, you know, no they didn't approve.
And the Presbyterians, too, I know they didn't.

No, they didn't. No, no, that was sinful to do that, that was a sin, you know. So -- but the youngsters didn't pay any attention to that. It was really the only thing they had to look forward to, you know, for diversion or for recreation.
You mentioned, I think, on this part of the tape before, that a lot of your work for the band came from Catholic functions.
Yes, indeed, oh, yes, sure.
They didn't disapprove of dancing.
Oh, no, indeed. No, they have never, no.

The only time they don't -- they don't dance is during the Lenten season, you see, and this is when they observe, I think it's six weeks, a six week period, and at that time, well, the poor musicians, you know, we were just -- we wouldn't fare too good at that particular time, because the Protestants, it was nothing, you know, they didn't believe in dancing or anything, but jazz music they considered a sin, you know, and just as soon as -- now, for instance, on the Good Friday -- well, no the day after Good Friday, which is a Saturday of course, and the Catholics would have this great big dance or whatever, and then it would be all opened up again, you know, full blast, until the next time. Until the next season, next year, when they would get back to -- and that particular season follows the Mardi Gras. I guess you know this, but that Mardi Gras season, the Mardi Gras season is about two weeks, and it's usually the first part of the year. There's no certain date. I don't remember now how they judge or govern whatever day it's going to be. It has something to do with the moon or something, you know. I can't remember. But nevertheless, the Lenten season does start right after Mardi Gras, the day after Mardi Gras. And that goes for six weeks.
Was that area predominantly Catholic, or --
Well, no, it wasn't predominantly Catholic, but I would say -- well, Pat, I would say about --
maybe about 70 percent, which is almost -- I guess I could say predominantly Catholic, yeah, about 70 percent.
Yeah, well, I think it probably is around New Orleans, but I didn't know about all of Louisiana.
Well, it's that way all over Louisiana practically, uh-huh. It was at that time.

We talked before about women with bands and I asked you wasn't it rather unusual for you, especially at your age, to be playing with a band, and you mentioned that there were several women around New Orleans. You named one, Jeanette Kimball. You said she was with --
Papa Celestin, , right. She was marvelous, marvelous pianist.
Were there any others?
Offhand --
That you can remember the names of.

Offhand I -- isn't it funny, I can't think of any other names right now, but Jeanette was outstanding, because she was with Papa Celestin. Her husband at that time was also with the orchestra. He was a marvelous guitar player.
What was his first name?

What is it? Kimball. Kimball. I can't think of his first name now, but he is right now working in New Orleans with the -- at the Preservation Band, I think. A guitarist. But he and Jeannette -- well Jeannette, as I say,
she was just a marvelous pianist, and she was with Papa Celestin's orchestra oh, for quite awhile.
Did bands like Papa Celestin's ever get to Lake Charles?

Oh, yes. Yes, they used to come through there. Sure they'd come there. You know, they played one nighters. They could never play more than one night there. You know, the people just wouldn't support it, but they would support that one night. They used to come to Lake Charles, and then they would go into Texas, you see, go maybe as far as San Antonio or El Paso.
What other bands came through there that you got to see, that you can remember?

Well, I can remember -- I can remember Don Albert's orchestra. I can remember -- I don't remember Alphonso Trent's orchestra, because I think Trent's orchestra was a little before this time, a little before my time. I can't remember that orchestra too well, but I do know that Alphonso Trent had a marvelous orchestra. And some other bands used to come through from like Alexandria, Louisiana. We had Crome, Taft Crome, who was very well known in that area. And we had bands that used to come from, oh, come from Houston, Texas. We had quite a few marvelous bands around Houston. Funny, I can't even think of any of their names right now, but there are some -- there are several musicians who have

really gone on to big times that were from Houston, Texas. One of them was -- what did they call -- used to play with -- a saxophone player, used to play and sing. Sort of a -- he's just terrific. He's still around. I can't think of his name, but it'll come back to me. But he was from Houston.
Arnett Cobb is from someplace around there.

Well, Arnett is from Houston, I think, too. But this guy that I'm talking about is a -- he's a saxophone player. He worked with -- I can't remember now even who he worked with. Now, that bothers me, because he's still around. But he was marvelous. Anyway, he was very well known. He was from Houston.
There was a lot of music in that --
A lot of music. There was a lot of music at that time, uh-huh.
And you mentioned -- well, that was later on in L.A., you mentioned a lady named Cleo Brown in L.A.

Cleo Brown was very popular when I first came to California. You see, she -- before I left Louisiana, as a matter of fact, she was, you know, just -- she had made a record called, 'It's a Heavenly Thing,' and this -- she sort of started the trend really for girl piano players, you know, piano players and vocalists. She started this trend.
Oh.

And she was just -- oh, as I say, when I got here, Cleo Brown, that's all you could hear, Cleo Brown. Cleo Brown. She was from Chicago. And when I came out here I think that was the one thing that, you know, made people -- you know, every time they'd see a girl piano player they'd expect you to sing. Well, I really didn't concentrate on singing, as I said before. I always played, you know, because I had been playing for a long time, and I played and was used to playing with orchestras. And when I came out here, well of course when you go into a thing where you are vocalizing, and see this is a whole different bag. It is, it's absolutely completely different, and I really had not -- this was far from my mind, it really was, it was very far from my mind. I was thinking when I got out to California what I would do is get back into arranging and really study and work at that. But the public changed that when I got here. And I'm glad.
Well, I'm glad you're glad. Well, you have such a distinctive voice, it's a wonderful style, that nobody has ever sounded like you.

Well, I'm glad of that too. I'm glad of that too. But you know, of course I suppose I had the same experience that Nat King Cole had, and there are a few other musicians too that has had the same experience. When I went to work, for instance my very first job here was at the
Dunbar Hotel. Did we talk about this the other day? I don't know.
On the part of the tape we're doing over, yes.

Oh, well that's good, we can use that. Anyway, I lived -- my mother's sisters, my mother had two sisters that lived out here. Well, one lived here in California -- Los Angeles, rather, and the other lived up north in Oakland, and then I had some cousins here. She had two sons. And then I had, oh, just a host of friends, and of course the gentleman who I mentioned earlier, Clarence Hart, had moved out here. I think we mentioned that before, did we not?
On the part that we're doing over, yes.

Uh-huh. Well, Clarence Hart had moved out here, and of course when he got moved out to California, well he had gotten into painting and decorating and this was his thing. He did this at home. But when he got out here he really went full, you know, just full scale into that particular thing.
No more music?

He didn't play music hardly, no, after he got out here. No, he did not. And strangely enough, his children didn't get into music. I think his son used to play a little, his son named Herbert Hart used to play a little saxophone, but I think Herbert just -- they just got away from

it completely.
But getting back to the Dunbar Hotel, the singing bit, they would come into this Dunbar Hotel and they would request a song. And I kept begging off and saying, 'Well, you know, I don't sing. I'm not a vocalist.' Well, they'd say, 'Well, hum it. Hum it. We like your voice. We just want to hear something.' And then I would say, 'Well, I just don't know too many songs.' Or maybe I would sing a song or two, try to sing, or hum it. Then finally I realized that this was something that they wanted from me, and I began to think about it and concentrate on it, and I said, 'Well, my God, they're expecting me --,' and I used to make a little extra money. This was when I realized what the kitty was all about.
(Laughter)

We didn't have this back home, you know. People would come up and just give you money sometimes, but out here most of the clubs had what they call a kitty. They even had a man here that used to make the kitties. Very pretty little cat, you know, on a stand, and with the lights and everything. Some of them were very fancy. But I didn't have anything like that.
You mean the kitty actually started out looking like a kitty?
Yes, oh, yes.
I didn't know that.
Oh, yes, it was made like a kitty, yes, and they'd have this little hole for you, somebody'd come up and request something and they'd just throw this money in the kitty.
How big was the kitty?
Well, it would be maybe about two, three feet tall.
Oh.

And with a little hole in it, you know, and they'd throw the money in there to you. But I didn't have anything like that, but they would get a glass, I had them to even just get a glass, say, 'Give me a glass, bartender,' and they'd sit the glass on the piano and put money in there.
I've seen that. Well, did the kitty start on the west coast, do you know?
I don't know where it started, really, but I didn't know about it until I got out here.
That's interesting.

Yeah, I didn't know about that until I got out here. And then after -- you know, when I got out here and got to working around, I noticed all of the clubs did this, and of course the musicians weren't making hardly any money you know. You're just making a little $2.00 or whatever a night, and -- but you made tips. The people were used to tipping. And as a matter of fact even today there are

a lot of people today who are accustomed to tipping at that time, they wouldn't think of asking for a tune unless they tipped you. I don't care who you are, no matter how big you are, you know, because really, when you have arrived, you know, you just feel like this is something that you should do. You just don't expect this. And at that time you sort of expected this, you know. I don't meanto say you wouldn't do it if they didn't give you -- you didn't get a tip, I don't mean that. But I'm just saying that when you have arrived you just don't expect that, you really don't. You're making good money, you know, so you just think that what you're doing you should just do it, you know?
Well, it was an accepted custom.
It was an accepted custom, and it really was in every place that I worked in. You know, they had this.
Did the club own the kitty?
No.
You carried your own kitty with you.
Oh, you carried your own kitty. That was your money. That was your --
I knew about the money, but I meant physically the kitty.
Oh, it was yours. It was your kitty.
And you carried your own.
Everybody had their own kitty, yeah.
That is really interesting.

Yeah, they had their own kitties, everybody had their own kitties. But that started, really started me to singing, you know. What I did, I used to get -- and then I started getting certain tunes, and what I would do, I'd get them and style them the way I'd want them, you know, I'd want to do it. And --
Do you remember the tunes you were doing when you first started singing?

Oh, I think, 'Under a Blanket of Blue,' and -- right now, offhand, I can't think of some of the other tunes, but I remember that because I was doing that when I first came out here. And, 'The Object of My Affections,' was a tune I used to do all the time. That was a very, very popular thing and I used to do that. And there were some special lyrics and some of them were mine and some of them were other singers', you know, because it was the type of song you could do many things with and write all sorts of parodies and everything else to it.

But that started me really to realizing -- when I realized that -- what the people wanted, and I said, well, you know, this is good. Then I enjoyed it, I loved it, you know, and I'd get a song and I would style it my way and do it my own way, and the people accepted it.
So by the time I -- later on, of course we haven't

gotten to that yet, but by the time I did get ready to record and was discovered, I had a repertoire already built. I had a built-in repertoire all ready, and this was one of the things that sort of annoys me, is the fact that my material was already established, well established years before I even, you know, thought about making a record. And today, I mean, you can't even buy a record today, you know, a Nellie Lutcher record cannot be found unless you find it in a rare record shop or an auction or something like that, because there are many people who have told me that they buy them at auctions. I don't know. But I'm getting ahead of myself.
That's all right.
This leads into that.

We don't have to -- we want to talk about that. We don't have to stay chronological. However, before we concentrate on Los Angeles, I want to go back to Louisiana and Texas for a minute, because the other time we talked you told me a couple of stories that I want to get on this tape, and they were -- I asked you had you had any unusual experiences travelling on the road with the bands, and you told me a story about when you were travelling by car with the band, I believe it was --
The Imperial. Yeah, it was the Imperial.
And you were on your way to Galveston via Beaumont, Texas, and what happened?

Oh, yes. Well, it was in the summertime and of course travelling in old cars with old tires, you know, we used to -- if we were going a distance like that, which must be close to 200 miles, I imagine, from Lake Charles, we travelled in two cars. We were at that particular time travelling in two cars, so there must have been about 10 of us, I guess. And we were going to Galveston to play a -- it was a holiday, I think it was pretty close to Labor Day or something like that, one of the holidays. And we were supposed to have stopped in Beaumont, Texas, both cars. Well, the one car that left ahead of us, when they got to Beaumont, Texas they did not stop, they went on, you know. They were trying -- what they were trying to do was to get to where they were going before day, you see, because it was awfully hot. I don't know if you know how hot it gets back there, but --
I know.

-- it does get very hot. So anyway, this car did not stop. So when our car left, I guess we must have left maybe about 45 minutes or an hour after they did. Well, we had already made plans to stop at a very popular little restaurant in the black neighborhood called the Sweet Dreams Cafe. And we were supposed to meet there and have coffee before we journeyed on. Well, this group went on, so when we stopped at the Sweet Dreams, well they told us that they hadn't been there, they didn't stop, they just went on. And so we

said, well, there's no need of us tarrying, so we stayed there maybe about 20 minutes or so, just enough to have coffee, and then we went on and we got to this little town, China, Texas is the name of this little town, and in this area, particular area, they have roadhouses. I don't know if they still have them, I imagine they do, I don't know. But they used to have roadhouses and these roadhouses were sometimes like a block or maybe a couple of blocks from the highway, and they had flood-lights all over the place, all around, you could see them from the highway, from the main highway, you know. And so somebody spotted, one of the guys spotted it, and said, "That looks like our car. Look at that car at a distance there," you know, because there was nothing in between, and they said, "That looks like our guys over there, it looks like a car with instruments on top." That's how we could really recognize it. So he said it does, well let's go over there and see. Well, we drove to this establishent, which was a roadhouse, and sure enough when we got there our musicians were there and some of them were standing out in front, most of them were standing out in front of the club, you know, in front of this area, and one guy had his hood up and doing some work on the car. And so one of them said, "Oh, my God, I'm so sorry you people came here, I'm so sorry you drove here." Well, we had no idea what had happened, you know. And so finally, these three caucasian -- one caucasian gentleman came to the door and he

says, "Oh, here's some more of them. Here's some more of them," ha, ha, "Here's some more of them." So he said, "Come on here, here's some more of them." Said, "We're really going to have some fun tonight." So then his other two buddies came over and these men said, "Oh, yes, oh, yes, and here's a bunch of them, and there's a girl in there, there's a girl in there." Said, "Yes, they've got a girl piano player. That means she must play the piano." And so they called me -- they came over to the car. And I acted like I was asleep, you know. So one of the guys nudged me and told me come on, he says, "Girlie, girlie, wake up. Come on in. Let's have some music." And they started applauding, you know, and "Let's have some music, let's hear some music." And I says, "Oh, I'm awfully tired. I'm sleepy."

Now, this was about, Pat, this was about 3:00 o'clock in the morning, 2:30 maybe, I'll say about 2:30, 3:00 o'clock in the morning. Yeah, in the morning. So he says, "Come on out and let's have some music." And so one of the other guys said, "Oh, we're tired, we can't." And he says, "Oh, we'll wake you up. We'll wake you up." He says, "Come on. Come on here."
How many of them were there?

Well, there were three of these guys, three of them. And then they went and got their guns, and naturally when they saw these long guns, these huge shotguns, you know, he says, "Oh, yes, we're going to have a little music

here. We're going to have a little fun here this morning. We're going to have some fun." So one of the guys said, "Go ahead on. Go ahead on. Let's go. Let's go." Because they had had this experience. They had already played, in other words. This gang, the crew before us, had already played. They had made them perform, see, so they knew what was coming. And so what we did, we then went -- we just got out of the car and went on in and started, you know, the guys started tuning up, and he said, "Come on, girlie. Come on, girlie." They wanted to be sure I was in, because they knew I was the piano player in the band. So we started playing. They had a ball. Oh, they just started applauding, you know, so there was one guy with us who was not a musician. He was a schoolteacher, really, but in the summer months he did odd jobs. (Pause)
Go on.

He did odd jobs and he went with us to take up tickets, like I was telling you before. This was a percentage dance that we were doing, and he took up the tickets for us. So the guy said, "What are you doing? What are you doing?" So he says, "Oh, I'm to be ticket man. I take up tickets." He said, "You take up tickets? Well you're not taking up tickets tonight. There are no tickets here to take." He says, "Well, this is what I do for them. I -- you know, it's a percentage dance, we play a percentage dance, you know, and I keep account of the tickets." And he says, "Well, there

are no tickets here tonight. Come on, you've got to dance a little bit." And he says, "Well, I'm sorry, I don't dance." So he says, "Well, what else do you do besides take up tickets?" And he says, "Well, I'm a schoolteacher." He says, "School-teacher? Well, you're not taking up tickets here tonight and you're not teaching school tonight, so come on, let's have a little dance." And he kept saying, "Well, I'm sorry, I can't dance." So they got -- they said, "Oh, yes, you can dance, yes, you can dance. All Negroes can dance, so come on and dance." And they shot -- they held this gun at this guy's feet to make him dance. And he was just walking around in a circle, you know, and two of them were walking around in a circle, making him walk around, and one guy went and shot out the back door, to let us know that they weren't playing. The guns were loaded. And he shot this gun, bang, bang, you know, and just frightened the heck out of us. Oh, we were so frightened. And this guy, I was afraid that they would hurt him. We were all afraid that they would really hurt him, you know, because they thought maybe he was being stubborn, but the guy was just not a dancer. He was not a dancer, and he was trying to explain this.

So the drummer in the band, and also the driver of that particular car, the first car, was named Joe Wynn. Joe Wynn was a man from -- I think originally he was from Philadelphia. But he had an awful lot of experience as a musician,

travelling around with bands, circus bands, minstrel bands and everything else, you know. So Joe said, "Oh, wait a minute." He said, "He can't dance. That man can't dance. Let me show him how to dance, and let me show you how to dance." He said, "He can't dance. Get back. Get out of the way." So he got there and pushed this guy aside. When he pushed the guy aside, then he got in, because he had -- as I say, this was what he had done on the minstrel shows, you know, he was just a natural, just a natural minstrel man. So he got to dancing and kidding and making jokes and singing and carrying on.
In the meantime --
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
