Reel one ran out right in the middle of that story, so you were talking about Joe Wynn, who came to the rescue of the schoolteacher. What was the schoolteacher's name?
His name was Babbins. His name was -- I'm trying to remember his first name, but his last name was Babbins. He was a nephew to Tony Babbins, who became the manager of the Imperial Orchestra.
I see. And so Joe Wynn came to his rescue.
He came to his rescue and danced and clowned and, you know, sort of got the people in the mood to forget about this other guy. So the guy in the meantime slipped out. He slipped out.
Good.

When we picked him up, my God, he must have been about five miles, better, better than five miles. He had walked down the road. And it was dark, you know, naturally, at night, and he was so afraid and so frightened. He had gotten out of the way.

So these characters made us play until they got -- you know, they just got tired of listening. And then when we finished they told us, 'Oh, now, you can put your instruments away. This was wonderful. Come on, let's have something to

eat," and they had beer and they had sandwiches, you know, and coffee, and says, "Come on now, let's have something to eat." Then they said, "We want you to come back here and play for us, we'd like to hire you. You've got a doggone good band. We want you to come back and play for us." So that the manager, who was Tony Babbins at the time, Tony Babbins says, "Well, okay." And they wanted to know how much money would we want, and he gave them a figure and made them think we was coming back. Well, we had no intentions of ever going back, not even going near that place.
Uh-uh, I should think not.
And that was China, Texas. Yes, sir, that was an experience I shall never forget.
I bet not. You say Tony Babbins was the manager --
Of the Imperial Orchestra. See this was the Imperial Orchestra.
After Hart had left, or --
After Hart's left, yes.
Was Babbins the leader then?
Yes, he was the leader, uh-huh.
I see.
He was the leader, that's right.
And so it was -- that was right before, shortly before you left for California.
Right, right.
Did you have any other experiences like that?

Well, offhand, that was the one that really stood out in my mind all these many, many years, because it was a frightening experience. I personally don't think that they would have harmed me. I never did feel afraid for myself. I was afraid for this fellow, you know. But it was such a ridiculous thing to do to a person, you know, and knowing the type of guy this particular fellow was. And I thought about it, and I just couldn't -- and I got back home, and I'm glad that my dad wasn't along at the time, because it would have been a terrible scene with him, you know, because he would have been afraid, I'm sure, that they would have hurt me or something, and he was a very mild mannered man, but he didn't tolerate any foolishness. He didn't give it and he didn't take it, and he wasn't afraid of anybody and he had -- everybody had the greatest of respect for my dad, you know. So I was very happy that he wasn't there this particular time. So I began to think to myself, I didn't say anything to my parents or anything about it, but I began to think then and there, I says, 'Well, I am not going to spend the rest of my life like this.' And you know, we had never had any trouble in Lake Charles, not every, not any of my family or any of our friends, not with that type of thing, you know, because we all got along
very well there in that little town, and --
Was that sort of thing more apt to happen in Texas?
Well, at that time I would say so, yes. At that particular --
I've heard a few other stories from musicians about Texas and guns and usually Texans who have been drinking and then make demands with their guns.

Yeah. Then of course later on this happens -- while I'm thinking about Texas -- I'm not really pro-Texas, but another thing comes to mind. My sister who -- I'm getting a little ahead of myself, too -- travelled with me one time. We were touring. This was after I recorded. And we stopped at a little place in Texas to get some gas. We were doing, oh, I guess about 10 one nighters, you know. It was in the summertime, and we were in this little town near -- en route to Corpus Christi. And we needed gas. My brother said we'd better get some gas here. So he stopped at this little filling station, you know, to get gas, and so my sister, who was much younger, she jumped out of the car and she said, 'I'll go to the restroom,' and of course this was before the segregation thing, you know. This really did exist, where you couldn't go to certain restrooms, you know. You couldn't just go to a restroom just anywhere you -- unless it was so designated. And so she jumped out of the car, and my brother told the --

the attendant said, "What do you want, boy?" Of course everybody was boy at that time, you know. My brother must have weighed well over 200 pounds, but they still called him boy. And he says, "What do you want?" And he says, "Well, I want some gas." He says, "You want some gas?" He says, "Yes, as a matter of fact I want a tank of gas, fill it up." So just as this guy got the hose to fill the car up, my sister gets out of the car then to go to the restroom, you know, and the guy says, "Hey, where you going, gal?" So my sister said, "Oh, I'm going to the restroom." He said, "Well, you can't go there. That's for white ladies only." You know.
This was what, late '40s?

Well, yes, this was in the late '40s, that's right. I'm saying I'm getting a little ahead, but just thinking of different unpleasant things that happened, you know. This was a ridiculous thing. This was about -- it had to be around '49 or '50 when this particular thing happened.

So my sister says, "Well, I've got to go to the restroom." "You can't go, because that's for whites." So I told my brother, "Well, tell him to stop putting gas in the car." He had only put about maybe two or three gallons, you know. I said, "Well, you're not out of gas." He said, "No, I'm not out, but I don't want to run out." I said, "Well, you don't need it. Let's go." So I said, "Well, pay him. Ask him how much, see how much you owe him and pay him. My brother said,

"Hold it, hold it. Halt. Halt." He says, "What do you mean?" He says, "I don't want any more gas." He said, "Well, you said you wanted --," and he said, "Well, I don't want it anymore." So he stopped there, and whatever we owed him, you know, we paid him and we went on.
Was it hard to find a place where your sister could use the bathroom?

Oh, well, the next town, wherever it was, a little larger city. You get into a larger town, you know, it was a little different. But we did find a place. As I say, some places just had two sets of restrooms, you know. They had white and colored, and you know, this was an acceptable thing at that time.
Oh, yeah, I know. I know. And for quite awhile afterward, too.

Uh-huh. And but you see in a little town like this, well they just didn't provide anything for that, so that means if you weren't, you know, a certain color, you just didn't go to the restroom, that's all, which was a terrible thing, when you stop to think of it. It was just like waiting rooms in train stations, you had the same problem, you know.
Yeah, and in bus stations.
Bus stations, yeah. You couldn't eat in certain places and all this. It was terrible, a terrible
thing.
Which brother and which sister was this?

Well, this sister died. She used to travel with me. I haven't gotten to that yet. We'll talk about that a little later too, you know, when I started travelling I took her with me. And you know, I just happened to think of this now because it happened in Texas.

Yeah, well I asked now because when I was listening to the first part of the tape you said that you were one of 15 or 16 children and I asked you the names of your brothers and sisters and I counted and we got 10 names. Now, you make 11, so there's four more. I was just trying to --
Well, some of them died you know.
I see.
I don't even remember the ones that died. But --
We got Florida, Bubba or Isaac, Jr., Joe, Charlie, James, Florence, Eugenia, Vida, Margie and Bennie.
Right.
And that was as far as we got.
Those were my mother's -- the others died, the other children died, you know.
I see.
At birth or -- I think we had one brother that I do remember, was named David. I remember his name. But the other children died before I was born. My mother's other
children.
I see. All right. So were there any other experiences of any kind out of the ordinary with travelling with the bands during that period that stand out in your memory?

Well, the one bad experience was of course living places, living quarters. You know, you had a difficult time trying to find a nice place to stay, and I don't care who you were, how big you were, how famous or popular you were, you just didn't stay in, you know, certain places. So --
This was true even after you were famous?
Well, it was of course, up until, even after 19 -- was it '54, when the segregation thing, you know, was passed, the segregation law. Well, even up until that time.

Well, of course they still had separate facilities after that, even on busses, because I remember in Texas in '56 or '57, separate waiting rooms, I was there, and a separate section of the bus. And my husband and child and I sat in the back of the bus because we were travelling with a baby and the back seat was empty and we weren't depriving anyone of a seat and it was just more comfortable for us to let the baby lie down.
But legally it wasn't right.
And we got more looks and told we
couldn't sit there.
Yeah.
Because here we were in the back of the bus when we were supposed to be in the front of the bus.
Right, right.
And everybody looked scared.
Uh-huh. Well, they were.
You know?

They were. It was a terrible thing, you know. It really -- you know, when you stop to think about it now and I guess it's a marvelous thing to have lived through this, because so many people today, the youngsters today, they only read about this. They really can't imagine what it was like. They really can't. But to be able to say that you have lived through this and had this actual experience, well it really was something. It was something.
So when you went to a town, if you knew someone or if someone had made arrangements and they knew you were coming, there'd be a place in private homes, but --
Yeah, in private homes. This is right.
Were there times when there weren't any places arranged for? What did you do?
Well, you just wouldn't sleep or maybe you'd just have to stay in the car until somebody arranged a place, you know. But there was no such thing as

going to a hotel. And a lot of the houses, if there were rooming houses, you know, maybe some rooming houses or something, if you were lucky you could get in those places. And sometimes they weren't really, you know, really kosher.
Were there ever colored hotels in the south?

There were a few. Not -- they weren't really hotels. You know, they called them hotels, but they weren't really, but they were quarters. I'd rather call them quarters, that's really what they were. Now, for instance in my little home town we had a place in Lake Charles, and this place was called Cox, Effie Cox. Mrs. Cox's place was one of the nicest places. I think Duke and the guys stayed there. Did you ever go through Louisiana with them?
No, I never went south with them.
You never went south with them.
No.

Well, they played in Lake Charles, and I think Ellington and some of the larger bands that came through there stayed at this particular place in Lake Charles. She had a terrific place, and it was an old place, but she kept it up beautifully, it was nicely furnished, she had a restaurant, she had good food and it was just a class, a really nice, class spot.
Another thing, I don't know if I mentioned the other
day, I'm thinking about this in going back to Lake Charles, I don't know if I mentioned the fact that when I was a kid that Ma Rainey came through Lake Charles.
No.
Did I talk about that?
No, you didn't. Do talk about it.
Well, this comes to my mind, too.

You know, this comes to my mind about Ma Rainey, of course the very famous old blues singer, came to Lake Charles from Texas, and with her little five piece band. She needed a pianist. Her pianist had quit in Beaumont, Texas, and so they played this little theater in Lake Charles called the Palace Theater, and whoever the leader was, I don't even remember the musicians now, wouldn't remember any of their names, but they wanted -- they needed a piano player, they had to have a piano player for her. And so they asked the proprietor of the theater, who was a Mancuso, Buster Mancuso, said, "Do you know where we can get a good piano player? We have to have a piano player. Our piano player left us in Texas and we have to have a piano player." I think they were going to play Lake Charles two or three nights or something like that. So right away Mancuso said, "Well, there's a little girl that lives down the street, the little Lutcher girl. I don't know if her parents will let her, but she plays very well. She plays well enough. She's a good little musician, a good little piano player." And he

said, "Well, I wonder do you think we could get her to help us out?" Because there really wasn't anybody else around that time who read too well, you know. And so he says, "Well, I'll ask her." So then he came down to my home, and we lived about a block and a half from this Palace Theater, on Boulevard, and so he came down and he asked my mother if they would let me -- if she would let me play, and she says, "Well, you'll have to ask her music teacher if she thinks she can play well enough." So my music teacher was Eugenia K. Reynaud, as I previously stated, and so he says call the school -- I was at school -- so he says, "Call the school and talk to --," my mother said this, said, "Call the school and talk to Mrs. Reynaud and ask her if she would, you know, if she thinks it would be all right, if she thinks Nellie can play." In other words, she didn't want me to do it if she didn't think I could. And so Mr. Mancuso called the school and talked to Mrs. Reynaud, my music teacher, and she says, "By all means yes, she can play. Yes she can play. Sure she can play for her. She certainly can play well enough to play for her." And so he said, "Well, I wonder if she could get excused, because we need her very bad. These people don't have a piano player, and I couldn't think of anybody else but Nellie, and would you let her." She said, "I will excuse her, yes, we will." So Mrs. Reynaud's husband was naturally the principal of the school.
What was the school, what was the name
of the school?
It was the Second Ward School, at that time, the Second Ward School.
And Mrs. Reynaud taught there?

Mrs. Reynaud taught there. She taught there and her husband taught there, and of course she taught music also, but she taught private music, and she had classes at school, and then she taught private. Well, I was one of her private students, you know. She had many private students. She was a marvelous musician, just wonderful. And so I played for Ma Rainey and that was one of my experiences, you know.
Oh, how marvelous.
Playing with a big name, and I don't know, many times I've even forgotten to mention this, but that's the one thing that stuck out in my mind.
How old were you?
Well, at that time, Pat, I must have been -- I must have been maybe about 12 years old, 12 or 13.
Really?
Yes, I was very, very young. That was -- you know, I was very, very young at the time. About 12 or 13.
Can you remember how you felt playing for Ma Rainey?
I don't know, for some reason I wasn't

timid, you know, I was never timid about anything like that. I was always sort of assured of myself, because I worked with my -- even at that early age I worked with my talent, you know, I developed it, and this is what you have to do, you know. If you have something, and everybody has something, and whatever you have, you know, if you love it -- I loved it. I loved my music, and as a matter of fact I still love it. But I loved it and I didn't bother about it. Other things didn't mean anything to me. It was my music that was everything. But I was thrilled, I was excited, I was so very excited to think that, you know, that I was going to play for Ma Rainey in this little orchestra. And they just were thrilled. And they even said, some of the guys, 'Oh, we wish we could take you with us.' But you know, my mother and father wouldn't have heard of that. No, that was out. So I played and they, oh, they thanked me and she did too, and she thanked Mr. Mancuso and told us, 'Be sure and thank her mother and father and thank her music teacher for letting her, because she really, --' you know.

So that was an experience, a wonderful experience for me at that time, too, because you know, I learned to accompany people, you know, which I could do, you know, and can still do today, and you know, before I even became a singer myself I could accompany people, because I worked behind the singer, you know?
Uh-huh. Was that the first time you
had accompanied a singer? Or in church maybe.
In church I had, but I mean in this particular medium, you know, I had never -- I don't think I had. No, I know I hadn't. And particularly with a very world famous blues singer like Ma Rainey.
And you did realize at that age how famous she was?

Well, I did, because see she had records out, you know. We used to have the old wind up, crank Victrola, they called them Victrolas in that time, and we had her records, you know. So we did realize that she was a very famous woman at that time. I think even moreso at that time than Bessie, in our particular area you know, neck of the woods. I don't know why, but it seems we heard more of Ma Rainey than we did of Bessie at that time, Bessie Smith.
Do you have any particular recollections about her as a person or about her approach?

No, not really. I know she was very kind, she was very kind to me, you know, and she says, 'Listen, darling --,' you know, she'd name whatever the tunes were, and they had music. They had -- not too much music. They didn't really have that much music, but I just could follow, I could follow what she was doing, you know, and I stayed behind her. But she was very nice, she was very nice to work with.
How big a band was it she had with her?
Just about five pieces. A small group.

A very small group. In fact they had four pieces because the piano player would have made the fifth person, I think. Just one horn, you know, one saxophone, one trumpet, bass, drums. Yeah, bass, drums and piano. You know. Now I'm trying to remember if they even had a bass, but I'm sure they did. They had a bass. I'm sure they had a bass at that time. But she had a five piece group, but she, you know, she really did -- she tore it up, as they say.
(Laughter)
How exciting for you, though, at that age.
Yeah.
Regardless of how accomplished you were, you obviously were accomplished, but at that age to be able to do that.

Well, I don't think I really realized at that time what it meant. That's why I say many times now when I'm talking about, you know, things that happened in my past, I somehow forget about it, and just very recently we were talking or something, and I happened to mention it. I think some friends of mine were here from South America, and they are very, very into, you know, the history of musicians, black musicians particularly, and I happened to mention the fact, because they were thinking about another woman. Oh, somebody said that Ma Rainey is still alive. I don't know if this is
true or not. And the thing came up as to whether or not she was still alive, and somebody said she was still alive. I don't know, but if she is still alive, my God, she must be over 100 years old.
I hadn't heard that she was still alive.

Well, we heard this. We heard this recently, that she was still alive. But as I say, I don't know if that's true or not. But I didn't realize really, Pat, until just this short time ago, just a few months ago, you know, just what this really meant.
Really, yes. Did you have any other encounters, or work with anybody else that was well known?

Well, I remember one time Step 'n Fetchit, who you know who he was, the old comedian, Step 'n Fetchit came through Louisiana, and he was sort of a scout, he was scouting around for talent for the studios, you know. He was quite a big man at that time. He was, you know, he was the thing. And he came through Lake Charles and they were looking for talent. And I think I had to play with that group also. I played with the little band that he had with him. They didn't have a piano, they needed a piano player or something, but anyway, I became involved with that, and they wanted me to stay with them. They wanted me to go to New Orleans with them and play a couple of other dates with them, and my folks said no way. My dad says, 'No, no, no. We can't let her. She
can't leave here." Said, "We can't let her go." So he offered me $65.00, I think, $65.00 a week or something like that. "We'll pay her $65.00 a week," he says. They wouldn't. They wouldn't let me.
Well, what kind of an act did Step have? Was it comedy? Was there music?

I think it was a revue, something like a little revue, but really what he was doing was sort of scouting around, you know, he was sort of scouting around. At this particular theater, the Palace Theater, where they used to have, as I say, shows, you know. They used to have vaudeville and different revues would come through, and this was what he was doing. He had a show with him. I can't remember now exactly, but it was a little variety show, and he of course was the star of the show, see, but he was going through Louisiana and into Texas and in through the south, and he was really sort of scouting and looking for talent also.

I just looked in Chilton here, and according to the John Chilton book, Ma Rainey died in Georgia December 22nd, 1939, which would seem like a more reasonable date than -- well, I don't know, but that's what it says here.

1939? Well, I've got to check that. Because I didn't believe she was alive. I didn't believe it, but these fellows were saying that she was alive. And I said, "Well, my God, if that woman is alive, she has to be, oh, my Lord,
she has to -- because she was --" I don't really have any idea how old she was, how old a woman she was at that time.
Well, it says that she was born April 26th, 1886, in Columbus, Georgia.
Uh-huh.
Her name was Gertrude Mælissa Nicks Pridgett, her real name.
Oh, for heaven's sakes. That's interesting.
Uh-huh. She was retired and lived out her life in Rome, Georgia.
Rome, Georgia. How about that.
She retired in 1933, it says.
Uh-huh. Well this guy, I don't know where he got his information, but he said he heard she was still alive, so I couldn't -- you know, we couldn't argue that.
Yeah.

But the point is when I mentioned the fact that I had accompanied her, he said, 'Oh, you did? You mean to tell me --,' I said, 'Yes, I did.' 'My God,' he says, 'That's wonderful. That's wonderful.' So that, of course along with the fact that I started playing in the orchestra with Bunk Johnson, well that was something else that was really of great importance to my career.
Yes. Whom do you remember that may have

The Palace Theater? Well, I'll tell you who played there. As I say, at that time you had -- you had Ida Cox. Ida Cox. I'm sure she's in your book too. Ida Cox. And I'll tell you who was with Ida Cox at the time. No, no, it wasn't Ida -- it was some sisters. The Whitman Sisters. The Whitman Sisters. The Whitman Sisters were very famous. They used to come through. You know, all these groups used to travel through. These were shows or revues, or vaudeville, whatever you called them, vaudeville, at that time. But now they would call it a revue.

The Whitman Sisters, and let me see who else used to come through Lake Charles. Well, as I told you before, the minstrel shows used to come through there. But these are people that I can remember as a child, coming through.
What do you remember about the Whitman Sisters' shows, or about Ida Cox's performance?

Well, I remember they were marvelous shows. This was old fashioned good showmanship, you know. Of course Ida was a blues singer and the Whitman Sisters were dancers. And at that time there was another very, very marvelous performer with the Whitman Sisters, and that was Peg Leg Bates. Peg Leg Bates, I remember him. I think Peg Leg is still around. And I can remember him performing and dancing with this peg leg, you know.
Uh-huh.

I remember this very well. And then later on, of course, you know, when I came out here and I got to see him and got to know him -- he didn't know me then, you know. He didn't know -- they would just come to Lake Charles and play there a couple of days and they'd be on their way, you know. But I did get a chance to see people like these people.
So you came to Los Angeles, then, in 1935, is that right?
Uh-huh, right.
And you were staying with -- was it your aunt?
My aunt. My mother's sister.
What is her name?

Lucille. Her name was Lucille Avery. And she lived just a block from Central Avenue, on the east side. And my cousin, one of my cousins, knew everybody on the avenue, because they lived in that neighborhood, they'd been living there for many years because my aunt had been out here for a number of years. And he was instrumental in introducing me to some of the folks, you know, on the avenue.
What was your cousin's name?
Irving. Irving Jordan. Irving Jordan. And Irving introduced me to the folks from -- you know, at the

Dunbar Hotel, and at the club. At that time the Club Alabam. I don't know how I got into the Club Alabam. I didn't talk about that, oh my gracious me, well that was something. The thing that was so exciting, Pat, when I first came here, was the fact that everybody, anybody who was anybody went to Central Avenue, you see. This Club Alabam was the living end. It was just something else, really. I saw people there that I, you know, had heard about, read about, you know. You couldn't say you had seen them because you didn't see them unless you saw them in the movies, because that was before television. But I had seen these different people, and to go to the Club Alabam, well just any time you'd go there there was just always going to be somebody there that was well known. There were some real famous persons.

Eddie Anderson, who later became Rochester, was working there with a partner, and this partner's name was Johnnie -- Johnnie, Johnnie, Johnnie, I can't think of it. Johnnie Taylor, his partner's name was Johnnie Taylor, and they had the most -- honestly, this was the funniest, the most comical act, together. They used to do acts with mops and brooms, you know. They'd be mopping the floor and going on, and all of a sudden they'd stop and tell jokes or something, and wisecracking at each other, you know. And Rochester, with his very funny voice, and Johnny Taylor was a very sharp guy, you know, very sharp comedian, and a marvelous dancer, which

Rochester was too. But this is the calibre of talent that was around. And my friend Lillian Randolph, who is still around today and doing very well. She has been in, oh God, so many marvelous pictures. She really went from the nightclub scene into the movies, you know, and to television, when television became -- in fact she was into radio first, because she did the Gildersleeve, and she was on Amos and Andy, and incidentally, the woman that was her sister, that was the mother on Amos and Andy, who was Amanda Randolph, was Lillian Randolph's sister. Do you remember her? Mama?
Yes, uh-huh. I didn't realize that was her sister.

Well, that was her sister. And, well, Lillian and I became very dear friends when I first came here, and they -- she and Paul Howard's wife, who was Sue Hoye (PHONETIC), and oh, so many of the guys, so many of the people that I met at that time, they were all working on Central Avenue. And of course at that time, there also -- there were other clubs too, like the Cotton Club, where Les Hite's band was playing. And then --
In Culver City.
In Culver City, that's right. And then out south you had the Bell Tavern.
That was in Gardena?
Right. I think it was in Gardena, because
you had all those little towns, but I think it was in Gardena. But, you know, you had those things.
Then on Central Avenue, my gracious me, every little place, every little bar on Central Avenue or anywhere, had entertainment, some type of entertainment. It was just marvelous.
What were the names of them? Which clubs were operating when you first came out here?

Well, as I say, I mentioned the Club Alabam, and I mentioned -- I think there was a club at that time called the Apex also that was down the street, and of course Curtis Mosby had a place, I think he had a place that later became the Apex, I think. And later on Curtis Mosby became the manager or something, or the owner of the Club Alabam.
Yeah. I know he did run an Apex and --
An Apex, yeah.
-- an Alabam, but at one point someone said the Alabam was run by a couple of Italian brothers.
Yeah, well it was, but I think this was after -- I think it was before, I mean, before Mosby's time.
Uh-huh.
I think Curtis came into the picture later, see. So --
And the Alabam was the largest club on Central Avenue, wasn't it?
Well, in that area.
In that area, yeah.
It was the most popular, I can tell you that. It was the most popular.

It was later on that I went to all the clubs, but at the time I went to them the Alabam was still open and the Alabam was the largest and the most lavish and it had floor shows along with whatever music.

Tremendous musicians. Lorenzo Flenoy (PHONETIC), he was a terrific pianist, had the band at the Club Alabam when I first came here. And some of those guys have gone on, but some of the guys are still around that worked in that band. There was --
Who else was in the band?

Well, Lorenzo was in the pianist, and Lorenzo Flenoy's been dead several years now, and then there was Buddy Harper, who's still around, and doing a good job with the prisoners, you know. He's working in that particular area.
Well, he takes bands to the prisons. Doesn't he also work with prison musicians?

Right, teaching them and whatever. He was one of the featured musicians in that band, because he played the guitar, he did arranging, and he also played the harp, you know, the mouth -- what do you call it, the Jew's harp, what do they call them, the Jew's harp? He played that.

Then there was Red Mack, who is still around, a marvelous trumpet player. And then there was Bradley -- I can't think of his first name now, isn't that funny? But anyway, he was a terrific little drummer. Oscar, Oscar Bradley was in that band.

I'm trying to think of the other musicians, and I think -- isn't that funny, I can't remember the other musicians that were in the band at the time. But anyway, they were all terrific, terrific musicians.

Then, when you would leave the Club Alabam you would to upstairs to the breakfast club. This was something. The clubs would close at 2:00 o'clock, you know. Then everybody would go to the Club Alabam -- to the breakfast club. And then that was one of the first breakfast clubs, above the Club Alabam. After the Alabam closed, you see, they would all go upstairs, and the entertainers from downstairs would go upstairs, and there was Sylvester Scott, who is still around. He's still around. He's from Texas, incidentally. He's from Beaumont, Texas, originally.

Well, Sylvester Scott would go upstairs. He would be the piano player, and he would have Lillian Randolph, you'd have Sue Hoye, Paul Howard's wife. You'd have Betty Treadwell. Well, these three people. There may have been somebody else, but I can't think right offhand. But these three people were featured, you know, entertainers. Now, they had already worked

downstairs, but they would also work this breakfast club, you know. And so Sylvester Scott played for all of them and they used to make money like it was going out of style. Now, that's another thing where the kitty came in, because nobody was making any, you know, big salary. $2.00 a night, you know, that was the extent of it. I don't think anybody was making much more than that. And they -- but they made tips, they made very good tips.
And the Alabam and breakfast club were next door to the dining room, right?
Well, a couple of doors, yes, a couple of doors away.

Then shortly after the -- when this club became so very popular, the breakfast club, so successful, that was such a successful thing. I suppose it must have been the first real breakfast club in Los Angeles, or in that area, anyway. And that's why I say people came from everywhere to come to the breakfast club. And they had delicious food. The food was out of sight. You could get a whole breakfast for about a dollar, maybe less than that.
Was there ever any additional music? I mean did anybody go in and jam with the piano player or --
Not in a place like that. Not in a place like that they didn't. They -- they didn't jam, not there, but there were other places where they used to go and
But there weren't jam sessions in the '30s? I don't know --
Well, there were sessions, but I'm just saying they didn't do it at the breakfast club, you know, at that particular club.

Now, a little later, when they did get into the jam session thing they used to go to the -- there was the Apex and there was Lovejoy's and there was another place -- of course Ivy Anderson, Ivy had a chicken place.
They didn't have music there, did they?

They didn't have music, no, no. But there was another place. I can't even -- I can't think -- isn't that funny, I can't think of the name of that place now. But this was a very popular place there. They used to have jam -- the guys would go there and jam, you know, after hours.
Then they began to open up all over town, you know.
Yes.
Everybody then got the idea of going into that, because the musicians loved to have someplace to go. When they got off from work they liked to unwind, you know.
Uh-huh.
And this was a way of unwinding.
Lovejoy's was upstairs at Vernon and
Central.
Right.
And then I guess it was a little later on that Stuff Crouch had the Backstage.
Right.
A little down Vernon, a few doors.
Right.
Down Vernon and just east of Central.
Uh-huh.
And -- well, I don't know about any other -- I'm sure there were other after hours places on the avenue.

There were other places. There was a place down at 54th and Central Avenue, and that was called -- oh, Brown's, the Brown House, or something we called it. The Browns, Mr. and Mrs. Brown ran that place. That was quite a place, and they had very good entertainment. They had a regular group that played there, and as I say, people used to jam and sing.
