So on this particular show this is what she did. So I -- my aunt said, "Well, why don't you --," and I said, "Well, Talmadge mentioned --," that's my son -- "Well, Talmadge mentioned the fact that he would like to hear me and see me on the show." Then I told her what I told him. And she says, "Well, why don't you call them and ask them. I think it would be wonderful if you could get on. If Betty can get on, you ought to be able to get on there too." I said, "But Betty has made records and I have not got a record reputation." I said, "When you have made records already, well the people have heard your records, so even if they're not hit records, you know."
Uh-huh.

They would be played. She said, "Well, people know you. You've played around here a long time." Because I'd get on a job, one job I was on -- I think I talked about that, where I was on that job for about two and a half years or so. So anyway, I did. I thought, I think I'll send a telegram. So I sent a telegram to -- what's his name? He turned out to be a big sportsman, and now I understand he's

deceased. Used to be on KFWB. Isn't that awful? I can't think of his name now. That'll come back to me too. We'll have to talk about it later. He was a big disc jockey on -- Frank Bull, that's the man.
I was wondering if that was who it was.
My Lord, how could I ever -- Frank Bull, Frank Bull. Well, Frank Bull was a big man on KFWB.
Yeah, I remember, uh-huh.
And then of course you had Gene Norman on that same station and those two guys were very tremendous, you know.
Right.

They were just out of sight. So I sent a telegram. I said, well, I think I'll do that. So I sent a telegram. I sent a telegram, and Frank Bull was so marvelous and so warm, you know, and so personable.
Right.
So he read this thing, he says, well, we've got a wire here from some gal named Nellie Lutcher. ('Lootcher) (Laughter)

He says, 'I've never heard of her, I've never heard of this gal, but I think it's mighty, mighty nice for her to, you know, to want to be on her show, and we would just love to have her come. You know, we'd love to have her come. We'll see what we can do about that.'
Oh, how wonderful.

So anyway, I called, I called him and thanked him, you know. I called and got through to him -- his secretary, I talked to his secretary, not him. So she said, "Yes, Mr. Bull would like for you to come to be on the show. He'd like for you to be there," and she told me what time, you know, because see, what happened, the way the thing was arranged, it would start like at 6:00 o'clock and we'd go from 6:00 until midnight, you see, and each jockey would have -- conduct one hour of the show, see. So they wanted me on, and naturally in the slot where Bull was, see?
Uh-huh.
And so that's the way -- it did work out. It worked out that way.
Was that a show inside or outside?
It was outside. They built an outdoor, outside platform.
I would think that they would have to, because the Hollywood High School auditorium wouldn't have been big enough.
Oh, no, no, no. It was outside. Strictly an outside thing.
Like on the athletic field or something?
I guess so. Pat, it's been so doggone long I don't remember how they did it, but it was huge, you know,
space.
Uh-huh.
It might have been just on the campus. I don't know what kind of campus.
Well, that would have been during the '40s, right?
Yeah, right.
What, early, middle '40s?
Did they have a huge campus or something there at that time?

I'm trying to remember because I was in high school then, but not at Hollywood, but I was at Hollywood High School. We used to go there for special programs. And it seems to me that the only place that there was a lot of space would be out on an athletic field.
Uh-huh.
You know, with bleachers and everything.
Yeah.
And probably that would have been where.
Yeah, well, they built this, you know, they built this platform, and it was just marvelous. They had all kinds of entertainment there.
What year was this?
This was in '47. Uh-huh, 1947. So Frank, when he introduced me he said -- and I only had a chance

to do one number, because he told me -- I went up and introduced myself to him when I got there, and he says, "Now, I don't know if you'll have a chance to do more than one song," he said, "because the program is so loaded, you know" but I was just so grateful to him, so this is a case of being in the right place at the right time.
And doing the right thing.

Right. So he said, "The program is so loaded I don't know if you'll have a chance to do more than one tune." He said, "But anyway, we'll see. You may get a chance to do it." And I didn't have -- there was nobody there to play with me, to accompany me, you know, so he says, "Can you work by yourself?" And I said, "Yes, I'll have to." So I went on and did my little number. I did, "The One I love Belongs to Somebody Else," you know. So Dave Dexter from Capitol Records was at home with his wife, and she was pregnant with their daughter, and he heard me. You know, it was broadcast.
Uh-huh.

It was broadcast. So he -- the whole six hours I think was broadcast -- so he heard the show and he contacted me in the next few days through another friend, Joe Alexander, who was also on that label. Joe Alexander was a marvelous vocalist and a bass player, but he was a better vocalist than he was a musician, really. And he was on the label. So he contacted me and told me that Mr. Dexter from

Capitol Records wanted to hear from me, wanted me to get in touch with him. Well, I didn't do it right away. I hesitated. It was two or three days. Because I had been disappointed. And I said, well, two or three days after that, I said well, I'll give Mr. Dexter a call. So when I called, well his little secretary, who was Marilyn Hammond --
Yeah.
I don't know if you remember her.
Sure, I remember Marilyn.

Marilyn Hammond who was just a darling, she was just a darling girl. And so Marilyn said, 'Oh, yes, Mr. Dexter's waiting to hear from you, Miss Lutcher.' I said, 'Well, would you give him my number and tell him to call.' And she said, 'Well, he will call you as soon as he gets in.' So sure enough, he did call me and he and I chatted and he told me he wanted me to come up, you know. He said, 'Well, I'd love for you to come up to the office here. I'd like to talk with you.' And so in the next two or three days, well, it ended up that way. I went up and had a chat with him, and it all -- you know, he asked me had I ever recorded before, which I had not. I had never recorded for any label or anything. I had made some home records, because I used to have a little Packard Bell, which was -- Packard Bell at that time used to put out a tremendous recorder. It was absolutely terrific.
Really.

Yeah. I think I have some of those old home records now, and I just made them at home, you know, just to hear how my material, stuff, would sound. You know. And I said, "No, I've never recorded for anyone." And he said he had heard something of mine. My brother Joe had taken some little things, little home records or something, you know, up there for him to hear, and he didn't particularly care for what he heard, you know, on the record, but he said, "I like you. Your brother brought some things up here and I told your brother to have you contact me," but my brother didn't tell me. I don't know if he forgot, I just don't know, but all I know is I didn't get the message, you know. And I says, "Well, I didn't know that you had told him to tell me." And he says, "Yes, I told your brother to have you get in touch with me." And he said, "I want you to make some -- I just want you to make some tests." At that time you could go to some of the studios. There were a lot of studios around, and he said, "I want you to go to the studio, Nellie, and make a few things. I just want to get an idea of what your voice sounds like on records," you know. Because everybody who maybe has a style and can sing or has a voice, you know, they don't record well. There are a lot of people who don't record well. Like Arthur Lee Simpkins was one of the finest vocalists ever, but he never really recorded. He never. The quality of his voice never came, and why I've never been able to figure that out. But he was just
a tremendous vocalist, you know.
Oh, I remember, yes. I remember hearing him many times.

A tremendous vocalist. A tremendous range, you know, because he worked with Heinz years ago, years, years, years ago. But anyway, and so I made -- I just made a few things, and things, as I say, that I had arranged and had been doing, you know. And some of these things. So he liked all the things that he heard. You understand? He liked all of the things that he heard that I had been doing, you know, just for them to test. So he said, 'We'll do these things.' And Capitol, they have these things. That's why I'm saying, you know, I feel it's unfair because they got all of these things that I had been doing long before I ever thought of making a record, you understand what I'm saying?
Right.

And these things are on records. This material is all recorded today. But they weren't things that I recorded just, you know, just for the record thing. Now, I did write some things for Capitol. I wrote, like, 'Hurry On Down,' for instance. I had been doing that in clubs. I had been doing it in nightclubs, and it was one of my big things in nightclubs, you know. I used to do it. And I used to do, oh, 'St. Louis Blues,' and some of those things, which was the old standard things, you know. There were quite a few things
that I used to do, but all of the things practically that I did on Capitol were tunes that I had been doing, you know, many years in nightclubs.
So anyway, they ended up wanting me to do these particular things, see.
What were the tunes that you did as demos for him?

Those were -- one of them was -- let's see, "Hurry On Down." I think it was, "Hurry On Down." "The Lady's in Love." "Let Me Love You Tonight," and -- and I did a thing, I wrote a thing called, "You'd Better Watch Yourself, Bub." "You'd Better Watch Yourself, Bub," I did that. It was about five things. But he just wanted to get an idea of the -- he saw that I had a -- you know, I was versatile. I could do ballads and pop things, you see.
Uh-huh.

And so he wanted to get an idea what it would sound like on records. So he was pleased with what he heard, so as I say, the next thing I knew, you know, I was in the recording studio doing records, see? And this -- this went on, but --
So did you then commercially record all these things?
Oh, yes.
Every one of them?

Yeah, all of those things are recorded. They wanted to record it, see, they wanted to record the music. But as I say, the point is it was unfair in a way for me to have-- for them to have gotten this material from me and then put me under a lousy contract or something, you see. I feel like this is -- I didn't realize it at the time, but it really was taking advantage in a sense, you see --
Yes.
-- of my creativeness. That's really the way I feel about it, and I --
But you did retain ownership of the things that you wrote, did you not?
Yes, well, of course that was through a publisher.
Because some record companies try to get rights to --
Yeah.
-- the compositions of artists, too.
Yeah, well some of the things -- as I say, I still manage to -- you know, through ASCAP I find out that I still --
Good. Good.
I still own some of the things. I own the -- I even own part of the copyrights to, 'Hurry On Down,' I own that.
Well, you should.

But my publisher, he still holds on to it, but I think in time to come that will be straightened out too. Because I'm so grateful for the help of ASCAP. As I say, ASCAP has been the greatest protector of anybody who's doing this kind of work, you know. I just can't say enough about them, you know.
Wonderful. I'm glad that -- back to the Hollywood High School program. Did you do just the one number?
Just the one number. Just the one number.
And that was what attracted David, although he did know about you from before.

Yes. Well, as I say, this was what attracted him. This caused him to, you know, want to get in -- he heard me do the thing and so when he called, when I did talk with him, he told me he heard me on the show, and he says, "I was hoping that you'd get to do more." Said, "I want to hear you do more." And I says, "Well, I was just lucky." I really was. I was very lucky to even have done that, because you know, what are you going to say with people like Betty Hutton, who was hot as a cracker at that time, a firecracker. She was so very hot at that time, and of course Bob Hope, who's endless, you know. And these -- I even think Dale and Roy Rogers were on the show, if I'm not mistaken. Well, the biggies, you know?
[Evans]
Yeah.

And here was poor little Nellie Lutcher, you know. You know, I had worked around various -- I had worked around quite a few big places all right, you know. Not big places, but popular spots, I'll say, you know.
Like one time I remember -- I remember -- I don't know if I talked about this. I think I did. When I went into the Club Royal -- did I mention that?
Well, we -- that's on the part of the tape we had to do over, and we haven't mentioned it today, so tell me about the Club Royal.

Well, the Club Royal, and this goes back to of course before recording, before I made records. I had worked -- before this I think I had worked with Dootsie Williams, who was a -- we had a little group known as the Chocolate Drops or something, the Four Chocolate Drops, and that group was Dootsie Williams, who now owns Dooto [Records], and myself, George Reed, who's still around, a fine vocalist and drummer who never really got big. He used to work with Horace Henderson also. George never really made it big, but he's a tremendously talented guy. And let's see, there were three, and then Joe Lewis, a guitar player who's gone. He's gone on now. He was not a sensational guitar player, but he was good and he was very -- he had loads of personality, you know. And he used to -- we had a beautiful little act, that was with
Dootsie Williams. So in that group we worked in -- I don't know if I -- I thought I mentioned about us coming home in the blackout. Wasn't that on that first tape?
That was on the first tape, but that was on the part we lost because of the interference noise. So no, you won't be repeating it. I have it down here to ask you about it in case you didn't get to it.
Uh-huh.
So you also mentioned that Dootsie Williams played what, trumpet?

Trumpet, yes. He played trumpet. Yeah, Dootsie Williams played trumpet, and he was a very fine -- a very fine vocal arranger. He had tremendous ideas, you know, for a four piece vocal group. And we were very, very -- you know, we were very lucky, because we worked all the time and we worked in nice spots, very nice spots.
What were some of the places where you worked?

Well, we worked with Lena. We worked with Lena Horne, when they first brought her out here. Her first nightclub engagement, I think, was at the Little Troc out on Sunset Boulevard. I worked -- well, this group was of course just an intermission group, you know. But I worked with Lena, and then prior to that, let's see, we worked at Curran's Merry-Go-Round, this was a very popular spot on Vine Street.
This very little place not any bigger than your living room here, but this bar would go around and around and around.
Whereabouts on Vine Street was it?
It used to be right down the street from -- you know where the Radio Room was, you remember that?
I remember, but I can't remember where it was. I remember seeing the sign, but I don't remember where it was at.
It must have been on the other side of -- it had to be on the other side of the -- it seems to me it was in that neighborhood with Sy Devore's, if I'm not mistaken.
Yeah. Was the Radio Room on the east side of the street?
It's on the west side.
On the west side of the street?
It was on the west side of the street.
What, in the block between Selma and Sunset?
I think so. Yeah, I think it was in there. I think so. Yeah, I'm sure it was.

That's the block where Sy Devore is. And that's the block where the club that later became Tom Brenneman's, what was it called? It started with an M. It became Tom Brenneman's and then became the Hollywood Empire.
Uh-huh.
Before that it was -- oh, I can't think of the name of it. Morocco, was that it?

I don't know. I can't remember, because the Four Spirits of Rhythm worked at this place. The place that I'm trying to think of, they worked at this club, because they were working down the street from us. See, we were at this Curran Merry-Go-Round and they were at this spot when they first brought them out here. Radio Room. Wasn't it called the Radio Room?
Yeah.
The Radio Room.
Yeah, right.
That was the name of that place, the Radio Room. I think that's what it was. But anyway --
But this was radio row.
Right.

They had all the radio studios around there. It was across the street from NBC and CBS had the theater that was -- it was called the CBS Vine Street Theater and then it became the Lux Radio Theater and now it's the Huntington Hartford Theater. But yeah, all the radio activity was --
Was in that neighborhood, right in there. So anyway, we worked -- I'm trying to think of some
other places around town where we worked. But anyway, we were together, I guess this group must have been together about a good two years, you know.
From when to when? I know that you were together in 1941, because you mentioned the Pearl Harbor experience which you were about to recount.
Oh, my Lord, yes, yes.
But when did you form the group?
Well, it must have been around '41, because Pearl Harbor was the latter part of that.
Uh-huh.

So it had to be around the early part, you know. The early part of '41, I imagine. Because we worked at Curran's and then we went to San Diego, and we worked at Curran's seemingly, and then we went back to San Diego, and then we came back to Curran's, I think, if I remember correctly. But anyway --
In San Diego you were working at what club?

We were working at the -- now, I'll have to think of that, too. But we stayed there quite awhile, and as I told you in the early conversation, I was never so glad to get home. I was never so glad to see my home as I was that night after coming home in the blackout from San Diego.
So you were there on December 7th.
Yes.
Okay. Yeah.

That's where I was. I'll never forget it as long as I live. I will never forget it. And he wanted to renew the contract, you know, because we had done very, very well there. Well, San Diego at that time was loaded with, you know, service men.
Uh-huh. And was about to have more.

Oh, yes. Oh, Lord, yes, they were just coming in like crazy. So all of the spots -- San Diego was one of the hottest places in this whole area at that time, you see. And Long Beach, even Long Beach out here was a very hot spot. But San Diego was especially a hot place, you know. So anyway, I was with that group, and well, I guess we were together, I would say, about three years. And then later we sort of -- everybody sort of spread out. And then I went to -- that's when I went to the Club Royal. I went there to work with these two brothers from New York, the Daniel Brothers, William and Douglas Daniel. They came out here with the Four Spirits of Rhythm.
And the Club Royal was in Los Angeles.

The Club Royal was on Florence and Broadway, and the owner of that club was a Leonard Castille, and these two guys came by my house one afternoon, I guess it must have been about 4:00 o'clock, and I wasn't working at the

time. I wasn't working at the time, and they said -- I think I had just closed a job. They said, "Listen, we want you to -- we'd like to get you to help us out because our piano player is ill and he's going to be out at least a couple of weeks and we want to know could you work with us a couple of weeks." And the piano player happened to have been Rose Murphy's husband. I guess it was her first husband. Pickens, his name was Pickens. I don't remember Pickens first name, but he was a tall, lanky guy and he was a marvelous piano player. And he was ill, he took ill at that time. So I said, "Oh, sure, I'll be glad to." So I went on to work, you know, in his place, and unfortunately he did not get well, you know. He died. And so the guys said to me, said, "Well, Pickens is gone. Would you like to keep the job? We'd like you to stay on with us." I says, "Well, I'll stay on with you until, you know, something else comes up." So there were just three of us working, the piano player, trumpet player, and a tipple* because Doug played tipple and trumpet and the other brother played bass violin. Wilbur played the bass violin and tipple. They both were tipple players. But they were marvelous entertainers.
So we worked at the Club Royal, and then they began to get along so badly, these two brothers.
Excuse me. I was trying to get the light turned on. Would you turn the light on, please? Thank you. Okay.
*A small ukelele-like instrument.

Yeah. They worked -- not they, I didn't mean that. We, rather, worked the Club Royal and Doug and Wilbur somehow they could not and did not get along well, and the longer the job lasted the worse they got. Brothers, two brothers. They fought like dogs. And unfortunately, one of the brothers, who was Doug, he was an epileptic, and then he began to have these seizures, you know, the epileptic seizures, and this happened a couple of times on the job and scared the heck out of everybody, me and everybody else in the joint, you know. So the proprietor of the club said to me one time, he said, "Nellie, I want to talk to you." And I says, "Okay." And so he said, "You know, these two guys are tremendous. They're just terrific entertainers," he says, "But I can't have this foolishness. They're fighting on the job, they're cursing each other out, which is terrible," he said, "And now this one is having these seizures." He'd had two or three of them. He'd just be playing his instrument sometimes and just would fall backwards, you know, which was most unfortunate, you know. And I know he disrupted the whole club, you know, with these things.
Uh-huh.

Now, what was bringing these seizures on, I don't know, but he had them. I had never seen anybody, you know, just quite that bad off with this particular thing. So he says, "I'm going to have to let these guys go, because

I can't keep them. I'm not going to keep them here." "Now," he says, "If you want to come back and bring a group, a trio, you're welcome to come. As a matter of fact I'll let you bring four pieces." Bring somebody else with me, you know. "But," he said, "I cannot keep them." So I says, "Well, I don't want to take the guys' --," you know, I didn't want to feel I was taking their job. He said, "You're not taking their job. If you don't do this, I'm going to have to get somebody else. I will get somebody else, because I have to have music in here." And the Club Royal was quite a populous place, and this guy had an awful lot of -- well, he was an athlete, and he was a sportsman, you know. A lot of sportsmen used to patronize this particular club. And he said, "If you don't I'm going to have to get somebody else, because I can't keep them. They disrupt everything. They're good, they're marvelous entertainers, you know, when they're with it. But when they're not with it, you know, I can't have it."

So I thought about it, and I thought about it to myself, and I said, "Now, I don't want to feel like I'm taking the guys' jobs, you know." And I thought about it and thought about it, and then after awhile I began -- so I talked it over with Leonard again, and he says, "I want you to know you're not taking their job. I'm going to replace the guys and I want you to come in here. I'd love to have you come. The people like you. You have a following here, and one of the reasons why they

come, they like you." Well, you know, by that time I was well into the singing bit, you see. I was into playing and singing. And so I said okay. So I took the job and I stayed on that job -- well, I guess I stayed there about two and a half years after that, almost three years.
So whom did you take in with you?

I took in -- I'm trying to remember who I took in on that job. Well, there's a guy named Tiny, Big Tiny Mitchell, who was a guitar player. A great big guy. My God, he was such a huge man. He was a very fine guitar player. And I think I had another guy named Herschel Coleman, who was -- Herschel? Yes, Herschel Coleman, was a trumpet player, he was a very fine trumpet player. And then at one time I had Shirley -- what is Shirley's name? Well, anyway, a bass player, he was a bass player. Then at one time I had Norman Bowden, who is still around. Norman Bowden is still around town. I would change, you know.
Uh-huh.

Something would happen, a guy would get sick or something, because I think Herschel Coleman passed while he was on that job. Then Norman Bowden. Then I had another little -- fine little bass player, George Mason, one of the Mason brothers. There are three brothers here, Mason Brothers, and they're all marvelous, excellent bass players, and this guy was the youngest of the brothers. Never studied music, you know.
But he is so talented. He can just hear something and just fall right in, just a natural. He's just a natural.

But anyway, I worked with George and I helped him with his instrument. I didn't have much luck teaching him to read, but I did, you know, teach him chords and everything to play, the right chords and everything, and he was very, very attentive and paid close attention to everything, you know. But at that time he had a family, and I think that was maybe one of the reasons why he just didn't get in to study, you know. Like some people do, they just don't want to sacrifice the time. But he was a natural talent.

But anyway, we did very well on that job, and then at one time Monk MacVeal, Nathaniel MacVeal, worked on that job with me, and Lee, Lee Young worked there. He didn't work too much with me. He worked two or three nights. Dexter Gordon worked on that job once or twice with me. And before I went to work there, Lorenzo Flenoy had worked there, and I think Lorenzo worked there with a little trio or something, and then he got a bigger band and went on to something else, you know. So that's why -- I think that's why the Daniel Brothers got into the scene.
But this was quite a spot. It was quite -- you know. And it was way out on -- around Florence and Broadway, you know. So anyway, I stayed there and --
That would have been what?
About '45, '46, until '45, '46. Something like that.
We didn't actually describe the San Diego job on this tape. You talked about it before. You said you worked there what, was it five or six days a week, and one day a week you'd come home.
I'd come home.
To see your son, who was living here in Los Angeles.
Yes, yes, and I had a baby sitter that would look after him, and I'd come. We did this for quite awhile.
How many days a week was the job?
Six days.
Six days?

Yeah, and we were off on Monday, so we would leave San Diego, and this was before freeways, for folks that don't know anything about doing it the hard way. We used to have to leave San Diego -- we'd have to leave home, rather, like on Mondays, for instance, and we'd go back not on Monday, but Tuesday. We'd leave here, say, about 2:00 o'clock or maybe 1:00 o'clock, and we'd get to San Diego -- it would take you about 3-1/2 hours to drive to San Diego at that time.
Right.
You had to do it the long way, you know.
And so you were telling me after Pearl Harbor you drove back and there was a blackout, a blackout being when they just pulled the plug. There were no lights.

Oh, that was the worst feeling. I shall never forget that feeling. That experience was something. That's another thing. There have been many things, several things that I've talked about that were things that I should never forget, but I can remember this just as if it happened yesterday almost, because naturally earlier in the day you heard this thing about the Pearl Harbor situation, you know, and in the meantime the proprietor of this club was trying to get the band to stay. He was trying to get us to stay in San Diego, and he offered us much more money, and nobody was interested. So Dootsie Williams said, "Well, after all we are getting -- he's offering us much --," I don't even remember now how much money we were getting, but whatever we were getting he was offering much more because he -- you know, he really knew that we had done a good thing for his business, you know.

And I said -- Milan, that man's name was Hank Milan, he was the proprietor of that club, and I can't remember the name of the club, but I remember the proprietor, Hank Milan.

And Hank tried to get us to stay. He said, "Well, if you stay down here --," he just made all kinds of propositions, trying to get us. And so I told him. I said, "Well, you guys can stay if you want to, but I'm going home. I don't want to come

back down here. And the war has broken out now," and I says -- because, you know, my son was a very little fellow, a very young child. And I said, "No, I'm going to be home. I want to be home with my child." Because my husband and I had separated, incidentally, at that time, too, and in fact I was in the process of getting my divorce from him. And I said, "No, I'm not coming back to San Diego, so get somebody else." So then Dootsie Williams -- nobody wanted to stay. They did not want to stay. So that's how we -- you know, we just gave up and came on back to Los Angeles, and as I say, I think that we went into the -- went back to the Merry-Go-Round when we got back to town, see.
Uh-huh.
And we managed to work several places. We were always busy, you know. And of course when the opportunity came for us to work at the Little Troc with Lena, well of course that was quite a thing.
Who was backing Lena at that point?

Well, she had Phil Moore. I think Phil played for her awhile, and then Eddie Beal. Eddie Beal played for her first and then Phil Moore came in and accompanied her, and of course she was -- I'm trying to remember which of the bands was there. It was Matty -- is it Matty?
Malnick?
Malnick, I think. I think Matty
Malnick.
Uh-huh.
I think, had the band there. But Lena had her own accompanist, you know.
Uh-huh.

So I think Phil Moore -- well, Eddie Beal somehow didn't work out well with her. He's a marvelous accompanist, but he didn't work well with Lena, seemingly. Then Phil Moore worked with her for awhile, but he had other commitments. But he did work with her and help her, to coach her. And then she finally got a guy named Arthur Twine, who was a very fine little pianist, and he had a lot of experience accompanying people, you know.
Uh-huh.

So then Arthur went to work with Lena, and I only worked on that job about two and a half weeks. We had a six weeks contract there, because Lena was going to be there six weeks, see, and as I said, we were an intermission group, and we were well received. It was just wonderful, and we met a lot of people, you know, important people at that time, and I would say it was one of the most important jobs that we had had. It was really, because it was in Hollywood and the other jobs were not in Hollywood, see.
Well, it was on the Sunset Strip, and the Sunset Strip at that point was a very prestigious location.
Right, absolutely. Absolutely.
The Little Troc was what, adjacent to the El Trocadero, right?
Right.
Which was the big, fancy nightclub where the movie stars went.
That's right.
And they also came into the Little Trocadero.

That's right. See Lena was the -- they brought her out here. This was before she got into the movies, you see. And the one thing I must say about her, she is -- was and still is a marvelous person as well as a tremendous performer, you know. I just -- since that time I have really come in contact, because of my position -- I have had the pleasure of meeting many people, names, big names in the business, stars so to speak, but Lena Horne was always so very warm and cordial and so very kind, you know, and this left a great impression on me. I just love Lena today for that, because at that time I wasn't known. You know, I was just a little piano player with a little group, you know.
Uh-huh.
But the fellow who owned the club at that time, Felix Young, asked Lena could -- he says -- well, like most clubs they have a room for the band boys, you know,

and of course everybody during intermission time, when they'd take their intermission, we all sat in the band room. Well, you know how the musicians are, the guys are talking and cracking and making jokes and whatever. So Felix said -- he says, "Listen, I'm going to ask Miss Horne if it'll be all right for you to sit in her dressing room. Would it be all right with you if I asked her?" And I said, "Well, I don't want to impose on her. I don't want to bother her, because she needs her privacy." He said, "No, she's not like that. Let me ask her." And he went and asked Lena Horne. He says, "Miss Horne," he says, "would you mind if the piano player, the girl with the group, would you mind if she sat in her, you know, if she didn't bother you?" She said, "By all means let her sit in here." And he said, "Well, there's no place for her. She's in there with the band." But I was the only girl, you know. I don't know how many guys were in the band. I guess about eight or ten guys, no doubt, and then there were four people -- three people including myself, in our group, you know. So he said all right. So he came back out and told me, "Miss Horne said she'd be grateful --," not grateful, I don't mean that, but she'd be very happy to have you sit in there. You're most welcome. And so I went on in, you know, but I didn't ever bother her. I'd bring a book or something with me to read, you know. And she was just as kind to me, and she said -- every time she'd get coffee or get a drink or get

something for herself, she'd say, "Bring something for Nellie. Bring something for Nellie." And I would say, "Oh, no, Miss Horne." And she'd say, "Don't call me Miss Horne. Call me Lena. Just call me Lena." But you know, I was just used to that, giving her the respect. But I just loved her. But unfortunately I took sick while I was on that job. I had a terrible problem with a tooth, and this tooth had bothered me for, oh, I bet two or three years prior to this, and my dentist told me it was a dangerous tooth. It was aching me at the time, you know, and now when I went to him my husband and I were together, and he said, "Now, I'm going to pack this tooth for you." He says, "I can't extract it, but I'm going to pack it for you. This tooth is infected. You're going to have to have this tooth taken out. But in about two or three weeks I want you to come back and I'm going to extract it." But he says, "I'll pack it temporarily for you now." He packed it and it stopped hurting and I didn't think about it. I forgot the tooth was in my head. I forgot it was there. I didn't even think about it another time. Didn't hurt me one bit.

The moment I -- well, not the moment I went on, but say after the first week I was on that job, and as I say we had a six weeks contract. We did work -- I managed to make about two and a half weeks of that. This tooth started aching me and never did stop. It started aching me like I have never, you know -- when I was a very young child, we all, naturally,
used to have toothaches, ear aches, toothaches, I knew about all those things. And this thing started aching and just would not stop.

And then it began to -- my throat began to bother me. I began to -- it began to bother me to swallow, and I said, "Oh, my God, what is this?" So finally I said to my husband, I said, "Listen, my throat is bothering me. It bothers me to swallow." So he said, "Well, you'd better go to the doctor." And I didn't want to go back to the dentist. I didn't want to go back there and I didn't dare tell my husband what the dentist had told me. I said, "No, I can't go back." So he said, "Well, you'd better go to the doctor." I said, "Well, it's my throat that's really hurting me." And I didn't want to think it was the tooth. I didn't want him to know it was the tooth.

So I called my doctor, who was Dr. Mermillion at that time. Not Dr. Mermillion, I don't mean that. What am I talking about. No, this was Dr. Hardiman. Dr. Hardiman was my dentist. So I went to Dr. Hardiman -- I called Dr. Hardiman, rather, and I told him that I had to come in and see him. He says, "Oh, is that so?" He said, "Oh, is that so?" I said, "Yes, Doctor, I've got to see you as soon as possible." So he made, you know, an appointment for me to see him, and I got in there and he looked at me. He says, "I told you to come back to me in two weeks. You waited two years." Yeah, really. He said,

"You've waited two years and I told you to come back in two weeks." And so I said, "Yes, well it didn't bother me, it didn't hurt." And he said, "But I knew it was going to hurt. I told you then it was a very serious thing, but I wasn't able to strike the tooth before because it was infected so." So he says, "Now, you're in a heck of a fix." He says, "Now, the only thing I can tell you now is you're going to have to go to the hospital." So he called the hospital, and I got to thinking about this. So my husband was waiting for me, and so he said, "You've got to go to the hospital." And I says, "Well, I'll have to go back home and see about my little boy." He said, "No, you don't have time to go back home and see about your little boy. You've got to go to the hospital right now. Right now." And he called the White Memorial Hospital. He didn't even bother about money or how I was going to pay for it or anything, because we were as poor as you know what at that time, you know, and he says, "You've got to get in the hospital."

And this thing was aching, just a constant ache, you know, my jaw aching, and this throat, my throat was just aching. Every time I swallowed it hurt. So when I got in the hospital, immediately -- the White Memorial Hospital -- immediately they started treating me, you know. And at that time the sulfur drugs, remember?
Uh-huh.
Sulfur drugs was the big thing. And I

am telling you they were just giving me handfuls of them. You know, here take these, you know, a little cup with a whole bunch of pills? Take these. And it looked like every half hour I was taking these doggone pills. This was on a Friday. I even remember the date so well.

So this must have been about -- say around about noon, or one or two o'clock or something like that. And they started treating me with this. And he said, "I want her to have a private --," the doctor who treated me, I can't even remember his name right now, the dentist, the specialist. It was a specialist that he sent me to. He said, "I want her to have a private room, she'll have to have a private room. So they got me in a private room. Not even a word about money or how it was going -- like today they want to know what insurance you have, is it going to be paid, blah, blah, blah. So anyway -- but we did pay the bill. The bill was paid, because we paid it later. And when I did -- when I -- really, when this thing came to a -- you know, came to a head, it took two days for this to happen. I'm using the expression came to a head, but that isn't what I want to say. You know, where they had to lance it, that's what I'm trying to say. They lanced it, you know, and my face had swollen. My jaw was -- oh, my face was twice as big as it is now, and they had to lance it from under my chin here, you know. And I just didn't realize that I was so -- and then later the doctor told me, "You were just as close
to death almost as you'll ever dare be." This infection had just gone all through. You know, it had just gone all through my system.

And that Sunday, after they lanced it, well it took it about three or four days for me to get back to normal after that. And -- but after I -- you know, when the infection and everything all went down, I didn't hesitate then to have it extract it. He still wasn't able to have it extract it until maybe about three or four weeks after that. So I had to go back to my dentist and the dentist extracted it, you know. But by that time all the infection had gone, see.

But that was a traumatic experience. Well, I said all that to say I was working -- I had to leave this job, this six week engagement, you know, that had started off so beautifully with Lena Horne, and this experience of meeting this lovely, gorgeous Lena Horne. I -- you know, I had to leave that engagement after two and a half weeks, and that broke my heart. I just -- oh, every time I would think about that it would just hurt me so that I would just cry about it, you know.
And you couldn't go back at the end?
Well, it was over. By the time I was able to go -- see, I wasn't able to go back to work, see? Because I had already worked two and a half weeks of the engagement, you see.
Uh-huh.
And by the time I got out of the hospital and got well from this thing, you know, because I couldn't go back to work right away.

So I never had any more trouble. Naturally I had the thing extracted and I just never had no trouble like that since. I tell everybody now -- I often -- anytime anybody talks about a toothache around me now, I say --
Hurry.
-- "For God's sakes, go to the dentist."
And I tell them. I told Lawrence Brown. I told Lawrence Brown about this, you know, because he was having a terrible thing with a -- (Sneeze interruption)

But anyway, I have told many people when I have heard them talking about a tooth, you know, to don't ignore it. I say, "For God's sakes, you don't realize just how very serious it was." So that, you know, and my recollection of this experience with this tooth, and as I say, causing me to have to give up this job at that particular time.
But later on I went on to other things, you know. That was a -- it was quite a thing, really.
I can see it. What a shame.
It was quite a thing, and to not realize the danger I was in, that was something else.
Yes. You know, you mentioned the first
time we talked about it, but I don't think we have it on this tape, about how you happened to go to work at the Dunbar, which you did immediately, almost immediately, after arriving in Los Angeles.
Yes.
You said that your cousin knew the --
The people at the --
The people at the Dunbar. Who were the people at the Dunbar?
I really don't remember, Pat.
I mean who ran it at that point?
I really don't remember.
And so you went into the Dunbar, which was what, a lounge?
A lounge, yes. It was a lounge in the Dunbar Hotel.
And that was on the ground floor.
Yes, it was on the ground floor. The lounge was on the ground floor, uh-huh, that's right.
Did it have a separate name, other than just --
Just the Dunbar Lounge, Dunbar Hotel Lounge. Incidentally, this is the lounge that you have been reading about in the paper -- the hotel, rather, that they are trying to restore.
Yeah. They've got a big grant from CBS too.
Yeah, they're trying to restore it.
Make it into a --

Museum or something, yeah. But I don't know. I personally don't think much of trying to restore it, because in the first place the community has changed, you know. It has changed tremendously, as we spoke earlier about the many wonderful things, the experiences that I had and many other people had on the Avenue, you know, in those days. I just don't know, the scene has changed tremendously now. Just as a landmark, I can see it as a landmark of course, you know.
Is it perhaps the idea is to rehabilitate the whole area, like an urban renewal sort of thing?
I don't know. I don't know, Pat. In all fairness, as far as I'm concerned, as I say, the neighborhood has changed.
Well, it's mostly boarded up now.

Yes, and you have a whole completely different set of people living in the area now, you see. The people that lived in that neighborhood have moved to the west side. They've moved all over, because now, in this day and time, you can live anywhere you want to live, and at that time of course you couldn't. So the whole neighborhood has changed, and even before -- before I left from the east side, you know, they used to -- things were beginning to happen then. I think

that was the one thing that sort of started the breakup of the breakfast clubs, because the neighborhood became -- you know, you sort of begin to have problems with theft, people breaking into cars and the underworld thing was going on. It started, you know, at that particular point. And my feeling is that it isn't any better now. If anything, it's worse, you know.
Uh-huh.

And I certainly think it's wonderful to put money into certain things, but I personally, you know, I don't see putting any money into a thing like that. I just don't. It's not any of my money, but I'm only speaking of what I feel, you know.
Yeah.

Now, many areas, there are many other areas that -- what I would like to have seen maybe would have been to even -- if you're going to do something, erect it in another section of the city and you could still carry the name, you know, of the Dunbar. Because, as I say, the Dunbar did carry a lot of old members, you know.
Yeah. Well, it was originally the Somerville, wasn't it?
I think so.
In 1927, I think --
I think it was built by the Somervilles, from what I --
And a year or so later it became the Dunbar. Do you know which was first, the Dunbar or the Clarke Hotel? Was the Dunbar first?
I don't really know, but I did know the Clarke Hotel was -- I think the Dunbar was before the Clarke. I think so. I'm not sure. Because it was in a different area, you know.
Yeah.

It was on Central Avenue, but it was farther north on Central Avenue, and at that time that section of the city -- well, that section of the city was pretty -- you know, you had some pretty nice people living in that area, and you had some businesses, nice businesses, going up in there.
The Howards mentioned something about a dance hall around the corner from the Clarke where a lot of the musicians would rehearse sometimes. They used it as a rehearsal hall.
From the Clarke Hotel?
Yeah, they said it was near the Clarke Hotel.

Well, they used to come to the Musicians -- oh, 767, our old union. That's the only place I can think of. 767 was in the neighborhood of the Clarke Hotel, I think maybe about a block and a half away or something like that, maybe a block away.
And the Clarke Hotel was at Washington and Central.
Washington, yeah, uh-huh. And I know they used to rehearse there. That was an old building. This was the old union that of course existed before they amalgamated, you know.
Uh-huh.
And all of the musicians that came to town used to come through that local, see, 767. But --
It had rehearsal facilities?

They used to rehearse, oh, yes. They used to have rehearsals and sessions, jam sessions, you know. So the amalgamation -- when the amalgamation took place I was not here. I was travelling then. I had started recording and I was travelling extensively at that time. So I didn't -- I wasn't here when that happened. But all of the many musicians -- it's so very funny, when I was travelling you know I used to meet musicians. And I still talked to musicians who came in here at that time, and of course when they came they affiliated with 767.
Uh-huh.
As their local.
You told me, I think it was off the tape, that there was -- no, you mentioned briefly on the tape that Paul Howard was somehow instrumental in getting you into
the union.

Well, he was. Oh, he certainly was. He was a dear -- he's a dear man, and thank God he's still around. Paul Howard was -- well, he was a very union minded person, you know, and of course as I say, I was here about two years before I joined the union. Well, you didn't really have to join the union. It wasn't, you know, strong. There was a union, but it wasn't a strong union at that time. And Paul Howard took it upon himself to approach certain people, and I was one of the people that he approached, and he told me, he says, "Listen, I want you to join our union." And I says, "Well, I'm going to think about it. I'm thinking about it. I'm going to think about it." Because I had never joined a union, you know. And I was working. I wasn't making much money, but I was working all the time, all the time. I was never without work. And he said, "Well, we're going to have a drive on," he said, "and we're going to make it very reasonable, so that you can get in and you don't have to pay it all at one time." And the fee was $25.00 to join.
(Laughter)

And you'd pay $5.00 down, you know, and they give you, well, forever to -- I don't say forever, I don't mean forever, but they gave you so much time to pay the $25.00 off. So anyway I joined, but he really encouraged me to join.
I think Buddy Collette told me he did the same with him.
Yes, he did it with --
He found him and talked him into it and gave him installments.
Yeah.
Yeah. It was a good way of building up the union.

Yeah, well he was instrumental in getting most people into the union, because you didn't have to belong to the union to work, you know. You know, you didn't have to belong. The little money, you'd get to thinking, "Well, my God, I'm not making but $2.00 a night."
(Laughter)
And I think when I got in the union I think the salary was like $3.00 a night. I was making $1.00 more than what I was making before.
Well, it was worthwhile, right?

But, when you stop to think of it -- and not only that, Paul Howard, bless his heart, he explained all the benefits, you see. He would tell you, "See, when you're in the union, after you've been in the union a period of time," blah, blah, blah, so many years, 30 years or so, you don't pay dues. You're a life member. You become a life member and you get this insurance and you get the benefits. He explained all

of this, you know, he explained all of this to you, and he would take the time and go on to explain to you the advantages of being in the union. He says, 'Now, when you work you have a chance of making more money.' And he says, 'Not only that, if you don't get your money the union can protect you. The union is a protective association and they will see that you get your money.' So all this sounded very good to me. It did sound (Inaudible). And he just took the time to explain all of the advantages of being a union person to me. And he said, 'And we'd love to have you. And it's prestige for you. Suppose you leave here and go to some other city.' He says, 'And you go to some other city and you say that you are a union member, because you can't go to any other city and work without being in the union, you see.' Well, naturally, down in Lake Charles we did not have a union, you know. The closest union to us, I think, was in Beaumont, Texas. And he says -- it just was so beautiful, so wonderful, and he was so sincere and dedicated to the union, he really was. He worked night and day with the union, he really did. He was just wrapped up in it. And at that time, when I got in, this was before Ed Bailey was President. I think Mr. Johnson had just left office, and they were starting over sort of a whole new administration, new people.
Well, Paul Howard was the Secretary. Florence Cadrez, who is still around and a very lovely, wonderful woman, and she was the corresponding secretary.

Paul was the financial secretary. I'm trying to think who was the Treasurer. Well, I guess Paul was both, Paul Howard, because he really, he just took good care of that money and those books like you would never believe, you know. He was both. And then later on Ed Bailey I think was the President, and he served for awhile, you know, while I was in the union. And, well, that was it.
Later on, Leo Davis, after Ed Bailey got out of office, I think Leo Davis, who's still around. Now, these people are still around. Leo Davis, I see him.
What did he play?
He was a saxophone player.
Whom did he play with?

He played with different people. There was a guy who used to be around here called Leon Herford, who I did not know. I did not know Leon Herford, but he was one of the older musicians around before my time.
Uh-huh.

Well, he worked with -- he worked with that band and he worked with different bands. He was a very fine musician, very fine saxophone player. So anyway, when he became President, of course, I don't think he didn't play anymore, you know.
Uh-huh.
And then, when the union did -- as I
say, Paul was just always the -- he was the one person there that seemed to have drawn everybody into the union, you know, and he just made you conscious of the union and the benefits, you know.
Buddy said he gave a lot of encouragement to young, up and coming musicians.

He really did. As I say, he just made it possible for us to -- for you to get in, you know. So I'm very happy that he did, because I've been a life member now for a long time. And I never dreamed that some day I would be in the position today, you know, where -- that I'm --
You're on the Board.

I'm on the Board at Local 47, and I considered that a -- when they asked me to -- I started as a trial board member, when there was an opening there. Harvey Brooks, who was a very wonderful guy. Harvey -- did you know Harvey?
Yes.

Well, Harvey Brooks was a dear friend. He was a wonderful man, a wonderful friend and a very talented man with many, many wonderful tunes to his credit. He was a great ASCAP man, also. He was one of the guys who encouraged me to get into ASCAP, you know. In fact my publisher was the first one to encourage me, but Harvey was really the guy who explained what ASCAP meant, you know, and the benefits of

belonging to ASCAP, you know. So he was just wonderful, and when he passed, that's how I inherited the trial board seat, you know. They asked me -- Marl Young, who is our secretary, the first black secretary that Local 47 has had, he asked me chi if I would serve. Then John Tran/tella, who was at that time the President of Local 47, he asked me first, and then Marle -- I said, "Well, I'll have to let you know." It was just -- it hit me just like something out of the blue, you know. I had never dreamed of nothing like that, really, you know. And then he talked to Marl, and Marl Young, who I had a lot of respect for, Marl had an awful lot to do with the amalgamation also.
I remember when that was going on.
Oh, yes. He --
Marl and Buddy both --
Marl and Buddy and those guys, they were just marvelous, you know, in getting into this amalgamation thing.

So Marle -- I said, "Well, Marl, I don't know. I've never done anything like this. I don't know if I could serve. Maybe you could think of somebody else who could serve better than I, you know." I said, "I haven't had any experience." He said, "Never mind. You're the type of person we want on this, you know, on this Board." And Tran/chitella was the first one to think about it. He said, "When he mentioned your name, well I just figured we didn't need to go any farther than that, and if
you say no," he says, "I'm going to be very angry."
(Laughter)
So I'm very thrilled today that --
So that was what year you went on the trial board?
That must have been -- because -- let's see. That's I guess about 10 years, Patty, maybe a little longer than that, but it had to be at least 10, because Harvey's been dead about that long, I think.
And you've been on the Board how long?
I've been on this Board about -- let's see, this is my second -- I think I'm on my third term now on the Board of Directors.
And a term is how many years? I don't know.
Two years.
Two years.
Two years, uh-huh.
I know it seems like a long time you've been on the Board. It seems to me. How does it seem to you?

It does. Well, when I got into it I enjoyed it really. I didn't -- you know, I just didn't know if I would, but Harvey -- I mean Marle explained to me and said, you know, what your duties were and what was expected of you, and I liked it.
What exactly do you do? I know slightly, but I probably don't know it all. What are your duties?
Well, as a trial board member or as a Board member?
Well, both, all right.

Well, the trial board, you make decisions on cases, you know. You process cases and claims. If a member has been done in, we'll say. Maybe he has a claim or somebody owes him money, whether it's a proprietor or whatever, a record company or whatever, and he hasn't been able to get this money, well, this is what the union is supposed to be. They're supposed to go to bat and get your money, see that you get your money. Well, first they have to have a hearing, you see, and they have a hearing on it, and after the hearing the decision is made. This is the responsibility of the trial board. You have to decide whether or not you think this is a just claim or this person deserves it or whether you think he shouldn't be paid, you see. Now, the Board of Directors, their operation is completely different, because you're a policy making Board, you see. You make policy. And in a way they're both very responsible positions, but the Board of Directors, you're not just doing this for one individual. You're doing it for your whole union. In other words for the whole Federation, I should say, because the Board works very closely with the Federation

of Musicians, the American Federation of Musicians.
So it's policy making, you make policies. You do the hiring, you do the firing of people, like in certain areas, certain people have to be fired, well it has to come before the Board, which is a very terrible thing to have to do, but you know, you have to go one way or the other, you know. If it's a just thing, you go for it. If you feel that somebody has not fulfilled his obligation as an employee or if you feel that -- on the other hand, if you feel like -- and another thing, the Board of Directors is also the second, just like the Supreme Court. Well, the IEB, the International Executive Board, is your -- actually the third step. But after the case is heard before the trial board, and if you're not happy with the decisions of the trial board, you then have the Board of Directors to appeal to, see. So the Board listens to your appeal. And after the Board listens to the appeal, now if you're not satisfied with what the Board says, then you still have the International Executive Board, which is marvelous when you stop to think about it. You don't just have to take the first thing that comes along. You can exhaust -- when you get to the International Executive Board, then you have exhausted everything, you see.
Uh-huh. Is that in New York or --
It's everywhere
Oh.
It's in all the unions. All unions --
The International Executive Board is physically where?
Like it's in -- well, they meet different places, you see. For instance, Max Herman, who is the President, was just elected to the Board not long ago.
He's President of Local 47.
He's President of Local 47.
He's elected to the International --

To the International Executive Board, that's right, you see. So they're from various locals. I don't even remember now how many -- I think it's six men, if I'm not mistaken, but they're from all over the country, and of course the President is a part of this, you see. But they are the Supreme Court of the Federation, in other words. They make the final decision as to what -- you know, what the outcome of a case on appeal is. They make that decision. So after that, forget it.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
