This is February 23rd, and this is Reel Number 4 of the oral history with Nellie Lutcher. The wheels are turning and today your cold seems to be gone, Nellie, because you were suffering with it the last time we talked.
Yes, I was, Pat.
We just reheard it by relistening to part of Reel 3, and I'm glad you're better today.
Thank you. I am too.

I went back and listened to the previous reels, and a few things came up I wanted to ask you more about. At one point you mentioned that one of your sisters writes and has a group, and you didn't mention what sister.

Eugenia. We call her Dina, it's a nickname for the family. She has a little group, and it started with her children, some of her children. She has six children, incidentally. Three girls and three boys. One of the boys is a marvelous percussionist, and the other -- one of the other sons is inspired to be an actor. But anyway, when they were young children, in church -- she belongs to the Lutheran Church, they started as a group with the Negro History Week Program. She was the Chairman of this program. So she did so marvelous with this and got this program together, and the theme of course

was Black History Week, and what happened, and blah, blah, blah. And she did a marvelous job of it. And so it was so successful that she kept the little group together and they went to different churches, the Lutheran churches, and performed this little program. And then finally she sort of moved on into other areas, you know, and she's been -- they've been together now, this has been I guess, say, oh, about 8 or 10 years ago. And she's kept the little group together and they dance and perform, and of course the whole thing is, as I said, based on what has happened within the different people who have made some name or some stride in the black community.
Is she here in Los Angeles?
Yes, she is, uh-huh.
I see. Is there any name she has for the group, or --
She calls it the Coreal -- let's see, Coreal Actors, I think she calls it. Coreal, it's C-o-r-e-a-l, Coreal.
And it's both spoken and musical?
Yes, it's both spoken and musical, uh-huh.
That's very interesting.
And my sister Florida, who is the designer -- I think I mentioned this earlier -- she is a marvelous designer and she does the costumes for them. So
they've done quite well.
And your sister Dina, does she write music?
She writes a little, yes, she writes a few things, uh-huh. She has written a few things, uh-huh.
I see.

So, you know, she's -- she has through the years, she's come in contact with several people that I think she helped to get started, have gone on to really make names for themselves, including the little girl who -- what is that, boogie-oogie? What is her name, Janice Johnson? I think that's her name.
Oh, yes, uh-huh.

Yes, this little girl, well she was a part of my sister's little group. They were all youngsters, and she of course was around the same age as my sister's kids at that time, you know. And when I first heard her, I knew she was a very talented girl. She wasn't even playing the bass violin. That's what she does. She plays the fender bass. And she's gone on to really great heights since that time.
She's not the same Janice Johnson that used to dance here, is she? A girl named Janice Johnson danced at the Lester Horton Dance Theater some years back.
I don't know if that's the same girl or not, but this girl is a dancer. She's a dancer.
How old is she?
She must be in her -- about 20s, mid-20s.
Janice Johnson would be older.
Would she?
The Janice Johnson I knew would be in like probably her late 30s by now.
Uh-huh. Well, I don't think this is the same girl.
We haven't talked about Joe very much, except that he was up at Capitol and talking to Dave Dexter before you were discovered. Was he up at Capitol because he was recording for Capitol then?

No. He did record with Capitol later, but at the time he was trying to get started, and of course he was the type to go around to different people doing what you have to do, you know. You've got to go knock on doors. I never was much of a door knocker, door rapper. But he went to several places, of course, and he was writing. He always did write. He was a marvelous arranger. And he was trying to get started and get something going. So at the time he went up to see Dave Dexter, he had a little -- I don't remember what it was now, but some little something that he had done. I had a little home tape recorder, and I used to do things, you know, at home. And whatever this was, he took it up to Dave Dexter and Dave heard it and he said he -- whatever the material was, he didn't

particularly like the song or whatever, but he liked the voice and he mentioned to Joe that he wanted -- he said, 'I'd like to get in touch with your sister. Maybe we can do something, you know, something else, submit some other material or something, and have her to get in touch with me.' Well, Joe, I don't know, probably he forgot about it, but he never did mention it to me, and it probably wasn't important, or he didn't think it was maybe important at the time. But later, when I was on the March of Dimes Show, I think which we discussed earlier, that's when Dexter heard me, so it all started from that.
However Joe, since that time, he's gotten -- he's gone into the religious field, that's what he's doing now. He's, oh, a Seventh Day Adventist.
Is he a minister or does he play religious music or --
Well, he plays religious music. Well, he calls himself a -- well, I don't know, I can't say that he is a minister, but he does this type of work, you know, religious work.
I remember he left jazz for religion, but I didn't know exactly what aspect of religion, religious music or what.
Yeah, he's gone into religious music definitely, uh-huh. And he is not a minister, so to speak, but I guess you could say that he's into the -- what do you
call it when these -- they go around doing things to help people, help to inspire people into the religious fold? That's what he's doing.
I see. Joe -- when did Joe come to California?
Joe came to California in the '40s.
After you did.
Early '40s.
Oh, before you did.
No, I came here in '35.
That's right, excuse me.
I came in '35. He came in the '40s.
He came in the early '40s.
Uh-huh, he came in the '40s.
And Joe is what, younger?
He's younger than I, uh-huh.
And was he playing music back in Louisiana?

When I left home he was not playing music, no, he wasn't. He wasn't playing nor was my brother Charlie. I think I mentioned him, too. Charlie was a younger brother. Joe went into music after I left home, and he was very good. He almost was self taught, really, but he studied. He did do some studying, and he had a little group at home in Lake Charles, that is, and he played with little groups around

there, and finally, when he came out to California, then he got -- did manage to get in contact with some of the people that he knew, some of the musicians that he had met, and in their travels, you know, coming through Louisiana. And he did very, very well, and then he did do some things for Capitol on his own. "Rocking Boogie," was one, and he did a thing called, "Mardi Gras," and several other things that did very well. Well, he was somewhat ahead of his time, you know, because this was -- at that time it was before Rock and Roll, it wasn't even Rock and Roll, but it was a shuffle boogie type of thing. Most of his things were in that vein, you know, and something like the Louis Jordan shuffle rhythm type of thing. And he did very well.
But later something happened, I don't know, he just decided that he wanted to -- he didn't want to do it anymore. He just went into the religious vein.

We were all brought up religiously, you know. We were all Baptists, brought up in the Baptist church, in Lake Charles. But he got a little deeper into it and he just didn't -- he didn't want to stick with his jazz. I say unfortunately because he was so good at it. He's a marvelous musician, marvelous instrumentalist and a marvelous writer.
Joe played all the saxophones, didn't he?
Yes, he did. But his main instrument was the alto.
I remember seeing him play baritone. I remember alto and baritone more than tenor, but it seemed like he played all the saxophones. Did he play other instruments besides the saxophone?
No. No.
And he also wrote.
He wrote. A marvelous writer, marvelous arranger. He could have made a living, or could still make a living today arranging if he wanted to do so, because he's just marvelous at it. But --
Does he write religious music now?
He does. Yes, he does. This is what he's involved in. He's involved in religious, and he seems to get satisfaction out of doing that, you know.
There are some people making money recording religious music.

Well, this is true. I can't say that this is true about my brother, however. I wish it was. I would like to see him, you know, do something, where he was going to make a good living at it, because he's a good guy and he is a talented man, but I think he's like some people who when they get into a religious thing they get a little -- I have to say fanatical. I call it fanatical, and this is not a

criticism at all. But I think many times with some people you have an ability, you have a talent, and I think you might look at things in a little different way, in a way that it doesn't benefit you. I think that's what a talent is all about, really. I think when God has given one ability and talent, it's given to you for your use and for you to help yourself and to be able to help your fellow man. So I just hope -- I hope that some day he will be able to -- he's tried awfully hard to get into various fields, you know, in religions. But he just doesn't want to look the other way at all, and this is really -- what I'm trying to say is this is where it is with him. This is where it is. This is where he got his -- just like me getting my -- I got my recognition in jazz, you know, and I just -- I couldn't see myself getting into anything, into another phase of music. And this is not a putdown at all. But I started out playing religious music, you know, but the religious music was sort of closely associated, in a way, the type of music that we did in the church was closely associated with it, so it was no problem.
But anyway, that's the way it goes, as I say, with some people, and my brother is -- he's living up to his conviction.
Is he still here in Los Angeles?
Yes, he is. Yes, he's very active in the Seventh Day Adventist Church.
It's been a long, long time since I've seen him.

Yeah, and he's very well liked. One time he was ill. He had a very serious illness, oh, several years ago. Joe was very, very ill at that time. We thought we would lose him, and thank God he snapped out of it. He takes care of himself. He looks wonderful.
You mentioned the other day that you weren't sure when exactly your father was born, what his birth year might have been. You said you could probably figure it out.
You know, I didn't think about it, Pat, but --
(Laughter)

But my dad, let's see. My dad died in 1961 and he was 80, he was 80 when he died. So we'll have to figure that out. Now, I haven't even had time. I didn't even think about it anymore. I should have made a note of that.
That would be 1881, then.
Uh-huh.
Okay. That gives us an idea. You mentioned that you went into the Imperial Jazz Orchestra following a piano player named Al Freeman, is that right?
Uh-huh.
And he wouldn't have been any relation to the Al Freeman, Jr. who's an actor?
I think that's his father. Al Freeman, Jr. is this Al Freeman's son.
I wondered if it might be. I mean Al Freeman is not a terribly unusual name.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. That's his son. I think I met the actor Al Freeman, his son. I think I met him one time in New York. But that is his son. Al Freeman has passed on, the dad.
That's good to know about that relationship.

When you started writing for big bands at a very early age, was there any particular arranger that you were aware of or any particular band whose arrangements appealed to you that made you want to write?

Well, I can't really say so. I think I liked the idea of writing and had a good sense of harmony and a good sense of doing this type of thing, and being around people that were doing it. These guys were writing all the time, particularly this Al Wilson, and as I mentioned, Paul Barnes. These guys were always writing and it just sort of struck me that this is something that I would enjoy doing, see. And as I say, Mary Lou Williams was of course writing at the same time, but I can't say that -- I really can't say that I was really influenced by her. However, I certainly have great respect and admiration for her, because she was one of the first women, I
think, to really make a name for herself as an arranger.

You mentioned Jeanette Kimball as another lady who worked with bands in the same area you lived in, and she was in New Orleans, but you said there were others that you couldn't think of any other names. Have you been able to think of the names of any other women who were professional musicians working with bands?

Not right in Lake Charles. Now, there was a -- dear me -- there was a girl in Baton Rouge, Louisiana that was very, very well known at the time, around that area. You know, they just didn't used to travel around very much, the women didn't, for some reason. They didn't, and of course I can understand that, because some of them were -- you know, they had families or had other careers, no doubt.
I imagine it was a little bit more difficult --
It was difficult, it really was, you know, it was awfully hard. It really was. It wasn't like it is today. It was hard, very hard.
You mentioned, when you were telling me about kitties, which was all new to me, that they actually looked like kitties, when you arrived in Los Angeles, the custom of having a kitty.
Oh, the cat, yes, for the tip?
Yeah. You said there was one man here
in L.A. who made them. Do you remember who he was?
Uh -- isn't that funny? He was a piano player. I should have made notes, Pat. I should have taken notes. Isn't that funny?

Well, if you think of it you could still let me know and we'll put it down in writing. You also mentioned that when you got here Cleo Brown was very popular in Los Angeles, and you mentioned she was from Chicago. But did she record? Was she well known for in person appearances or was she also a record artist?

Yes, she was very well known. She really made her -- got her recognition on records. In fact she was responsible for the change, you know, and for the demand for women piano players and singers. Because before that time -- and she was doing a boogie woogie thing, you know, and before that time I don't think too much attention was paid to women, you know, to women piano players and singers. Maybe that's why you didn't see too many of them with the bands, other than maybe a singer, a girl just singing. Cleo, when I first came to California, well her records were just all over. Even before I came to California, Cleo Brown was -- you know, she was well on her way. And I think when I came here, shortly after I got here, she was booked out here into one of the spots. I can't remember now even what the spot was, but she was booked in Hollywood, into one of the big spots here, and she was just

absolutely the -- just the talk of the town and the talk of the country, for that matter. And then after that time, really, then attention was focused on women. I really feel in a way that this was what sort of helped me, because at that time they were ready for -- you know, they were ready for women piano players and singers, because she sang and played, and she had her own little style, which was a tremendous style, and she had a terrific left hand, terrific boogie thing.
You mentioned, talking about the band back home, a man named Joe Wynn, and then on the tape we did over you referred to Windy Joe Wynn.
Well, they called -- that was a nickname.
That was his nickname?
Yes, Windy was a nickname.
Okay. And your husband -- second husband's last name was Lewis, but what was his first name?
His name was Leonel. They all called him Buddy. Buddy was his nickname.
And your son, you told me on the tape we did over, but we didn't repeat it, he was born at 6-1/2 months and he weighed 2-1/4 pounds.
That is right, yes, indeed. He certainly was. Well, he was a 6-1/2 months baby. And I was working with a group -- did I tell you this on the other tape, about
the group I was working with at that time?
I don't think so.
I was working at a -- I thought I said this, but anyhow, I was working at a hotel downtown called Stillwell's.
Yeah, I think you did on the other tape, but we don't have it on this tape.
Oh, we don't. Well, anyway, it was at Stillwell's Hotel, this was a popular hotel downtown. It's either on Spring -- it's Main or Spring Street.
Around 9th.
Around 9th, right.
I've seen the sign. The hotel is still there.

Right. Well, I guess it's still there. And it was an old hotel then. You know, it had been a very prominent hotel at that time. I don't say it was as prominent as the Biltmore, but I guess you would call it about a second or third rate hotel, and it had music, and I was working with a little group. Ben Borders was the drummer and leader, and then Jim Wynn, who became very well known, and who passed on about a year and a half ago, a saxophone player. And there was another -- let me see, there was a trumpet player, Cortland Mason, and myself. There were four of us working this job. And my husband at that time worked at the Carthay Circle

Theater, he was a doorman there and doing other little jobs around. So we had decided that I was going to work about two more weeks and then take off and get ready for the baby, you know. And we were both anxiously awaiting this baby. And lo and behold, one day I went shopping and my sister Florida who was living with my husband and I at that time, she hadn't been in California but about six months, but anyway, she went shopping with me and we were shopping for the baby, you know. So I was working six nights a week. I think I had had that -- yes, I had had that Sunday off, because this was on a Monday. So we went downtown and we went to about three or four stores, shopping for the baby, and my sister had a little job in the afternoon, where she worked afternoons, and I guess about 2:00 o'clock, or something like that, but she went on to her job. And then I continued to shop around, and then I journeyed back home. Well, on my way back home I began to feel pains, you know, in my stomach. Well, I wasn't even thinking about -- you know, I knew it wasn't time for the baby to come, two and a half months ahead of time. And I said, well, I guess I'd better go home. So I got on the bus -- no, was it a bus? A streetcar. We didn't even have busses then. A streetcar. Well, we lived on the east side, I think it was 29th Street. And I got on the streetcar and started back home, and I had to change. I think I changed -- did I change there? No, no. Because the way I was at the time, I just got on this streetcar and went

straight down Central Avenue. And as I got close to home, I just began to feel so terrible, and I said oh, my God, I hope I can make it home. So I got off the streetcar at my corner, you know, and walked on home, and I just barely made it. I was so happy to get home. And we lived upstairs in an apartment, and I went on upstairs and the first thing I did was sit on the side of the bed, and then I would lie down a little while, and then I'd sit up a little while, I'd lie down. Then I said well, I guess I'd better pull my clothes off. I pulled my clothes off. I just kept thinking I would feel better. Instead of feeling better I was feeling worse all the time.

So there was an old lady who lived below me. Garland, her name was Mrs. Garland, lived below me, and it so happened that she was home that day. She worked also. And she was home, and I looked out the window, out my back bedroom window, and I saw her in the yard, and so I called her and told her. I asked her if she would come upstairs a little while, so she says, "Oh, yes, I'll be up in a minute." So she took her time and she finally came upstairs. And I told her, I said, "Look, I'm not feeling good. You know, I went downtown and I think I probably walked a little too much, because I was shopping for the baby, and because I'm going to, after the next two weeks -- this is my last two weeks at work and I plan to stay home after that and I don't want to have to be shopping or anything." And she says, "Well, just lie down and rest awhile." So I'd lie
down and I'd sit up and I'd lie down and I'd sit up and I'd go to the bathroom. Oh, I carried on, you know, never thinking that this was so close to happening.

And so finally, she said, "Well, maybe I should massage you." And she got the -- what did she get? She was supposed to get something that I had there to massage with. Instead of getting what she should have gotten she got some vinegar or something and was massaging me, and it was so cold. It's a good thing it was in June. My son was born the 15th of June.

I said, "Oh, my God, it's cold, it's cold." She apologized. She said, "Well, just lie down and just don't bother," she says. "Well, maybe I shouldn't bother you," she said. "I'll just sit here." We had twin beds and she sat on the other twin bed there, and so finally every once in awhile I'd get up and she said, "Oh, my God." I said, "You know, I have a feeling that I should let you call my doctor," and she says, "Who is your doctor?" And I said, "Well, I've been attending a clinic downtown," you know, and I said, "I think you should call them and let them know," you know, "that I'm having trouble, and maybe they can recommend or tell you something to do for me." She says, "Well, I'll do that."

Well, at that time we didn't even have a telephone, really. We didn't have our own phone, but we used to use the landlord's phone. He lived in the back, in the back of this apartment house. He owned the house in the back. So she said,

"Well, I'll go downstairs and call. I'll go to my house." So she went to her house, which was right below me, and she called and told them. I gave her my clinic card, and she got the clinic card and she gave them the number and everything. So they said, "Well, we have a doctor and a nurse out now. We will have them to come by and see about her. They're not too far from there and we'll just have them to come in and look in on her." And while this lady was down making this call, my son was born. He was born.
By yourself?

Yes. He was born, and strangely enough, he was almost born in the commode, because, you know, you keep running. Well, you know, you've had a child, so you know what. This water keeps coming. And I -- you know, you feel like every minute you want to do and you don't want to do, you know. When I got back to the bed, just got back to the bed in time, and I felt this awful thing happening, you know, something just coming, and here comes my son, here comes everything, well just everything. Well, the umbilical cord was broken. And I just don't know, I can't tell you where I got the -- I don't know what you would call it, the nerve or the whatever, the knowhow, that's the word I want to say, the knowhow to carry on or to do whatever needed to be done, but it had to be God in action.
Immediately after this all happened I was free. You understand what I'm saying, I was free of him, you know. And right outside of my bedroom -- it wasn't a big room -- was we

had an old refrigerator sitting there and on the top of this refrigerator we had newspapers and things like that, so I was able to -- by me being free, by this cord being broken, I was -- I'm sure that's why he was prematurely born, because the cord was broken -- and I was able to step outside of the room and get these papers and put the -- you know, to help cover up some of the goo that was there, and then my husband's robe was around, and I just wasn't worrying about whatever, whose was what, I just wanted to try to -- and my whole thing was to try to protect this baby, and he was so still and quiet I thought he was -- I didn't even think he was alive, you know.

So I used to hear my grandmother -- then I heard somebody talking about this on the radio the other day, about spanking babies when they're, you know, newly born babies -- I used to hear my grandmother talk about spanking babies and how they used to spank them, you know, when they were first born.

So I just happened to pat him on his little buttocks, you know, and when I did it the first time he moved a little bit, and then I did it the second time and he moved. Then after awhile I spanked him, and he started a little faint cry, and the more I spanked him the more he cried. He just (Imitating crying of baby). Then I got excited. I said, 'Oh, my God, I hope they hurry up so they can save him. And sure enough, in about, oh, -- it all happened so quickly, right now I have no idea, when I'm talking about time I can't even say how many
minutes or how long or anything. I haven't any idea as to how long it took. But -- because to me it's just like it happened yesterday, I can remember it so vividly.

This lady came, that woman who had gone to make the phone call, came back upstairs, and she was taking her own time, you know. Not intentionally, but she was just an older woman and she couldn't walk too fast. And she came back and said, "Oh, Mrs. Lewis, they will be here in a little while to see about you. They're in the neighborhood and they will be by to see about it." I said, "Come quick. Come quick. The baby is here." And she says, "Oh, no. No. Oh no, it can't be." So when she came up and saw this baby lying there, and I had him covered over, you know, and I wouldn't put it all the way over his face, just enough to keep him breathing, and I spanked him a little bit so she could hear him cry, and she said, "Oh, my God. Oh, what can we do." I said, "Well, we can't do anything. Let's not do anything. We'll just have to wait till they come." And I just spanked him and kept spanking him until they came.

Finally, when they came, which I guess -- well, as I say, I have no idea how long it was. It wasn't too long, that I can tell you, because now they weren't as busy then as they would be now, you know. I don't even know if this type of thing would have even happened now. If something like this happened I would have to be rushed to the hospital immediately. I didn't

even get to the hospital, didn't get to go to the hospital. So when they came, she says, "Oh, come up." You know, we lived upstairs where you pressed the button and the button opens the door. She says, "Come in quick. Come in quick, she's had the baby." "She's had the baby?" And they ran upstairs, this doctor and this nurse ran up the steps. "Oh, my, my, she's had the baby." So they came in immediately, and when they saw the baby and he was still alive and, you know, he was a little fellow, 2-1/4 pounds. Then they got busy, and they started asking me about the pans or something. I said, "Whatever you see in there that you want to use, use it."

So what they had to do was to make an incubator, you know. They had to prepare an incubator, and this they did. They prepared this incubator and put him, you know --they cleaned him up and put him in the incubator, and in the meantime they gave me -- the doctor -- well, he was so busy working on the baby he didn't do too much to me right then, but then they gave me a shot, you know, they gave me a shot. And they worked on him and got him all straightened and put him in this pot on top -- you know, made this homemade incubator.
How was the homemade incubator made?

Well, they sat it on top of the oven. They lighted the oven, you see. See, you didn't have the -- if this had happened today, because I have a modern -- I have a real modern stove today, you know, with the oven and the broiler

underneath, this type of thing, you know. But at that time you just had a flat topped stove, see, where the burners were on one side and the oven was on the other side, see. So on the side where the oven was, well that's what -- they lighted that oven and sat this big pot there and they had blankets -- they had a big blanket and they cleaned him and did whatever they were supposed to do to him and placed him in this -- and this is the homemade incubator.

No doubt if it had been even at a time when it was cold, he probably wouldn't have made it, you know, because he probably would have been exposed to the cold weather. But it was hot. It was warm. Not exceedingly hot, but it was warm. The 15th of June, you can imagine.

So they kept him in this incubator and took him on out to the hospital, and he stayed hospitalized I guess about -- in this incubator -- about six weeks before he gained normal weight. And at that time, you know, you used to stay about two weeks before you really felt free to get out. Nowadays you can get out in the next 24 hours.
Yeah.

And I -- when I went to the hospital, after the first two weeks -- oh, and I breast fed him. I mean I, you know, kept him alive with milk, with my milk, and they told me and told my husband, well take all the milk, get all the milk she can get for the baby. So I did have an awful lot of
milk at that time and he would take the milk out there to see him.

The one thing that really broke my heart was when my husband went out to -- when he went out to see -- when he came home -- I must tell you this, this is funny. Well, we were working at this hotel, as I told you, and my husband was working at the theater downtown, would stop by the hotel sometimes at night and would ride home. Would ride home, you know, with us, see, because we didn't have a car at that time, so he would ride home with us because he had to transfer from the Carthay Circle Theater bus to the Central Avenue thing. So this night he stopped to visit and to ride home with us, and this bandleader and Jim Wynne said, "Man, what are you doing here? Don't you know you're a father? You ought to be home." He didn't even know, because you know, I didn't bother about telling him. I said, "Well, he'll be home. He'll find out when he gets home."

So they said, "Man, don't you know? What are you doing here?" And he came looking for me, and they said, "You're a daddy. You've got a son." He didn't even know. So he ran, and when he got home he ran up the steps, you know, and here I was, you know. And he says, "Why didn't you have somebody to call and tell me?" I said, "No, I didn't want to excite you because I knew you'd be home later." You know. And I says, "I was all right, you know."
Well, my sister came home I guess about, oh, about

8:00 o'clock. So when she got home she didn't know, so she came and discovered that she was an aunt. (Laughter) And I had to tell her what happened, how it happened and everything, you know. And this lady had stayed with me all that time, you know, until my sister came home. And then I think my friend Jim Wynn came to pick me up to go to work that night. Yeah, so we didn't even -- I didn't get a chance to notify anybody.

So anyway, when he came to pick me up, the doctor, they were still there. Because this must have happened about 5:30, 5:30 or 6:00 o'clock or something like that, because we used to have to be to work at 8:00 o'clock. But still, it might have been even a little later than that. I'm just guessing now about time. I'm just sort of playing with time now. But I'm remembering that Jim Wynn came and rang the doorbell. Well, he picked me up, you see. He'd pick me up at 7:30. This is a good thing for me to remember that much of it. He would pick me up at 7:30 and we only had, say about 20 minutes to go from downtown, from where I lived. So when he came to pick me up, well this Mrs. Garland answered the door, you know, opened the door, and she says, 'Oh, Mrs. Lewis? She has her baby.' She never called me Miss Lutcher, you know, because naturally Lutcher was my maiden name and my professional name. So she said, 'Oh, Mrs. Lewis has had her baby.' And he says, 'Had her
baby?" He says, "Well, she wasn't supposed to have that baby now."
(Laughter)

She said, "Well, she's had it." He said, "Oh, for heaven's sake. May I come up?" She said, "Yes," and the baby was still there. The baby was -- you know, he was still there in this incubator, and Jim Wynn came and he never got over that. He never got over seeing this baby in this home-made incubator. And he said to the doctor, because they had the kitchen door closed, he said, "May I come in, please? May I please come in?" And they said, "Yes, yes, come in for just a second." So they let him come in, and he came in and there he saw this baby. He couldn't get over that. He said, "My God, that's the smallest baby I've ever seen. I wonder is he going to live." He didn't say that to me, but he asked the doctor, "Do you think he'll live?" And they said, "Oh, yes, he'll live. He's a healthy baby. He's tiny but he is healthy." They could tell. And he never did get over that.

Then this -- let me see. Let me see, now, later I think he must have called -- he called his wife, he called Lola Wynne, who was his wife, and told her, because they didn't live too far from us at that time, so he called his wife and told Lola Wynne to -- he says, "Be sure and go by Nellie's house. Nellie's had her baby." And Lola gave a scream, "What? Had the baby?" So then later she came by.

Well, now, here I had to tell it to my sister Florida. Then I had to tell what happened to my friend Lola. Then when my husband came home, well you know I had to tell him. He just was absolutely just baffled. He didn't know what to say. "Well, I wonder why this happened," he said. "Why did it happen?" I said, "I don't know. God did it. I don't know."
What an experience. And by yourself it happened.

Yes, by myself. Yes. Well, as I say, today I'm very happy to say that my son did grow up to be very healthy, you know. He was never -- when he was younger he used to -- maybe once or twice he had little spasms or something, like most children have growing up. But he grew up to be a very healthy guy.
That's great. What year was it that Talmadge was born?
'36. The next year after I came to California.
And you mentioned on the tape that had to be re-recorded, so we don't have it on here, that you -- he was originally interested in music and he took music lessons?
Yes, he did.
He played the drums?
Well, he started on piano. I wanted so badly, I suppose like most people in music, you know. I

don't -- you know, I don't say that I would have wanted him to be a professional musician, you know. That would be up to him to choose this, and I think this is the way it should be with any child. I don't think you should just force it on him. But I was hoping that he would have been musical, you know, would have liked music enough to stick with it. And he loved it, and he still does, you know. And he could get to the piano and he would pick out little things on the piano, you know, and I was so thrilled. I said, "Well, maybe he's going to play the piano." And I had him under -- oh, at different times, two or three different teachers at different times. Wonderful teachers. Marvelous. Very good with kids and beginners, you know. But he would do all right as long as he was with them, but he would never practice. He didn't like it well enough to practice. So they all said the same thing. They all advised me to stop him until he really showed interest. So this is what I did and he never did really show interest.

Later he said to me, he said, "Mother, you know what I would like to do? I would like to study the drums." Well, Sid Catlett was a friend of mine and a very marvelous musician, and he said, "I think I would like to play the drums." I said, "Do you really?" He said, "Yes, that's what I would like. I want to be a drummer like Sid." I said, "Well, that's wonderful." So naturally I was thrilled over that. And I got a good teacher for him and got him some drums, you know, and he did very well.
He did very, very, very well. And as a matter of fact he studied for about four years at Fine Arts Conservatory.

The young fellow that was teaching him had never travelled, you know, with a big band, and he wanted to travel. I think his name was Rosenthal, Lenny Rosenthal. And he wanted to travel, you know. But he was so marvelous with my son, and my son just adored him and he adored my son, and he did just very, very, very, very well. And then he used to call and tell me, you know, when I'd come to town. I travelled quite a bit at that time, but I had a housekeeper that used to, you know, keep me informed, and I'd call home sometimes two, three times a week, talking to Talmadge, you know, to see how he was getting along. And then my sister and her husband lived right next door in one of the apartments, and they looked after the place for me and helped with Talmadge, and this housekeeper kept me aware of everything. And he was practicing. Oh, he did practice. He loved the drums.

But when Lenny decided that he no longer was going to teach, you know, he was going to give it up for awhile, and he had all of his students assigned to someone else. And my son said to me -- his first assignment with this teacher, he didn't like him. He'd made up his mind he wasn't going to like him. And so he said to me, "I don't care much for that teacher, mother." I said, "Well, listen, you're not supposed to be in love with the teacher. The teacher's there to teach you. This

is for your good. He's a good teacher and he knows what he's doing. He's experienced." But I knew what the problem was. He was an older man, you know, and he probably didn't kid around with him and play with him. He was very sincere and -- I don't mean the other guy wasn't. The other guy was very good, but he was a younger teacher, and I think that made the difference.

However, he did not ever do anything with the drums, so I talked with the teacher and I told him. I said, "Well, what do you think?" He said, "Well, I would advise you to -- let's stop him." He said, "Let's stop him and see. Maybe later on he'll go back to it. But right now he's not doing anything. He doesn't show any interest." And I said, "Well, I don't want him wasting money and time, because he's wasting my money and your time."

So then this is what we did. We just stopped him, and he never did go back to it. He never did go back to it. And of course after that he decided -- he went to -- he finished high school in North Carolina, Palmer Memorial Institute in North Carolina was a marvelous school for black children. Then he finished there and he came -- when he came out of there did he go to Palmer? Not Palmer. Pierce. Pierce Junior High. He went out to Pierce Junior High.
Junior College.
Junior College. He went to Pierce Junior College a couple of years, and then he decided he wanted
to go into the service. He volunteered to go into the Air Force, and that's what he did.

So he stayed his full time in the Air Force, four years. And when he came out of that then he went into the aircraft industry and he worked there, and later he did marry and that marriage was not a success. It lasted about 10 months. And he was still sort of lost as to what he really wanted to do. He just didn't seem to -- he first thought he was going to take up technical writing. This is something definitely, he said, "That's what I want to do. That's what I want to do." And he went into that and he didn't stick with that, and several other things. But now he's in the exploration bit, doing an exploration thing for Standard Oil. That's what he's into now, and he likes it very, very much.
Oh, wonderful.
He also now is into computing. However, he's finished a course in computing, but he hasn't gone into it yet.
Whereabouts is he living?
San Francisco. And he just married again, oh, about last May, about 8 months ago. He just married again. And I don't have any grandchildren yet, but I'm hoping.
I hope so too.
(Laughter)
When you mentioned -- we were talking
I think Scatman Crothers.
What year would that have been?
That must have been -- well, it had to be in '47, because that's when I started recording, you see, and it was just before -- oh, it was just before I went east.
And the Lincoln Theater is on Central Avenue between 22nd and 23rd?
Adams. Somewhere around there, yes. Around Adams, uh-huh. I think now -- I think it's owned by some religious group now, if I'm not mistaken. It's a church or something now.
But in the '40s, and I guess before the '40s, it was the main theater in the Central Avenue area, wasn't it?
Yes, it was. It was.
Had stage shows?

Stage shows. Marvelous stage shows. I can remember Bard u Ali , who's out here, and Pigmeat Markham. They came out here from New York, you know. Bard u's still here. And they -- he used to sort of produce the shows at the Lincoln Theater. And there was another man,

Harry Levett, who's passed on. Harry Levett used to show the -- exhibit the local talent, any local talent that he'd think had possibilities, you know. He was very good, and he also wrote for the -- I think he wrote for the Sentinel for a little while, the Sentinel, the Los Angeles Sentinel, and he probably before that wrote for the Eagle, the Los Angeles Eagle. That was a black paper also. He wrote for those papers. But he was very good at staging shows and trying to show the local talent off.
Was that some kind of an arrangement where it would be like once a week with the local talent, or was it a full week show presenting local talent?
Like once a week. I think we did it once a week. Might hve been -- might have been two days, but I know it wasn't more than that, you know. At the Lincoln Theater.
And that would be, say, once a week, and the rest of the week would be what? Out of town?
Movies or -- no, the rest of the week would be just movies, you know, most likely. But on the weekends they would have shows.
There wasn't ever a period when there was live entertainment every day?
Yes, sometimes there would be. Yes, sometimes where would be. It depended, you know, on who. Now,
as I say, I think when Bardu Ali was there I think they used to have stage shows every night. The shows would run for maybe a week or two, you know, at a time.
Do you remember who, what artists were appearing?
Well, I can't -- the only person that I can really remember offhand would be Pigmeat Markham, who, you know, made quite a name for himself. "Here comes the judge." Remember him?
Oh, yeah.

He was one of the guys that -- and then of course they had Dusty Fletcher, who's gone on. Dusty was there. And Jimmy Bas.k.ette Jimmy Bas.k.ette I think was one of the Amos and Andy characters, I think, after awhile.
I remember the name.

Yes, Jimmy Bas.k.ette. Well, all of these people were brought out here from New York, you know, and they really -- it was so marvelous, and they had dancers. I can't think, offhand, really, some of the dancers, the other people, but I can think of these comedians, because they were so funny, you know, and this marvelous sense of humor. I mean and every one of them were different and had different -- you know, different types of humor.
Uh-huh.
And it was just hilarious, really.
That was -- was that the only -- that wasn't the only theater where they had live black entertainment. The Orpheum downtown had some black performers, didn't they?

Well, they would have some black entertainment, but at one time there was another theater. This was a burlesque theater. What is it? The Burbank. I think it's the Burbank Theater downtown. The Burbank at one time had their regular burlesque show and a black revue, you know. And Cooper -- what's his name? Ralph Cooper, I remember one time was producing the black show at the Burbank Theater. Ralph Cooper was also from New York, and I think Ralph is still around also. But he was very popular and a very -- they say he was a very marvelous producer, you know, shows done there for years.
About what year would this have been when they had the shows at the Burbank?
Well, it must have been in the latter '30s, I would say, because I came here in '35. This would have to be -- it would have to be in the '30s. It would have to be around the '30s.
Do you remember any of the people who appeared there in the revues?
Well, one girl I remember was Alma Travis, and I think Lillian Randolph, who I mentioned earlier also, who was a dear friend of mine. And let me see, who else
that I can remember right now? Offhand -- Leonard Reed, of course, was -- he was also in and out of the theater at that particular group. But I can't remember any of the other names right now.
When you got to Los Angeles in 1935, who were the people that were playing music here? Who were the people that you remember that had bands and were performing?

Well, the one person I remember -- I mean there were several. Lorenzo Flenoy, for instance, was at the Club Alabam. I think I mentioned this earlier. He was at the Club Alabam and he had about a 12 or 13 piece band. Some of the guys that were with him are still around. Lorenzo's passed on since that time. He had guys like Buddy Harper and Red Mack and Bradley. I can't think --
Oscar Bradley.

Oscar Bradley. And -- funny, I can't remember the other guys, isn't it funny, offhand. It'll come to me. But then you had C. L. Burke, he was around. You had I think C. L. Burke had the band out at the place called the Bell Tavern at that time. They had shows. And of course Les Hite was out at the Cotton Club with a big band, and then that band was Peppy Prince who's still around. Peppy was the drummer for them and also doing vocalizing. A very fine vocalist and drummer. And you had -- let's see, who else was -- oh, Lloyd Reese, who's gone on. Lloyd Reese was a very marvelous

trumpeter. Lloyd's gone. Then you had George Orendorff. George Orendorff is still around, a very fine trumpet player. And -- I can't remember the other guys, offhand, but quite a few of the guys are still around, the older guys.
And those were the people who you remember best as being --

They were the musicians. And of course earlier I did mention guys like Sylvester Scott, who was at the Breakfast Club. He was the piano player for, oh, all of the people who worked at the Breakfast Club.
This was the one upstairs?
Upstairs, yeah.
Over the Alabam.

At the Club Alabam. And you had people like Ned Stanfield, who was a piano player. Ned Stanfield was around here when I first came here, and he later went back into the profession. He's a doctor, and he played around Los Angeles in some of the spots as a single, you know. And also you have people like Dudley Brooks, Eddie Beal. These people were all here when I first came here. And Fred Skinner, who's another man who was quite a big -- who was quite a big name and a very popular local talent when I first came here. He was working at the Ambassador, would you believe that. Oh, yes, Fred Skinner. And I saw Fred Skinner about seven or eight months ago, and he looks just wonderful. And he worked at the Am-
-bassador Hotel for quite awhile.
As a leader?
As -- no, he was doing a single.
Oh.
he was working as a single. And I must not leave out --
Was he a singer?
He plays and sings. Oh, yeah, he's a singer. A marvelous entertainer, marvelous entertainer. And as I say, he still -- he's still doing the same thing.
He's still entertaining?

He still entertains. He's not living right in town, but he's a good guy too, so maybe it's time to contact him, because he's seen a lot of things, because he's always -- he has always been on top of things and worked in the very finest spots, you know, available.

Another person that was here and working as a single was Harold Brown. Now, Harold Brown, he has worked in some very fine spots in Los Angeles, as a single. He's never -- I have never known him to work with anyone, but he's always worked as a single.
That's Lawrence's brother, Harold.
Lawrence Brown's brother. And to my knowledge he probably gets on a job and stays on it longer than anybody.
Yeah, 10, 15 years, right?

That's right, and he has done this through the years, you know. It's just wonderful, but he's very competent. I mean he has a very distinct style. He's a very -- he's in command all the time, with his piano, you know.
And he has quite a following, quite a loyal following.
Quite a loyal following.
Whenever I've gone to see him I know the people there seem to be regulars, people who seem as though they must come every night.
Yes.
They all know him and they --

Yes, indeed, and it's been like that through the years. Well, he was here when I first came here, and guys like -- well, Elmer Fain, who we mentioned earlier. Elmer Fain has been around Los Angeles -- he was here when I first came here, and later I think Elmer Fain might have had an orchestra at that time. I don't remember. But later, Elmer Fain became a business agent for the black union, local 767.
And now he's the business agent for 47.
Business agent at 47, uh-huh.
When I was at Paul Howard's house, his wife brought out some old newspapers and entertainment journals

and there was an article in one of them about Elmer Fajn's group. It had some name -- the Jolly Jesters or something like that. And they'd been in some kind of a dispute with a club owner who hadn't paid them or something. It was a news article.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
That was the first time I'd known that Elmer Fajn was a leader.
Yes, he was a leader, and probably that's one of the things that really encouraged him or got him to get into the bit of trying to protect the musicians, you know.
What did he play?
Saxophone. He was a saxophone player, uh-huh.
Because I've only known him since he's been a business agent with the union.
Yes. Well, I've never heard him perform, because ever since I've known him he probably -- he's been into the role of a business agent, you know. Uh-huh.
You were mentioning today, when you first arrived, about two women performers here, one a lady who worked with the Spikes Brothers Orchestra. What was her name?

Her name was Roberta Hyson. Roberta from what I understand, from what she told me, was one of the first black women to record, in Los Angeles. And there was some connection with the Reb Spikes group. Reb Spikes and
his brother were music writers or music publishers or something, and seemingly there was some connection there with them. I --
She's a singer.

She was a singer. A very -- I worked with her, but also we worked at little jobs, a long time ago, the three of us. And incidentally, Sam McDaniels worked with us. He was also very popular when I first came here. Hattie McDaniels' brother. He was a drummer and a terrific entertainer. He had a terrific following.

But there was another woman also. In fact there were two other women. One of them has gone on. Her name was Lottie Gozier. Well, Lottie was a marvelous pianist, and she and Roberta and another woman named Ruth Lee, they tell me they worked together, and I think they recorded. I think the three of them -- Roberta recorded alone, but I think the three of them made records together or something, and they were very, very popular. Now this, of course, must have been around the early '30s, the very early '30s, before I came here. But I did get to meet them, as I say. I worked with Roberta, because at that time, when I first came here, every group had a vocalist, you know. Well, I wasn't singing at that time. I would maybe do one or two songs a night, but I really did not consider myself -- I still didn't, you know, go out as a vocalist, but I did sing a few songs. But each group, little trio, or sometimes just a piano player, would have a vocalist with them.
Would you call these ladies jazz singers?

Well, I guess you would call them that. No, they weren't just jazz singers. Some of them were -- at that time it was a thing where they used to go to the tables, you know. They used to have -- the clubs were all, naturally, intimate spots, and they would go around to the various tables. Now, they'd work with a piano player and they'd go around to the tables and sing intimate songs. So I don't think this would be so much called jazz, for all of these people that I've talked about. But this is what people wanted, they wanted to hear.

Some of them -- another singer that comes to mind was Betty Treadwell. I think I mentioned Betty. She was one of the singers from the Breakfast Club, over the Club Alabam. And these singers worked, they did pop and some of them did a little dancing. Anita Brown, who was a very beautiful girl, and she was very popular, and another girl was Billie Brown, and another one was Bonnie Bryant. Well, these women were all entertainers that could sing and dance, you know, and every little spot, as I say, featured entertainment. Every spot, I don't care where you went, what section of the town you would go in, you know, even on Central Avenue. There was entertainment.
Oh, there was lots of entertainment there.
Yeah, an awful lot of entertainment. Everywhere you went you'd be entertained, you know. So I'm

very glad that I came along at that time, because I got to see these people, because most of these people are gone that I'm talking about now, and they weren't that old. Anita Brown was certainly not very old when she died. Bonnie Bryant was not that old. Billie Brown was not that old. It's amazing how they died so very young, all of these women that I'm talking about. They were very young women.
You were -- when you worked at the Club Royal, that was with Dootsie Williams, is that right?
No. No, I worked at the Club Royal with my own little group.
So you were the leader there.
I was -- I went to work there with a group, with a trio, with the Daniel Brothers.
Whose name was it billed as?
Well, it was the Daniel Brothers Trio.
The Daniel Brothers Trio and you worked for them.

And when they came and got me to work with them when Picket -- I can't think of his first name -- Pickens, Pickens was a tall, slender guy, marvelous piano player, from New York. He was Rose Murphy's first husband, and he worked with these guys, with the Daniel Brothers, at the Club Royal, and when he took sick, they came to get me to work with them. I wasn't doing anything at that particular time.
I think I had just closed a job and they wanted me to work with them until Pickens got better. So I went on to work with them.
That would have been around what year?
Well, that would have been around the '40s, early -- let's see. It was in the '40s, it had to be in the '40s, uh-huh.
Well, in San Diego when you were working, then, you were there in 1941.
Yeah, during Pearl Harbor.
That was where you worked with Dootsie Williams.
That's right.
And who was the leader of that group?
Dootsie Williams. San Diego, Dootsie Williams.
Was'it called -- was it in his name, I mean, was --
Dootsie Williams. It was Dootsie Williams and the Chocolate Drops, so I was one of the Chocolate Drops.
Okay. When you were talking about your first recording and your test records -- was that what Dave Dexter called them, that he asked you to do?
Yes.

Then you recorded them, and you said among the numbers that you did in your first recording session for Capitol was, 'Hurry On Down,' and it was because of the success of those that you later got a better -- well, a better contract for which you had royalties. Does that mean that, 'Hurry On Down,' was your first hit, was it not?
Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
It became a hit and you had no royalties out of that hit?
Well --
Or did you?
At that time, when it became a hit, you know.
That was done for a flat fee?
It was done for a flat fee, with the understanding that I would have been given a better contract, see.
But whatever that made you didn't get anything.

Well, I don't recall getting -- I don't recall at that time getting it, but when I got a manager -- I did not have a manager at that time -- Carlos Gastel, when he came on the scene he changed all of that. He changed the contract and changed, you know, saw to it that I did get it.
Did you subsequently record, 'Hurry On
Down," again, or -- like when it appeared on the LP, that was the original?
That was the original. That's the original, "Hurry On Down."
So when it appeared on the LP did you then have a contract so that you got royalties?

Well, I don't know. I'll have to look into that. Because I'm thinking that Gastel. -- I was under the assumption that Gastel did get -- change the contract, because I was told if the thing is a hit we'll tear that contract up.
Oh.

That was the understanding, see. Because when I was approached to do a session for a flat fee, well naturally the first thing I thought, well, my God, -- not that I thought the thing would be a hit or anything. I wasn't thinking about that. But frankly, I had sort of lost some of my ambition at the time, to record, because I had -- you know, I had really strived so hard at the time to try to get on, you know, a label, and of course after it happened it was all to my benefit, because had I recorded prior to that, I probably would have recorded for a smaller label that wouldn't have -- would just have got lost in the shuffle somewhere, like those things do, you know.
Uh-huh.
So fortunately, it was worth my taking a chance, and then by me --
