And what was so amazing is the fact that the records of course are released -- were, I guess they still are -- were released in New York before they were released here. And when I was

approached by Barney Josephson to go to Cafe Society, who was the big thing, you know, he was the big man and Cafe Society was the most popular spot in New York at that time -- this was 1947 -- and when he heard this record, my record, I think he was -- he was very carried away because Frank Loesser was a personal friend of Barney Josephson's, and I don't know -- he heard it at somebody's house or heard something, but he knew it was a Loesser tune, and then he liked both sides of it, and he became very interested, so he came -- he had to come out to the coast, because he was coming here to visit Frank Loesser, and when he came, well naturally the first person he contacted was Dave Dexter, because he had heard that Dave Dexter, you know, had really discovered me on records. And he -- I was working in Reno, I think, at that time. I was working at some little spot there, and just was there about maybe three or four weeks, and Dave Dexter called me one day and he said, "Nellie, you've got a hit, gal. You've got a hit record." I said, "Really?" He said, "Yes. Your 'Hurry On Down' is a hit." He says, "And Barney Josephson is here." Either he was here or he was coming. No, Barney was on his way out. He had called Dave Dexter from New York, telling him he was on his way to California, and he was going to -- he wanted to see him and talk to him about me when he got here. So Mr. Dexter was alerting me to this. And I just didn't -- it didn't hit me really, you know, what was happening. He says, "Gal, you've

got to go to New York. They want you to go to New York. Barney is coming out here to talk to me about you going to New York." I said, "Oh, really?" He said, "Yes." So anyway, I told him when I would be home, and when I came he said, well, you've got to come down and see Barney. We'll get together with him. So I met Barney Josephson, and he was very, very, very interested in my coming to New York. He said, "You've got to come to New York. You've just got to." Well, I don't know, it just didn't hit me, as I said before, it didn't hit me what had really happened, you know. It's like really working for something, you know, that had taken what looked like forever for it to happen, you know. And today, when I see these kids just seemingly something happens right away for them -- see, I had been here, working on the coast, for 12 years. 12 years, and I'm working for peanuts. And at that time I had adjusted myself to getting along with a little money and, you know, my whole thing was to try to raise my son, because my husband and I, at this time, we had been separated, we were separated and divorced, and I was just trying to raise my child, raise my son, and that was the utmost thing in my mind, and I knew that I would always be able to hold a job. And I worked as a single and I worked with groups and whatever.
So finally, when I did -- when Mr. Josephson talked to me and said, "Nellie, you've got to come to New York," I said, "Well, I'll have to let you know." And I told him about

my little boy. I said, "You know, I have a little son, and I've just, you know, I've got to be sure that my son's going to be taken care of if I go." And he said, "Well, you've got to come to New York, because your record is hot."

This record, I think we did this session in March or April, I think. I can't remember exactly now, of '47. And of course it takes it about three months, I imagine, to really hit, you know, for the impact, because it's released in the east before it's hit here.

So I thought about it and I thought about it, and in the back of my mind I thought, well, now, how in the world can I afford to go to New York. Well, the money really that Mr. Josephson was offering wasn't much, you know, and I got to thinking to myself, now, I can't go to New York and live with that little money. But Mr. Dexter was saying, "Well, I think you should go and try it and see what happens, because you'll be able to make other contacts." In the meantime, he says, "I'm going to talk to Carlos Gastel , because what you really need is a good manager. You need a good, good manager and a good agent." I didn't have either one.

And sure enough, he did talk to Carlos Gastel and GAC, and of course Carlos worked very closely with GAC, you know, because he had Nat, Peggy Lee, Mel Torme, Stan Kenton, all of these people were GAC. So anyway, he talked to Mr. Gastel and got him interested in me, and well, it just started,

it just happened that way. However, I did agree to go to New York and work for Barney Josephson for the first, you know, for eight weeks at least. So after that time, then Carlos Gastel took over as my manager, and that's when things began to happen.
I worked theaters, nightclubs, and I continued to record, you know.
And Carlos handled everything for you?
Yes, he handled all of that.
In his loud sportshirts, right?
Yes.
When I think of him I always think of him going to elegant opening nights in those loud, loud colored sports shirts.
And loafer shoes.
And loafer shoes, and no tie and no jacket. And it didn't matter what --
That was Gastel.
-- how elegant a place it was or what their code was, nobody ever dreamed of turning down Carlos Gastel.
No, that's right.
And he never dreamed of dressing like anybody else.
No, not like anybody else. But he was
a very warm, personable man, and --
I think everybody liked him.

Everybody loved him, because he loved everybody. He loved people, you know, he was just that type of person. And -- well, I really considered myself lucky to be handled by somebody like him, you know.
He took good care of his artists.

Because he would see to it that you got recognition. That's one thing you did get, you know. And he didn't go for any peanuts, you know, he didn't go for that. So I was very fortunate, and I was very grateful to Mr. Dexter, because I'm sure Carlos Gastell didn't have to have Nellie Lutcher at that time, because he had Nat Cole and all these other people that I just mentioned, so he surely didn't need Nellie Lutcher.
I want to say something now, that recently there has been an article that Mrs. Nat King Cole wrote. It was the biography of Nat King Cole. Did you read that?
No.

Well, she did. She did the -- she gave the information. Somebody else probably wrote it for her, on Nat King Cole's life story, which I think they're going to make into a film. I just heard this recently, they're going to make a film out of it.
This is a book?

Yes, it's a book. It's the autobiography of Nat King Cole, "The Autobiography of Nat King Cole," I think that's the title of the book. However, there was one item in the book that was -- that I'd like to correct right now, and this item involved me, and it was an untrue statement made by Mrs. Cole, that when she went into a certain club -- I don't know if you remember the Beaux Cards -- do you remember the little Beaux Cards Club, used to be above CBS, I think it was on Melrose, if I'm not mistaken. It was a very small room and there were two French brothers that owned this little club called the --
I remember the name, but I can't remember what the club was like.

Yeah, it was a small room upstairs, you know, and Gastel seemingly had some connections with this room, and he sort of used it as a showcase for his artists, you know, to break in. Because I had already recorded, and he booked me, got me booked into this little Beaux Cards room, and it was a small room, very small room, very intimate. And I think that was the first time I met Maria Cole. So Maria Cole, Nat introduced her to me. That was before they got married, of course. And when she wrote this -- when the book came out there was a statement stating that Carlos Gastel walked into this Beaux Cards room, and here was a woman sitting there playing the piano and singing -- let's see, singing and playing the

piano furiously. This is the statement she said, that Carlos Gastell walked over to the gentlemen who owned the club, which were two French brothers and said, "Who is the woman playing the piano?" So they told him, gave him my name. This was what she said, which was not true at all. I don't know why I should have even come into the picture, because it wasn't necessary to even mention my name. The story was Nat King Cole's autobiography, you know, so it really wasn't necessary, unless you could add or say something that, you know, really related to this. I did know Nat King Cole, as I said previously, earlier. I knew him when he first came to California. I also knew his first wife very well, and he used to rehearse with the big band at my home. That's how well I knew him, you know. And I knew him before Capitol or Carlos Gastell or anybody knew him, you know, and I just admired his work so much. At that time he wasn't doing very much singing, you know. Just like I was. He was really playing the heck out of a piano and he wasn't hardly singing. People made him sing, just like they made me sing.

But Mrs. Cole went on to state that Carlos Gastell asked how much was I being paid, and this proprietor of the club -- this is in this autobiograph -- says, "How much are you paying her?" So the proprioetor says, "We are paying her $125.00 a week." And said, Gastell went over to Mart Ruby who at that time was his assistant -- he also was a road manager.

He used to take care of Nat's people on the road, you know, particularly Nat. He travelled with Stan and some of the other people too, but particularly Nat King Cole. He handled Nat's road business, road manager. He was a very fine road manager. Incidentally, he's still around too. He's still around Los Angeles, from what I hear.
Well, Gastel , he said Gastel said to Mart Ruby, "Well, here, fire her. Pay her off and tell her to go home."
Oh.

Yes, this is in the book, and I want to state this is not true. This was not true at all. And I'm saying this because I'm not too proud to say if I was fired, and it wouldn't be the first time. I wouldn't be the first person nor the last person to ever be fired from a job, but this was definitely not true. And I was very, really, annoyed about it.
I should think so.

Because it had nothing to do with, you know, it wasn't a fact. It wasn't the truth, those statements. Had it been true -- because what I'm trying to say, after the Beaux Cards room -- this was before I went to New York City. This was before. This was in 1947, what I'm telling you, and I went on to New York City and I went on to, God knows, to the Clique in Philadelphia, and everywhere else I went, plus going to England. I went over to England. I went to Scotland, and

all the other things that I did, Carlos Gastell was responsible for this. But this was not stated in this book, and the reason why I'm saying it is because people, many people, read the book and saw it and wanted to know why. Well, this is not true. Many people who remembered me knew this was not true, see?
Did you work the Beaux Cards room?

Sure I did. That's what I'm saying. This was where I was working when Gastell came in. You know, she said he came into the room -- in other words, she spoke as if he walked into the room and just like you'd go in a room and catch me someplace. But he was responsible for me playing the room. This is what I'm saying, you know. So I can't understand why it was even necessary. It was a personal -- some little personal vendetta, that's all I can think of.
But you say you don't know her.
Yes, I know her. Yes, I know her. I met her at this particular place, this establishment, you see, because she and Nat Cole were engaged at the time, to get married. This was before they got married.
Odd that she would go out of her way to put that in print.
Well, I don't know. I still can't figure that out. Really, I can't. And as big a man as her husband was and as successful as he was and as well loved. He

was one of the better loved people in the business, you know. I would compare Nat's -- people loving him and really appreciating him to Crosby or Sinatra or any people of that calibre, you know. I held him in very high esteem as an artist, and as a person. He was a wonderful man. He was just a very beautiful person, and you know, he would not -- now, he would not have condoned anything like that. He wouldn't have said anything to really harm or hurt anyone, Nat wouldn't. He was a great artist, a great artist and a great person, and I'm very happy for his daughter today, who has made a big name for herself, you know, in a different capacity, completely different. Her type of singing isn't the type of singing that I would run around or break my neck to hear, but nevertheless, she is in the business, and she's doing, as the kids say today, she's doing her thing her way, and she has proven herself to be a real trooper and a wonderful girl, a marvelous girl.
She's got a talent, and I think whatever she does it's done tastefully.
It's tastefully, and it's her.
Uh-huh.

It's her, you know. She's not trying to do anybody else. Well, there's one time -- I have to take that back. There was one time I thought very much she sounded -- she was greatly influenced by Aretha Franklin. That was my personal opinion. I very much -- you know, I listened and

said, 'My God.' I couldn't hardly tell, really, that it wasn't Aretha, because Aretha had been so big for so long, you know, and this was all you could hear, and when Natalie Cole -- to me she reminded me very much of Aretha Franklin. I'm not saying that she -- that she was copying her. I'm not saying that, but I'm just saying the style was similar, to me. But I think she has gotten away from that, you know, now.
Yeah, she seems to have. When Nat used to rehearse his big band at your house, who was in that big band, do you remember?

I can't remember, frankly. The only person, I think, that I can remember, was his brother Eddie, who was at that time a bass player, and Eddie of course has gone on also. Eddie later got with a group, he had a group, I can't remember what they called themselves, but he had an entertaining group, something like four or five people in it. And I can't -- I can't remember anybody else in the band, I just can't, because when they used to rehearse, well they -- not only would his band be there, some of the other guys would come in and they would start, and before you knew it it was a jam session.
He was such a tremendous pianist, you know, and all the guys just loved to play with him, you know. All of them would.
Who all can you remember from the jam

sessions at your house? Who used to play there? Well, let me see. As I mentioned, Panama Francis was one of the guys. Al Morgan, who's gone on, a marvelous bass player, used to be with Calloway years ago. And Al -- not Al Wilson -- Lloyd Wilson, who was a trumpet player from Detroit, he and his wife shared a house with us, and guys like Forest Powell, a little trumpet player who's also still around, and -- oh, gosh. Well, of course Marshall Royal. Marshall, I've known him and worked with Marshall, I had the pleasure of working with Marshall too.
Where was that?

Oh, that was in the -- that must have been in the '30s, the latter '30s, the latter part of the '30s. Before I started working with -- before I started recording or anything, naturally. But I can't --
Where was it you worked?
We worked in San Pedro. We worked a little club in San Pedro. Alton Red was the leader and Marshall Royal was the saxophone player and I was the piano player. Three pieces.

But that was a marvelous, marvelous experience, working with Marshall, and in later years, you know, he went with Basie, and the same marvelous talent, he had it all the time. But it took a long time for him to really get the
recognition, but I'm glad he did get it. A marvelous musician.
Yeah, Lawrence Welk has just discovered him. Did you know that?
Isn't that something? Did you see the show that night? Wasn't that something?
And Marshall has said that Lawrence wants him to come back and do another one.

Well, honestly, it was so fantastic, I'm so glad you mentioned that, Pat, because the night he was -- I didn't know he was going to be on. I watch Lawrence Welk, Lawrence's show, every week, and my mother, incidentally -- I don't think I mentioned too much about my mother, who lived with me. Did I mention this earlier?
No.

Well, my mother, after my dad passed, my mother, we brought her out to California. She stayed with me, and she -- every Saturday night, you know, she would listen to Lawrence Welk, whether I was home or not. He was her favorite, and she would listen to him, whether or not, on Saturday night, Lawrence Welk. She just adored him, just absolutely adored him.

So I got in the habit of looking at him also, and of course I know Sam Lutz, because at one time Sam Lutz was with Gabie Lutz and Heller, and I was with them for awhile, for a short time, Gabie Lutz and Heller.
They're artists' managers.

Yes, artists' managers, that's right. And I used to watch the show with my mother, and she just loved the show. So when -- when Saturday night came, as I say, this was one of the things that she had to do. So this particular night when Marshall was on, a few weeks ago, I had been shopping, and I had just got in the house, and as soon as I got in the house I turned the television on. I do this, you know, when I get in, I turn the television on. And here was Lawrence Welk introducing Marshall Royal. And I said, 'Oh, no,' and I sat right down and listened to this, and I was so thrilled over this performance. It was just absolutely just grand, you know?
It was, yeah.

And of course I've heard Marshall. As I say, I've worked with him and I've heard him many times with Basie. Of course when he was with Basie he didn't get to really do too much, you know, because he was a section man, you know. And -- but this particular night, it was his show, it was his spot. And he played like I have never heard him play before. I was so thrilled. I had to call him. The moment the show was over I called him and I told him how marvelous he was on that show.

And incidentally, while I'm speaking of Lawrence Welk, I think that this is one of the great programs, really. Probably he never has gotten the recognition for the show, although he has made the money. I'm sure he's made more money than anybody

else, hardly, in the business, doing that type of thing, you know, and he has lasted longer than anybody else. But I think it's just marvelous to be able to sit for an hour and see this type of show. It's an awful lot of -- there's an awful lot of talent there and there's a lot of thought going into it. It's well done, very tasty, and I just think it's just beautiful, and I'm just very grateful that Lawrence has lasted through the years and will continue to last with that type of entertainment, you know, family, where the family can sit down and look at this. And unfortunately, this is not happening today. It's unfortunate.
You mentioned that Big Sid Catlett was a good friend of yours.
Yes, he was. He was a good friend of mine.
Did he ever play at your house, too?

Oh, yes, he played at my house. In fact he did one record with me, record session. He did -- I can't remember all of the things. What else did we do on that? We did, "The Song is Ended, But the Melody Lingers On." He was on that session with me. Also, Irving Ashby, the guitarist, second guitarist with Nat King Cole. He was on that particular session. So he was a very good friend of mine and a very marvelous, very marvelous drummer.
Oh, yes.
A very marvelous drummer.
I remember when he was here with Louis Armstrong, in 1949.
Uh-huh.
Which was when I first met him.

Yes, he was a marvelous drummer and he was one of the few drummers that, you know, you could sit -- he didn't care to see how much noise he could make. When I say noise, I don't mean it that way. I don't mean noise, but what I'm saying, whatever he did you could sit and listen to him and could tell what he was playing. He followed a melody. And this is sort of unusual, because most drummers have their own little pattern or their own thing that they're doing, you know. They want to see how many sticks they can use, how many brushes, and how many things they can hit on. But Sid was -- he was just like a guy playing a melodic -- an instrument, you know, that carried a melody. You could follow along what he was doing. Very fine. Very fine.
Were you aware of Charlie Mingus growing up in Los Angeles?

Yes, I worked with Charlie one time, I don't know whether it was one or two nights, when the Downbeat Club was going, and that's on Central Avenue, was on Central Avenue, and it was in the neighborhood where I lived. And I worked with him, Illinois Jacquet and his brother, Russell Jacquet, and funny, right now I can't even remember who the other

guys were in the group, but I do remember Mingus, because Charlie Mingus was the type of bass player that would dictate to the piano player what to play, what notes and what chords to play, you know. I don't know if he bugged everybody else, but he used to bug me.
(Laughter)

He had a certain idea, and I read a little something about him not long ago, and I could understand it, because I suppose he was a guy who never really got to prove himself. That's the way I feel about him. And he was a very talented, very talented musician. But he had certain ideas, and everything had to be a certain way, the way he thought it should be played, you know. Certain chords, you're used to playing something a certain way, and he worked with a player, he's going to tell the piano player. Well, that was my experience with Charlie Mingus. And the last time I saw Charlie Mingus was in New York, when I was in New York in 1973. I was doing a stint then at the -- for Barney Josephson, at the new club, the Cookery. Barney Josephson has this new club there. It isn't new now. I suppose it's been going maybe about 10 years now. But in 1973 I did two stints there, one in the spring and one in the fall of the year, and in the spring of the year, the latter part of the engagement, when I finished the engagement, rather, I was there in time for the festival.
Newport.

The Newport Jazz Festival. And at that time Mayor Lindsay had a program on Sunday. It was a, you know, program with people from different walks of life, and by the festival starting at just about that time, well I think he had several folks there from the jazz festival. He interviewed them on his show. And Charlie Mingus was there and I think -- oh, I can't think of the other trumpet player's name right now, but another very fine trumpet player was on there, and several -- well, about four or five of the other musicians were there, guys that I knew them -- I remembered them by name, but I didn't know them as well as I knew Mingus, because I knew Mingus here. I met him on the coast. And at that time I sort of noticed a little something about Mingus that sort of bothered me. He seemed to not have been in command, you know, of himself. He seemed as though he was worried about something. He seemed a little distressed about something. I don't think he was well at that time. I think his passing recently, probably he was getting into this then, you know.
Yeah, it's very, very likely.

He was still performing, you know, and of course he was highly recognized, and -- but I have a feeling that he was never able to really do the things, or prove the things that he really had in mind proving, you know.
Uh-huh. Yeah. He was here in '73. He worked the new Shelley's Manhole.
Did he?
Yeah, he worked here for about 10 days, I think.
Uh-huh, in '73.
Uh-huh.
And then I remember we took him out to a radio station, out to KBCA, for an interview, and he -- Gerald Wilson interviewed him, and he would answer in like, 'Huh? Huh?'
Yes, this is what I'm saying, yes.

But when Gerald could manage to dig something out of him, or challenge him, he would speak up and say a few things, and it was obvious that he had a lot to say, but he just couldn't bring himself to say it. So we set up another interview, and we got Buddy Collette, Brit Woodman and I think Red Callender out there, to all reminisce about --
Different --
And then Mingus got excited and he talked.
Uh-huh.
But it took a lot of --
It took this to prompt him to do so.
Yeah.
I don't know what it was, as I say. It

could be that he had, you know, he wasn't well or something, at the time, because he would -- seemingly he was in a daze at times, and sitting, just sitting there, talking to Mayor Lindsay, who was a very controversial person, you know, and very intereted. He's really very interested in jazz, you know. And I thought it was wonderful for him to devote a part of that program to the festival, you know. He was still the Mayor of New York at that time.

But I really noticed it, I noticed then, because when I came back to the coast I was telling some of the musicians, some people here, that I had seen Charlie, you know, and he and I had talked a little bit, but he didn't have too much to say, you know. He just sort of looked like he was kind of out of it, you know. He might have been worried about his health then. It might have been the beginning, you know.

Buddy Collette tells a story that Mingus used to get into his playing so much that he couldn't quit to go take a streetcar ride to a job or something, and so he would take his bass on the red car and play on the red car. And so Buddy said sometimes, he said, 'As long as Mingus was playing, I'd take out my flute or something, or one of my horns, and we'd play on the red car. Passengers seemed to enjoy it.'
(Laughter)
He was a character, there's no question
about it. He was quite a character.
You never got in on any of Mingus's streetcar concerts.

No, no, no, no. As I say, the only time I ever worked with him, really, was at the Downbeat, you know. I worked with him there. It was a couple of nights or so, and well, it was an experience that, really, I wouldn't have wanted to work with him too much, because he was a bug as far as a piano player was concerned, you know, and his conception of what should be done, what should be played chord-wise, you know, it was just altogether different from what I would have done, you know. But this is the type of a musician he was, you know, and I imagine he did this to any piano player, because I've talked to other piano players that have worked with him. He was the type of guy that would dictate to the person, you know, what to do and what to play, the piano player particularly. He didn't bother anybody else, but he was on a piano player.
(Laughter)
We were going to talk a little bit more about your involvement with the union. How did you -- you were a member of Local 767, right?
Yes, I was, uh-huh.
Did you say Paul Howard got you into it?
Yes, Paul Howard got me into the union. Well, of course, when I first came here in 1935, the union was,
you know -- there was a union. I don't even remember where it was located, but there was a union on Vernon or someplace, but it was nothing.
Someone said it started in somebody's garage.

I think so, I heard something to that effect. But it was just nothing, you know, just nothing. And Paul was very interested in building the union up. They had this old building -- they got this old building, later. They bought a building down on Central Avenue. And incidentally, Lee Young, Lee Young and his parents lived right next door to the union. They bought that house. I guess they lived there probably all that time. But the union bought this old house and made a union hall out of it. And that's the thing that got me into the union.

They had a drive on, to get people in, you know, involved in the union. At that time we had an awful lot of musicians. They were coming in here from every direction, you know. And most people, well like me, they had never belonged to a union. Well, in Lake Charles we didn't even have a union, and nobody had any intentions of setting one up, and I don't think today there's a union there. However, they are affiliated with Beaumont, Texas. I think that whatever happens in Beau -- in Lake Charles, is handled through the Beaumont, Texas union, you know.

But Paul Howard was instrumental in getting me into it, and he made it financially possible, because they had this drive where I think you paid $5.00 down and $5.00 a month or something, until you got your joining fee paid, you know.
At the time you joined what were union benefits? What would it do for you, particularly?

Well, I think, if I'm not mistaken, I think you only go -- I think it was $250.00. That was, you know, your death benefit. That's what you got out of it, $250.00. And of course the dues, I don't remember what the dues were at that time, but it wasn't very much, you know. And this is -- you know, naturally, if you were sick you got a little help from the union, but they didn't have any money to really do too much for you. But the union was important, you know, it was important to you. It helped -- it did help us to better meet our obligations, to get more money, to earn more money, you know, put you in a better earning position.
If you were a union member you had to get whatever union scale was.
Whatever the scale, surely.
Did it ever put you in the position of having to turn down work because an employer wouldn't pay union scale?
Well, that's true, yes, oh, yes. Yes. Even as little as it was then, there were some people who they

were so used to not, you know, they were so used to paying a little $2.00 a night, or whatever. That's all I was getting when I first worked, when I came here, as I told you, at the Dunbar Hotel. I was getting -- for six hours work I got $2.00 a night. But I made tips, you know, and the tips, of course, that helped an awful lot because people were good tippers, and many of the clubs, many of the better clubs didn't pay -- they didn't pay much more than that.
Did it take a while to get employers educated?

Well, yes. They got -- well, it's like anything else, this is the purpose of a union. As the union grew, the membership grew, naturally the union became strengthened and with people saying, "No, I can't afford to work for that kind of money. I can't work for that." You know, even though it hurt, because you needed, you know, you needed the money.

So, as the union -- as the membership, rather, grew, then you know, we got in a bargaining position. We got to the place where we could really make a living and a fairly decent living, according to the times, according to what you were paying, 15.00 and $20.00 a month rent. Can you imagine that? I can hardly believe that ever happened.
I remember the first apartment, when I first came here, as I told you before, I lived with my aunt, and my aunt had a five room house, a very nice five room house, on the
east side, one block from Central Avenue. She was paying, I think, $18.00 a month for that. A five room house with a nice lawn, a big house.

Then later, when I got my own apartment, or my mother's sister and I got an apartment together, her older sister, and my aunt -- that sister didn't stay here. She was going to move down to Los Angeles from Oakland, and she just didn't like here, so she left, and of course the apartment was mine, see. And I think I was paying $16.00 a month for this little one bedroom apartment.

So at that time, as I say, money -- nobody was making money, but everything was, you know, in accord with what you earned, because you could at that time take maybe -- you could take as little as $5.00 and live a week off that. Less than that, no doubt, you know.
Uh-huh. What year was it you joined the union, do you remember?
It was -- it must have been about 1937. It was -- because I've been a life member for a long time now.
That's great.

And the one nice thing, the one thing I have to say, the benefit, when the union finally -- when the unions, rather, when they amalgamated, part of the bargain was for us to maintain our -- I was going to say seniority, we'll

use that word. You know, your membership standing. Whatever time you had spent or put in, that would go with your new record, with your record, over to 47. So -- and then they also had a policy, 47 had a policy, where you'd have a $1,000.00 death benefit, so we inherited that also. We turned over all the assets from the old union, which was a building -- which was a building and maybe a couple of pianos or something like that. And this piece of property, of course, wasn't a very -- wasn't a valuable piece of property. It was in a business neighborhood, you know. But all of the assets were turned over, so all of the members became -- we were recognized as full members of 47, with the death benefit shared by the other members.
Did the negotiations take a long time? It seems like I remember a lot of fund raising and campaigning at the time of working for the amalgamation.

Well, I wasn't here at the time this happened. This was in the '50s when it happened, and I wasn't here at that time. See, I was travelling at the time, and I missed all of that, but there was an awful lot and there are a lot of people, several people that really should bet credit. Marl Young and Buddy Collette and Benny Carter and Red Callendar. And these guys were, you know, they were very, very instrumental in really getting the show on the road. And it was something that would have had to happen in later years, and that was really the time for it to happen.

Of course they had some opposition, from what they tell me. In fact I think some of the older members that are still around, they naturally did not see the advantage, you know. They were so used to going down to the old union. But the wonderful force behind the whole thing really won over, and it became a very marvelous thing for everybody. It was advantageous to everybody concerned, really; particularly to the black musicians, because they -- I don't think at the time that they were in a position to really remodel the old building or put money into it, and at that time it was just breaking, getting to the point where the black musicians were being accepted. There were some spots around town, they tell me, that really were not interested in employing black musicians. And I think just about this time, that this was all, you know, coming to pass. This was sort of behind us all, because fortunately, I always worked in the white establishments. I didn't have that problem, and I'm glad. I'm awfully glad of that. But I didn't have any problem. I worked, really I worked more in the white spots than I did in the black spots. I didn't work that many black spots.

So when -- that's why I think when finally, when the big thing did happen to me, when I did get, you know, get my break through records, well many people remembered, and I'm very grateful for that. I'm very grateful for that, because I've met many people who have told me, said, 'You know, I

remember seeing you at the Club Royal, and one time I even worked the Swanee Inn, and that was -- oh, that was long before I made records. And I worked there one time with wonderful Ivy Anderson. That's a person whose name -- I think we mentioned her earlier, when we were talking about the Chicken Shack.
Uh-huh.

But I remember Ivy, and I just adored her. She was a wonderful, wonderful woman, and a marvelous artist. I knew her and we worked the Swanee Inn -- that's the place where Nat worked, Nat King Cole first organized the King Cole Trio.
And that place still exists on Vernon Avenue.
Yes, it does.
I don't think it has music anymore, though. It's just a restaurant.

I don't think so. But that's the place -- at that time -- it shows you how everything has changed -- at that time, they had not one entertainer, but they had continuous entertainment. Because I remember the time I worked there. I worked, accompanying myself, and then Ivy worked there, and then one time Margaret Bonds and Calvin Jackson -- that's somebody -- Calvin Jackson and Margaret Bonds came out here when I first met them. Margaret who, bless her heart, is gone on today, but she was a very marvelous musician,
very marvelous. Did you know her?
No, I didn't.

Well, she was a marvelous pianist. She was sort of -- really, she wasn't what you'd call a jazz pianist, you know. She was more or less a classical. Because I understand Margaret had a tremendous classical background. I think her mother was a teacher, music teacher, in Chicago. And from people that knew her, and I also got to know her husband later, and her husband was telling me, and other people have told me, that she had a marvelous-- but anyway, she and Calvin Jackson were featured at the Swanee Inn.
What, dual piano?
Yeah, dual, uh-huh. Double piano. And it was just out of sight, really. But this was the type of thing that used to happen in Los Angeles.

So this is -- I haven't been in the Swanee, and the last time I was there, oh, I guess it's been about -- maybe about four years or better, maybe four or five years ago. Someone was working there then. I can't remember who. I think -- I think Duke Burrell -- do you know Duke Burrell, the piano player?
No, I don't.
Duke Burrell was working there at that particular time, but I --
Well, I go by there from time to time, and they have dinners and cocktails out there, but no sign of
any entertainment.
Yeah.
According to the sign.

That's unfortunate, because it -- it's a smart room, too. It's a very smart room, you know. You know, that comes to mind too, another room that I worked that I loved, and it was a room called Shep's --
Playhouse.
No, it was called Kelly's. Shep Kelly, this was a place down in Chinatown, Shep Kelly. Was it Shep's? No, that was Shep's Playhouse.
I've heard that Shep's Playhouse was down in --
In Chinatown.

Well, the way it was told to me, because I was never there, was that it was in a section that became known as Bronzeville during World War II, when all the Japanese -- it was in the Japanese section of downtown, when all the Japanese people were put in the --
In the concentration camps.

Yeah. And so then the area was empty, and so part of the neighborhood became black and became referred to as Bronzeville, and it was during that period that Shep's Playhouse opened and had jazz, was the way it was told to me. Is that right?

Bronzeville, yeah. I can't remember. It wasn't -- Bronzeville wasn't the real popular name for it. They called it another section, a section I can't think of. I can't even remember what they called it at the time. However, there were many breakfast clubs up in there at the time, and Shep's Playhouse of course was a regular nightclub, and a fantastic, beautiful place. A beautiful nightclub. And let me see, Roy Milton worked -- he worked in that area. He worked at a club there. And I think at that time Camille Howard, of course, was with Roy Milton at the time. And Lou Jones -- I used to work with Lou Jones, who's a marvelous saxophone player. He's not playing so much now. He's a barber. But he at that time had a little group, used to have little groups at one of these clubs down in that area, you know.
But that whole area was really --
Well, what was Kelly's?
-- all black. Huh?
What was Kelly's? Was that there? You just mentioned the name.

No. The Kelly's that I mentioned, when I said Shep Kelly, but this was the man's name. This man's name was Shep Kelly that I was thinking about. He used to have a little place on Ivar, right across the street from the Knickerbocker Hotel, and the place was called Kelly's. The man's name was Shep Kelly, but everybody called it -- well, I went to

work there, and I guess I worked there for about a year, and I met an awful lot of people, and some of the stars used to come in that place, you know, and I enjoyed it. I just loved it. I was doing a single there, you know.
What year was that?

That must have been around -- it was around maybe about '39 or something like that, '39. About '39, I'll say. And I'm trying to think of another spot that I worked. Another spot that I worked was a club called -- this was in the '40s. I'm trying to think of places where I lived. That's how I get my thoughts come to me. I worked at a club that was known as the Valli, the Club Valli, also. This was a club that served curried foods. It was right at the corner of -- is it Holloway? Holloway Drive, where Holloway Drive comes up, you know?
From Sunset Strip?
Yeah.
Yeah, uh-huh.
It was at the top of that. I think at one time Mickey Cohen had a little haberdashery there at this place.
Oh, uh-huh. Yeah, I know the section.
This was before Mickey Cohen, you know, but it was called the Club Bali, and I worked there -- oh, I worked there for about a year, and the star of the show was

a guy named Burrows Fletcher, and of course I was just sort of an atmosphere piano player, you know. And I used to do a thing -- I used to do Fats Waller's, "You're Feets Too Big," and I met an awful lot of people there, and I made a lot of wonderful friends with the people in the industry, you know, and most of these guys that used to come in there were designers, you know, and stars and people that were very, very prominent people. And I worked there for about a year, and I -- well, I knew guys like Orry Kelly and -- I knew all of them. I can't even remember all of their names. But these are the type of people, and as I say, they served this curried food and the waiters wore sarongs. A real special, this was a real special thing, you know, real elegant club. And it was really, really nice. I liked that. That was really one of my first nice jobs. Now, I think I was making $5.00 a night when I went there. And my friend Lillian Randolph was responsible for getting me that job.

She had been working there, and at that time Lillian Randolph was going -- was going into acting and doing -- she was on the Great Gildersleeve. She was going into, you know, the radio thing, shows and whatever. And so she was sort of getting away from the nightclub thing. She had been working there for quite a while, and they wanted somebody -- they wanted a girl. They told her they'd like to have somebody -- a girl to play and sing. So she, being a friend of mine, she recommended me for this job, and the guy who owned the club at

that time was a guy named Icky Arthaway. He owned the club and Burrows Fletcher was the main attraction for the room. And that was a very enjoyable engagement. I've met many people at that place, you know, since -- after I had started recording, that remembered me from there.
Somebody told me that they saw a piece of film with you. What would that have been?

Oh, I did a short with Ina Ray Hutton, Ina Ray Hutton and her Girl -- I think it was called, "No Men Allowed," or something like that, because she had all girls, you know, an all girl orchestra. And she was a charming person, I thought. She sort of faded out of the picture. I don't know what happened to Ina Ray, but I did do this with her for Universal.

Oh, because there's a book out called, Jazz On Film, * and your name isn't listed in it, but they do have some of the Universal shorts listed in there. Yet somebody told me they saw this short with you in it.
Uh-huh.
Do you remember what you did in it?

Yes, I did, "Real Gone Guy." I've got to find out about that, because I tell you, you see, I wasn't a member of the Screen Actors Guild, and this was one of the things that I did -- Taft-Hartley, you know, the Taft-Hartley thing, where they allow you to do one thing, see, because it
*David Meeker, author.
was filmed. I think it was probably the beginning of some of the things that were done on film for television, you know.
Uh-huh.

Not for television particularly, but they did them in theaters like short subjects, you know. They used to call them short subjects. I don't know if they still call them that, because I don't know -- I don't really go to theaters that much. I don't like what's happening with some of the things, you know, on the screen, so I don't frequent the theater scenes too much now.
What year did you make this?
This must have been about -- it was in the '50s. It had to be in the '50s, because I'm just thinking, it had to be maybe about '50 -- '53, '54, something like that. It had to be around that time.
Also, another thing that I want to touch on a little bit is the -- I think this happened in '51. I was a subject on "This is Your Life."
Oh, I missed it. Tell me.

Yes, I was a subject on that, and I think -- I don't know, my memory might not serve me too well -- I think I was one of the first -- one of the first artists to do the thing live, you know, to do it direct. Because it was -- what do you call it, kinescope? The kinescope process that they followed. So I think my show was the first one to be

done live, and anyway, I was -- I was so surprised. I was completely -- there are some people that still remember this, as long ago as that has been, and I still have the film of it. It's kind of -- some of it's a little worn. I have to see if I can have it processed and --
Oh, yeah, you should have it restored.
And restored. I must keep that, you know.

But this was a marvelous thing, and I used to sit, you know, whenever I could and watch the different subjects on the show. And Ralph Edwards, who is a wonderful man, and such a personable man, and he -- he had -- isn't that funny, what is the guy's name? I can't even think of his name now. But was instrumental in really getting me on the show, and he had a girl working for him, and this girl, she was a maid, and the girl was a friend of mine, and she was instrumental in getting me, you know, getting me on the show. I say she was instrumental in getting me on the show because she found -- he found out that this girl was a friend of mine, and he had my records. Pascal, Al Pascal, that was the man's name. Al Pascal.

He was instrumental in getting me on the show, you know. He wanted me -- but I of course didn't know that. I wasn't supposed to know that I was going to be the subject of the show. And I was told that I was going to do -- what is the woman's name? Oh, dear, used to be a dancer. She was a marvelous

dancer. I was told that they were going to do her life, and it was on a New years Eve night, and what I used to do, I used to always get home for Christmas, you know. I wouldn't be away from home. I didn't -- I was home one time, away from my son at Christmastime, once, and I was never so miserable in my entire life. I was never so miserable, and I promised myself that I would never do that again, regardless of how much money, you know, it meant I would miss. I must spend Christmas, because I was used to this, you know, and coming from a large family Christmas always meant so much to me and my family. We always just loved Christmas. It was the big thing with us, even in Louisiana, you know, we just loved Christmas, and to have been away from home at Christmastime just really tore me up. So I promised I would always be.

But anyway, they contacted me, Mr. Pascal, and said they wanted me to be -- to do a number on this show, and it was going to be on a New Years Eve night. Well, on New Years Eve night some friends of mine were having a party or something, and you know, this was already arranged, for me to go to this party. I was looking forward to it, because working all the time you just didn't get a chance to do other things, you know, and I said, well, I'm going to be home, and I looked forward to going to this party.
So they got in touch with Mr. Gastel', my manager, and told him what they wanted. Well, he knew the whole story. My family knew the whole story, and my little sister Vida, who

used to travel with me, I told you about her. Vida was instrumental, and another friend who has gone on also. Vida has gone on, of course, and this friend Eugenia. Well, they got together and got all these facts, and we have a darling little friend back in Louisiana, Mary -- what's her name? Mary Burn Elliott. And also Rosa Hart from Lake Charles, who has gone on. But Rosa Hart was very, very strong and very instrumental in keeping the little theater going in Lake Charles, you know.

But anyway, anything theatrical and anybody theatrical she was with it and for it. She was just a marvelous person and Mary Burn Elliott and her family were just tremendous. So they knew all of this was going on, and they did the works of getting this thing, putting it in action. Unbeknownst to me, you know, and I absolutely had no idea, really. Because I've had people ask me, "You mean to tell me you didn't know?" I say no, I did not know. I had seen the show, you know, but I -- the way it was put to me, and they were just wonderful in doing it. They said, "We want you to do a number on the show," and the song was, "Let's Start the New Year Right, 12:00 O'Clock Tonight." They said, "That's what we want you to do. We want you to do the show and --," Gilda Gray, that's the woman's name, the woman whose -- I don't know if she's gone on now or not. Gilda Gray? She was a dancer.
I know the name but I don't remember her.

Gilda was a dancer, and this was what they told me, said, "We want you to do -- we're going to do Gilda Gray's life and we want you to do a number to bring her on, you know, and we want you to do, "Let's Start the New Year Right." Well, I didn't know, "Let's Start the New Year Right." I didn't even know it, but I learned it, and I think I even forgot some of the words that night, I was so excited.

I had no idea that this was going to happen, and funny, you know, this was on New Years night. It was on New Years night, now, and I was so excited. Well, I was excited over the idea that I was going to do this, becuase it was the first time on national TV, you know. And this was the thing that I was really excited over, the fact that I was going to do this on national TV. And when I -- after the thing was all over -- before it was all over, it was revealed that they had set everything up in Lake Charles, my home. They had set a screen up. They had made arrangements with the Chamber of Commerce, the Mayor and everybody in Lake Charles were watching this. It was all set up there on NBC. And they tried to get my parents to come out, but they were not well enough to come, you know. My mother was -- she wasn't ill at the time too, but my dad had had a stroke, and he was, you know -- and she really wanted to be there. She wouldn't leave him, and I wouldn't have wanted her to, you know.
So they would not come, but they showed photos of them and -- anyway, when the show opened up, here I was, singing
"Let's Start the New Year Right, 12:00 O'Clock Tonight," or whatever, and later on -- what's the guy -- I can't even think of his name now.
Ralph Edwards?

I get so excited when I talk about it. Ralph Edwards came out and said, yes, yes, yes, something, we're going to have fun tonight. And then here comes a voice saying, "It's been a long time, Nellie Lutcher --," something, "since I looked down your throat in Lake Charles, Louisiana," or something. Then it hit me and I sat there and I looked and I looked, and I thought what is this voice coming from some foreign place, you know. And I looked and looked, and then finally she said, yes, and I think it was the first person they brought out, and that was Maude Reid, who was a nurse at the school where I went.
(Laughter)

At your now famous throat, or your now famous tonsils, or something like that, she said, and she came walking out on the stage. Well, I tell you, that was the beginning. And then they brought so many surprises out. You know the nature of the show.

They brought the principal, who was my music teacher's -- my music teacher had gone on. I didn't bring that up later. It was my music teacher who I loved so dearly and who was so wonderful to me, and so interested in me and my career, and I

just give her all the credit in the world for helping to steer me on and to train me. Well, she got drowned. She was in a terrible automobile accident, she and her husband's mother. Let's see, was it she and her husband's mother? No, she and her neice. There were four of them in the car. She and her neice were drowned, and the husband and the husband's mother survived. But that was a terrible thing.

But anyway, the husband came. They got him. He was the principal of the school and they got him to come, and each -- you know the nature of the show -- each one of these people would speak out something, you'd recognize his voice, and I would just go to pieces every time I would hear a voice.
I'm sure.

And all in all they must have brought about -- I guess about eight people, and whose voices I hadn't heard in years. And it was just tremendous, and my son at that time was attending school back in North Carolina, and he was supposed to have been visiting my parents at Louisiana. So when they brought him, you know, he was the last one to come out, I think, and they said -- Ralph Edwards would say, "Nellie, what about the song that you wrote for your little son Talmadge when he was a little boy." And I went on and started playing this song, started playing, "My Little Boy," and just at that time here comes this little boy, who was a big boy, and put his hands over my eyes. That almost killed me.

Excuse me. I had to cough. That just absolutely -- I just couldn't control myself. I became so emotional at that point, you know. And of course he expressed himself and said how grateful he was, you know, that I had sent him to school, to this fine, wonderful school, because the school where he was at the time, as I said, was one of the finest schools in the country, and incidentally, Maria Cole, who I mentioned earlier, her aunt, her aunt was the founder of this wonderful school for black children in North Carolina.
What was the aunt's name?
Charlotte Hawkins. Charlotte Hawkins. She was a great educator.
So it was she that Charlotte Saraty (PHONETIC) was named after.
Yes, that's right. That's right.
Maria's sister Charlotte.

Maria's sister Charlotte was named after her. She was a wonderful woman. I had the pleasure of knowing her and meeting her and she did -- she just did wonders with my son, you know. She took a great deal of interest, not only in my son, but in all children. She was just a born educator, you know. She was a wonderful woman.
But anyway, this all happened, and of course the folks back there were looking at the show, and all over the country, it was seen all over the country.
How marvelous.
And I just -- you know, even today, I haven't seen this in a long time, but when I see it now I sort of get a little drippy eyed.
Oh, sure. Were there any musical people also brought on to it?

Well, Dave Dexter, of course, that was instrumental in getting me on records. And one other person was brought on, was very comical, was a guy named Alan Prade, who I think I mentioned earlier. He was at one time the head of the -- he was the manager of the Southern Rhythm Boys Band that I played in before I came to California. He was also at one time, he had a band called Alan Prade's Syncopators, or something like that.

But nevertheless, he was brought out for this. He was living down south, in Port Arthur, Texas or somewhere, and he was a huge man. He weighed about 350 pounds, I guess, or close to 400 if anything. And they brought him out and he told some of the experiences, you know, how my dad used to take us around. I told this earlier too, how he used to take us around in the summer and we used to play little shows and little concerts at the various schools, you know, in the little towns of Texas and Louisiana. And this guy was one of the members of the troupe, and this was the one person that they brought out, you know, one of the musicians that -- well, he didn't play an instrument, but he was a great singer and a
great entertainer and a comedian.
(Laughter)
That's great. I didn't realize that. I wish I had seen it. I missed that.
Well, some of these days maybe we'll get to do the film. I've got a -- I treasure that film, you know.
You probably shouldn't try to look at it until you've taken it to be restored. Those things disintegrate, you know.

Yes, I know they do, and I was talking -- I talked to someone not long ago, and they told me they would help me to get it, because the last time we tried to do it, use it you know, parts of it were broken off, and I really don't want that to happen.
It's a kinescope, is that what it is, or is it on film?
It's on film. It's on film.
There are places that just restore, so you can have it transferred to a video cassette or onto new film.
Well, I must do this, and no doubt even NBC, I'm sure probably they could even --
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
