You mentioned that you went to England and Scotland and I don't know where else, Honolulu, you said, off the tape. This all happened after your hit record and when you went to Cafe Society in New York. You signed with Carlos Gastell, and then what happened? Did Carlos book you overseas, or what?
Oh, yes, he did, definitely. Yes, he did. As a matter of fact, I went twice, I think in one year, and it was just a tremendous success, really.

Well, my records had really -- they had known me through records for about -- well, ever since they first came out, see, because the records were released, and this was -- we're talking about like '50, '51, or something like that. And they were just warming up, and I can't remember the guy's name who was instrumental in introducing my records from Germany. They used to hear -- what do they call this? I can't think of what they called it, but it was one of those shows that you could hear records. They'd play them in Japan and they'd hear them in England.
Oh.
I can't think of the name for the doggone thing right now, but nevertheless, this fellow introduced my records through that medium.
Short wave radio?
Well, it wasn't really short wave. I don't think it was short wave, but they called it something else. It was like they were playing it for the soldiers.
Oh, Armed Forces Radio?
Something on that order, I think. And he played -- you know, would be playing the records, and the guys would hear them.

So this was how the people in England, from what I understand, got -- became aware of my records, through Germany you know. And they wanted me to come over, so I first hesitated to go. I hesitated. I don't know, I -- as I say, I guess I felt just like I did about the -- going to New York the first time. It didn't really hit me, you know, that it was -- well, that these people were aware of me. In other words, you know, I had arrived, but I guess when you take so long to arrive and you arrive you don't even know you've arrived.
(Laughter)

So I still wasn't -- you know, it didn't excite me too much. But Carlos Castel., of course, he kept harping on it and they kept after him. "We have to have Nellie Lutcher. We want Nellie Lutcher to come. She's got to come. She's got to come." So finally, I decided to -- that I would go, and it was so marvelous, and I took my musicians with me the first time. I think we did eight weeks, and then we went back the second time and did ten weeks. And I played

all over England, and then Scotland. I went to Glasgow, Edinburgh, and did what they called -- let's see, it was something like our vaudeville here, and they didn't call it vaudeville. They called it -- what did they call the theater shows? Oh, that'll come to me too.
But anyway, everybody did that, you know. You'd play in a place a week.
What musicians did you take with you?

I had -- when I first went I took Earl Hyde on drums, and George Duvivier, who's today one of the greatest and one of the finest bass players around, amongst the finest. They went with me the first time, and the second time, for that matter. And it was just tremendous, really. The response was so very great, until I couldn't believe it, when you'd play these halls over there, you know. I guess this was their chief form of entertainment. I'm trying to remember what they call them. They don't call them vaudeville houses. They call them something else. But anyway, these people would respond, and they knew, they knew you, who you were. They knew who I was and they knew my records, my works, and right today I still hear from these people.

Incidentally, there was one man that was a marvelous -- he was just a marvelous performer, musician, impresario, band leader, orchestra leader, disc jockey, whatever. His name was Jack Jackson, and Jack Jackson was very, very popular in

England at the time. So Jack Jackson travelled with me. He toured the whole scene with me, he and his wife, each time. And we had the most marvelous time and the most wonderful -- Jack Jackson just passed, I think, this past year. But he was a wonderful, wonderful guy, and I did get to meet many of the English musicians, people that were very important in the circuit, you know, and I had a chance to really see just what and how much they appreciate our American music. They really -- I mean there's no question about it. They are deeply concerned and they are really -- they are really responsive to what you do.

Scotland was -- I certainly didn't expect this in Scotland. When I got there and they knew every -- they knew my work. They just absolutely -- Nellie this and Nellie, Nellie, Nellie, play this, and they knew the songs that I did, could sing them right along, and this one little fellow, right now, he was just a youngster at that time, he was from Liverpool. Liverpool was my very first engagement in England, was Liverpool, and he and his little friend followed us all over, you know, all over England, everywhere we would go. Every Sunday they would come to see us in a different place.

Now, what I'd do, I'd work six days in one place and on Sundays we'd come to London and do -- I think they called it variety. They called it variety there. I think that's the name they called it, variety. Variety houses and variety concerts. But it was really variety, because you know

it was just something like our vaudeville shows here that we used to have, where they had comedians, you know, and dancers and singers and just all sorts of acts on the show, you know. It was just marvelous.

But it was a marvelous experience, and I got to know Lew Grade and Leslie, and Delfonte, who's a big man. In fact I think Delfonte was kind of responsible for my going over the first time, through an agent, Mumford, I think this guy's name was, Mumford. I think that's his name. I hope I remember the name correctly.

But anyway, Delfonte is a brother to the Grades. You know, they're all brothers, and they're all in different capacities, you know. But it was a marvelous, wonderful, wonderful experience, and as I say, today I hear from people, I still hear from them, and this young fellow whose name is Alan Hobbs, he's the little fellow who followed us all around, well he's now in California. He's been here for quite some time. He lives in San Francisco. So he keeps in touch and he goes back home. I guess his parents are still living in England, and he goes home about every year or every other year or so, and he keeps in constant touch with me.
Great. Loyal fans.
Loyal. Well, I'm very grateful for that, Pat. Through the years the people that were devoted fans, they still are, and I guess, like many people have asked me

today why I'm not -- they don't hear more of me. Well, the answer is, you know, I've been with several record companies. Capitol, of course, was my first company. And then I was with Decca awhile and I was with Columbia, and I did some things for Imperial and one of the things that I did was on Liberty. I did an album on Liberty which I consider a very, very good album, with Russ Garcia doing the arranging for me on that album, and he did a marvelous job. It's a marvelous album. It was one of the -- one of the few things, I suppose, that I did where I didn't play. I didn't play the piano at all on that particular album. But I just vocalized and just concentrated on vocalizing. And also on the Capitol thing I did a session where I didn't play, and that also, that was Harold Mooney did the arrangements on that, and that was a session that I was quite proud of also, because you know, I was experimenting with something different you see, getting away from the completely rhythm things. And of course this was what Nat did. It's the same pattern almost that Nat King Cole -- that they followed with Nat King Cole, you see.

But I was glad to -- it gave me a chance to really display some versatility, you know, because I could perform as a single artist or with -- when I say single I mean with rhythm and piano, and/or with a big orchestra. That was -- but the arrangements were built around me and for me, and I give -- really, I give both of these men credit. Harold Mooney on

Capitol.

Also, Billy May didn't do a bad job. I did some things with him on Capitol, although this is sort of coming to me in the --Billy May was also a very wonderful man, very wonderful. I did some things with him too, but the things with Harold Mooney were a little different, because that was my time to experiment with strings, you know, which sort of gave a little -- a little something extra, you know, to what I'd done, and I'm very proud of that.

The thing that I regret today is the fact that none of the record companies, they're not releasing any of my material, any of these things that I did, and it hurts a little bit because this is one of the ways that you make money in the business, you know. You're not just in it for your health or because you like to do it. I enjoy it. I love what I do. I love my work and I'm extremely grateful that my career turned out like it did, because as I say, I really did not concentrate on being a singer. This was far from my mind. I wanted to be an arranger.
Do you still ever have the inclination to write?

No, not for an orchestra or anything like that. You know, tunes, I've written many of the tunes that I've recorded, but including, 'Hurry On Down,' 'He's A Real Gone Guy,' and, 'Do You or Don't You Love Me,' and oh, just any
number of things.
What other titles can you think of, because we don't have them on here.
You don't? Well, "You'd Better Watch Yourself, Bub." Let me see, I can look at this and tell you some of them.
"Fine Brown Frame" is yours, isn't it?
That's not mine, it's my arrangement. No. "Do You or Don't You Love me." The only ones on here are, "He's A Real Gone Guy," "Hurry On Down," "Do You or Don't You Love Me." The rest are --
This is looking at your 10-inch Capitol record, "Real Gone."
Yeah, uh-huh.
What other compositions have you recorded?
Well, I did, "The Pig Latin Song." As I mentioned, "My Little Boy." Oh, gosh.
I should have given you some warning on this.

Well, yes, because it's hard to think of. I would have even brought a list with me, because I do have a -- I told you about the thing, the discography that Bobby Boatian (PHONETIC) gave me, that he got from an English -- I don't know whether it's English or not, but it's from a
European publication.
Could we get a Xeroxed copy of that for me?

Yes, I have it. I have everything that I have ever done, when it was done, the musicians on the date. I haven't seen anything like that. I think we talked about this before, Pat. I haven't seen anything like this in the States. But this guy got ahold of it, and he is a friend of mine, a dear friend, and he is one person in the business that is so knowledgeable. I mean he actually follows up and has knowledge on people, and records to prove, you know. This is his life. He has a little house by the old river bed and he has three dogs and he has about 6,000 records.
And he's a member of -- is he the founder also of the Society for Recorded Music?
I don't know if he's a founder of it, but he's a very active member, and probably the Secretary or the Treasurer or something in it. But he's very devoted. He is just absolutely just marvelous.

But anyway, he got this book and gave me -- he Xeroxed this list of things that I had recorded and things my brother recorded, everybody who has ever recorded, you know, up to a point. He's -- all of your things were listed, and this is a European publication.
Wonderful.
He could tell you -- if you talk to

him, he can tell you what -- where he got it from, but I have a copy of this thing. In fact somebody else Xeroxed it for me, so I have a list of all of these things, when they were recorded, who they were done with.
Oh, that's great.

And it's unfortunate, as I say, today, that none of this stuff is available unless you get it at an auction or unless, you know, you pay a big sum of money for it, which is -- it's a little -- well, it creates a little bitterness, because I feel that there's a place, not only for Nellie Lutcher's records, I feel there's a place for any creative work. And while I'm at it I want to thank the Smithsonian Institute for asking me to do this interview.

It's important, Nellie, because there's so little written down about you. You've done so much and you've been involved with so many marvelous people, you've contributed so much, and you can't find you in a book.
Yeah, well --
A couple of the encyclopedias give some brief information, but someone wants to find out about you they can't find it written down. Now we have some information.

Well, I'm very glad of that. I'm very grateful that they gave me the opportunity of doing this interview, and I hope that -- well, before I make it on home, as the old folks would say -- and I'm not homesick. As I say,

I want to make heaven my home, but I'm not homesick. I do plan to really get back into things, but I must say too that there have been changes that have come about, and where it does make one a little bit -- you get a little disgusted, a little bitter about certain things, because I feel that there is a place for every type of music, every type of music there is a place for it. And of course, as the time -- as we -- the time that we're into now, this period that we're into now, with the disco, well this to me is a great discredit to the average musician, because many musicians are not able to get a job because of the disco scene, you see.

Before disco, of course it was rock and roll. Well, I don't put the rock and roll scene down, you know. It's not my bag, it wasn't my bag. It was certainly very far from my type of thing or my scene, and the people who created it and the people who were fortunate enough to get into the act at that time, who were fortunate enough to get with the people who were promoters and people who promote this thing, and that's how rock and roll got to be so big, it really just boomeranged like nothing I've ever seen, you know. And jazz has never had this, unfortunately. It really has never had this type of thing. And the thing that hurts, the thing that bothers me, is that seemingly some people don't consider jazz that important, you see. They know what it is. They know it is definitely a creative thing. I think one of the most creative forms of
music ever. It's the thing that's created right here in our own country, and it's unfortunate that it's not recognized as widely and as much as it is in other countries.

I got a letter just a few weeks ago from somebody wanting to get -- bring me -- from a Scandinavian booking agent. And I've gotten calls within the last year from people wanting me to go into Europe, you know. But my feeling now is that I would like to do something like that, if I have something going, some records going, you know, if the records were resurrected or reissued or something. But I think just to go someplace now just to be going, in the first place you've got to dicker and you've got to talk about money and the kind of money that you should get now, because you can't afford to go -- I can't, and I speak for myself, and I'm sure I'm speaking for many other people -- it's too expensive now to attempt to go. And when I travel I use my own musicians with me. Not that I put any other musicians down. Unless I'm fortunate enough to go in a town, like when I go to New York, I have musicians there that have worked with me. Morris Edwards, for instance, who is a very fine bass player. Well, Morris Edwards worked with me out here in California before he even went to New York to live. He works with me. And of course, as I mentioned, George Duvivier, who's so busy now he doesn't have time to work with anybody, any one person too long, you know. He's so much in demand.

So, if I'm fortunate enough to do that, but when you are doing a certain type of thing and you feel a certain type of rhythm, that I do, because I feel that what I'm doing, it's a sensitive -- I feel every movement that I make. I work really by my feeling, you know. When I play, that's the way I play the piano. I work strictly by feeling. And every musician -- any musician -- I don't say every -- but every musician who comes along doesn't feel this, you see. So there are certain people that I enjoy working with because I know they sense what I'm doing. They're sensitive to what I'm doing, and this makes me a better performer, when I work with people who really understand what I'm doing and who really feel what I'm doing. I don't want to work for somebody who's just, 'Well, I'm working with Nellie and I'm going to get some money.'
Yeah.
You know what I mean, 'I'm going to get some money for doing this,' and so on. So that doesn't --
But here, here in Los Angeles, you usually work with the same two musicians, don't you?

Yes, I work with the same. Well, I work with either Billy Hadnott, who was on my very first record date, and he's still around, a very wonderful bass player. And then Benny Booker, who was the first bass player who went on the road with me. He went -- he was on the road with me about, I guess, a couple of years before -- before George Duvivier was

with me. George Duvivier went to Europe with me. Then I use -- right now I'm using a very fine drummer, Gene Washington. He's a very good drummer. And I have worked with -- I've worked with many drummers. Al Bartee and some of the other fine drummers around town. And, as I think I told you, Lee Young was on my first record session. He was on the, "Hurry On Down," session. At that time he was a playing musician. But now he's an executive, now.
Yes, I know, at Motown.
At Motown Records, yes. So he has come a long way.
So you are still performing, for the record, here. I know you are. But you work clubs here in Los Angeles. You don't travel much, though, do you?

I don't travel too much now, no, I don't. I sort of stay home. Well, I'm an old landlady. I love dealing in real estate, so I inveted money in real estate. That is in an apartment house. And a six-unit place. I rent five ofthem and I live in one, and that sort of keeps me busy, that and my little, you know, chore with the board,the union, because sometimes we meet two or three times -- well, we meet once every week, and sometimes it's possible we meet maybe twice a week. So I'm quite busy with that. But I still love what I do. I love my work, and I feel that the time has come or will come when, you know, when you won't have to butt your head

against a stone wall, trying to really get into the scene as it is today. Because it's a whole different ball game, and at that time -- there are still people, there is still a market for whatever anybody has to offer, you know. Once you've made it. This is the way I feel. I feel once you've made it or got the recognition, you don't lose the recognition. But there are people who are looking for the next what else is new, so what else is new. And this is the thing that's a little heartbreaking about the whole thing, because the people -- there are people around today that could do and promote and could -- the same thing that did happen can happen again, it can happen. Because you don't lose this unless you lose your voice or lose your fingers or a hand, or lose, you know, lose your cool, as the kids say. You lose your cool, then that's it, you know.

But I still feel that there is a market for the things that I do, and I'm very grateful that I still get letters from people out of the country, and incidentally I must tell you about -- I must say this, and then we'll close. I had a friend from South America. I don't know if I mentioned this to you sooner, about the young man from South America that was here, or did I? Do you recall?
Off the tape. You merely mentioned on the tape that someone from South America had asked you a question the other day. But you didn't really talk about it.
I didn't get into it?
No.

Well, I'm going to say this briefly. Well, this young fellow is a poet and he's a director and he's -- well, he's into music. He played guitar at one time. And his name is Emilio Bele de Cavajo, and he is quite busy, from South America. He's in Rio de Janeiro. And he was here with a show. Let me see, that's been about four years ago, I guess. They were appearing at Madison Square Garden in New York, then they came here to UCLA, and he called me from New York. He wanted to know if I was going to be in Los Angeles when they came here, and I said yes. And he said, 'Well, I must meet you. I have your records, I have all of your records, and I want to see if I can find some of your records.' And he said, 'I've had your records ever since they first came to South America.' And he had my album and he had some of the Capitol things, too.

So, when they did come here, and I got to meet him and the whole group, and he was the only one in the whole group that spoke English. I couldn't even understand the rest of them, but somehow they understood my music. And they told me that, some of them said they learned some of the English language through my records. I don't know how.
How marvelous.
Well, that's what they said. But anyway, he's been a very dear friend to me, and I hear from him.

As a matter of fact I got a letter from him today, and he's quite busy, and he's into the record bit, and he's into producing, he's into writing and poetry, and whatever, but he's quite a guy, in Rio de Janeiro, but I'm very grateful to have him as a friend and somebody who is interested in my work. And he tells me, "You've got to come to South America. You've got to come." And someday I would love to go.
It sounds like you've got all the ingredients for a good international tour.

Well, I would love to go to South America, I really would, because judging from what this guy says and some of his friends, when they come over here he tells them, "Be sure and call Nellie." He gives them my number and they call me and they tell me, "Emilio says to be sure and tell you hello and give you his love." And they're beautiful people. They are very dedicated people too. Very -- you know, there's no phoniness about them, that's the thing that I like, and when they enjoy and appreciate something, they really like it. And it's amazing, as I say, how many people in other countries dig what's happening here with us, and particularly with jazz, you know.

Now, I don't know, I guess the rock and roll scene has made quite an impact too, but somehow it hasn't lasted. It's not a lasting thing, unfortunately. Somebody makes money real fast, real quick and fast, you know. But the thing with

the jazz artists is that you knock yourself out a long time before you can even learn to play an instrument. You don't do this overnight, you know. And of course with the new electronic gimmicks and the instruments and all the things that's going on today, it has made it a faster thing. It's just like flying, for instance, and the train, you know. I just took my first flight last -- when was it, May? And I tried to -- I have it written down someplace. I think it was -- I went to San Francisco. I was en route to Sacramento, and I was a special guest at the Sacramento Jazz Club. I was their surprise guest at their 10th anniversary, so they wanted me to be their guest, and I flew. But I'm saying all that to say it was just like that, because that was my first time flying, and they had a heck of a time getting me on the plane then. But flying is something I just don't -- it hasn't really gotten to me yet, however I realize in some instances it is a necessity. But if I was travelling all the time I still couldn't -- I couldn't stand the, you know, the tension, the thing of flying. I don't think I could stand that. Well, I was spoiled, I guess, coming along in the era of the train bit, you know, before anybody even heard of the word Amtrak.
(Laughter)
You'd get on a train here in Los Angeles and get off when you'd get to New York, you know. Maybe you'd stop in Chicago. You'd have about two or three

hours in Chicago. You could stop and visit and do whatever, shop or whatever you'd want to do. Then you'd journey on to New York. That would take you about four days. And when I went to Europe, of course, I took the ship, which I love. I just love the ship. I loved it. Fortunately, I was on big ships. The Queen Mary. And that's another thing, the Queen Mary, which is now a historical thing here, out at, what is it, Long Beach?
Long Beach, yeah.
Well, I travelled on the Queen Mary. Yes, I was privileged to have travelled on that ship, and it was just absolutely just magnificent, just beautiful.

When they brought it here and it was first set up, I told many people, and I have visited the ship, and it was a real pleasure. You know, some of the sights on there, some of the old -- what do you call the rooms? Staterooms, I think that's what they call them, some of this came back to me, you know, and it was just such a marvelous thing at that time to travel that way.

And of course when I went to Honolulu later, I also went by ship. I went on the -- no, I went on a small ship and came back on the Lurlean which was a very famous ship at that time, you know. But all in all it was wonderful having travelled around, having met many wonderful people in my career, and I still think if I had to choose another profession I would

not have chosen anything else. I would still be a musician, an entertainer, because I love people and I love the scene, and again, I do want to thank the Smithsonian people for allowing Nellie Lutcher to be a part of your -- what do you call it?
Oral history program.
Oral history program. Thank you so very much.
Thank you, Nellie.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

segments.title: Copyright notice, Smithsonian project heading and start of interview
segments.summary: Standard copyright warning, Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Project headers for Reel One (January and February 1979), and the start of proceedings.

segments.title: Name, birthplace and birth date
segments.summary: Nellie Lutcher gives her name, Lake Charles birthplace and 1915 birth date, and says privately she is really a 1912 child.

segments.title: The sixteen Lutcher children and their names
segments.summary: She names her surviving siblings, including twin brother Joe Lutcher, and says all studied music but only she, Joe and Charlie stayed with it.

segments.title: Her father the bassist and the string instruments at home
segments.summary: Her father was a professional bass violin player who played all string instruments and taught her guitar, violin and mandolin.

segments.title: Her mother Susie Garrett and the parents' roots
segments.summary: Her mother wanted to be a pianist but married at about 13 and had children too fast; both parents came from the Franklin, Louisiana area and neither family was otherwise musical.

segments.title: Her father's career and his day job at the packing house
segments.summary: Her father played Louisiana and Texas towns but also drove for a packing house, so he could not play as often as he wished.

segments.title: The Imperial Jazz Band, Clarence Hart and Bunk Johnson
segments.summary: She describes the Imperial Jazz Band of Lake Charles, led by Clarence Hart, and Bunk Johnson who played with it and was later discovered; Willard checks his dates in Chilton.

segments.title: Bunk Johnson's humor and the sincerity of itinerant performers
segments.summary: Bunk was jovial and funny; she recalls minstrels, medicine shows and vaudeville that played Lake Charles for a single day with great humor and love of the work.

segments.title: Medicine shows and minstrel tent shows in Lake Charles
segments.summary: She describes how minstrel tent shows and medicine shows worked, what the medicine cost, and how big Lake Charles was.

segments.title: Earliest music and her teacher Eugenia Reynaud
segments.summary: She can hardly remember not playing piano; her parents started her with Eugenia King Reynaud, the main teacher in Lake Charles.

segments.title: Playing the Blue Danube and studying with Mrs. Foster
segments.summary: After she played at a graduation, concert pianist Mrs. Alton J. Foster took her briefly but said she was too advanced to teach much.

segments.title: Sunday school and church pianist at eight or nine
segments.summary: Trained by Mrs. Reynaud, she became the Sunday school and church pianist at Sunlight Baptist, being woken at night to play for collection.

segments.chapter: Imperial Orchestra and Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.title: Hart asks for Nellie to join the Imperial Orchestra
segments.summary: When pianist Al Freeman went home to Ohio, Clarence Hart proposed Nellie; her father agreed but her mother hesitated.

segments.chapter: Imperial Orchestra and Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.title: Church disapproval of jazz and her mother's feelings
segments.summary: Church women said the little girl was going to hell for playing jazz; her father backed her, while her mother worried because she was young and had washed laundry to pay for lessons.

segments.chapter: Imperial Orchestra and Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.title: Her early marriage that lasted two months
segments.summary: She married very young, refuses to name him, left after two months at about 16 and started traveling with a band afterwards.

segments.chapter: Imperial Orchestra and Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.title: Learning to arrange from Al Wilson in the Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.summary: With the Southern Rhythm Boys she studied arranging under saxophonist Al Wilson and arranged for the 15 or 16 piece band.

segments.chapter: Imperial Orchestra and Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.title: Personnel of the Southern Rhythm Boys (re-recorded section)
segments.summary: After a tape fault the interview redoes the band personnel: the Williams brothers, Al Wilson, Collins, Eldridge Joe, Snake Griffin and Lawrence Emerson.

segments.chapter: Imperial Orchestra and Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.title: Eldridge Joe, Don Albert and Snake Griffin
segments.summary: She says Eldridge Joe went on to Don Albert's San Antonio band and that Snake Griffin was a Creole who later moved to California.

segments.chapter: Imperial Orchestra and Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.title: Her father on piano and the string instruments she used in school
segments.summary: She never used guitar, violin or mandolin in bands, only in school clubs; her father also played piano at parties.

segments.chapter: Imperial Orchestra and Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.title: Young players in the band, Kermit Scott and wanting to be an arranger
segments.summary: Band members were in their twenties; Kermit Scott later played with Hines; she wanted to be an arranger like Mary Lou Williams, not a singer.

segments.chapter: Imperial Orchestra and Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.title: Percentage dances, guarantees and admission prices
segments.summary: She explains how percentage dances, ticket men and small guarantees worked, with no salaries or unions, and travel in old cars.

segments.chapter: Imperial Orchestra and Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.title: Church attitudes to dancing and the Catholic Lenten calendar
segments.summary: Protestants condemned dancing while Catholic functions supplied band work except during Lent after Mardi Gras; the area was perhaps 70 percent Catholic.

segments.chapter: Imperial Orchestra and Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.title: Women instrumentalists and Jeanette Kimball
segments.summary: Asked about women in bands, she names pianist Jeanette Kimball of Papa Celestin's orchestra and her guitarist husband.

segments.chapter: Imperial Orchestra and Southern Rhythm Boys
segments.title: Bands that came through Lake Charles
segments.summary: New Orleans bands, Don Albert, Taft Crome and Houston bands played one nighters in Lake Charles on their way into Texas.

segments.title: Cleo Brown and the girl piano-singer trend
segments.summary: Cleo Brown's records began a trend for girl pianist-singers, and people expected Nellie to sing when she reached California.

segments.title: Arriving in Los Angeles: relatives, Clarence Hart and the Dunbar Hotel
segments.summary: Her aunts and cousins were in California and Clarence Hart had moved there to work in painting and decorating; her first job was at the Dunbar Hotel.

segments.title: The kitty and tipping at the Dunbar Hotel
segments.summary: Patrons demanded songs, which drew her into singing; she explains the cat-shaped tip kitty, tipping custom and low club pay.

segments.title: First songs and building a repertoire before recording
segments.summary: She describes the first songs she sang, such as Under a Blanket of Blue and The Object of My Affection, and the repertoire she had ready before recording.

segments.chapter: Life on the road in the South
segments.title: Car trip to Galveston and the roadhouse in China, Texas
segments.summary: On the way to Galveston with the Imperial Orchestra, her car found the other car stopped at a roadhouse where armed white men were forcing musicians to play.

segments.chapter: Life on the road in the South
segments.title: Forced to play at gunpoint and Joe Wynn's minstrel dance
segments.summary: Shotgun-armed men made the band play and forced the ticket-taking schoolteacher to dance until drummer Joe Wynn clowned in his place.

segments.chapter: Life on the road in the South
segments.title: Reel Two: how the China, Texas night ended and Tony Babbins
segments.summary: After the reel change she names the schoolteacher Babbins, nephew of manager Tony Babbins, says he walked five miles, and that the band never went back.

segments.chapter: Life on the road in the South
segments.title: Deciding not to spend her life like this
segments.summary: The incident made her decide she would not spend her life that way; she says Lake Charles itself had no such trouble.

segments.chapter: Life on the road in the South
segments.title: Denied a restroom at a Texas gas station
segments.summary: On a later tour near Corpus Christi, her sister was refused the white ladies' restroom, so they stopped the fill-up and left.

segments.chapter: Life on the road in the South
segments.title: Counting the Lutcher siblings again
segments.summary: Willard totals the named siblings against fifteen or sixteen children; others died at birth or before Nellie was born.

segments.chapter: Life on the road in the South
segments.title: Finding lodging under segregation and Effie Cox's place in Lake Charles
segments.summary: Even famous musicians had trouble finding rooms before and after 1954; she praises Effie Cox's place where Ellington's band stayed.

segments.chapter: Ma Rainey and the Palace Theater
segments.title: Ma Rainey needs a pianist at the Palace Theater
segments.summary: When Ma Rainey's pianist quit, theater owner Mancuso recommended young Nellie and her teacher Mrs. Reynaud gave permission.

segments.chapter: Ma Rainey and the Palace Theater
segments.title: Playing for Ma Rainey at twelve
segments.summary: She felt confident and thrilled, was kindly treated by Rainey and learned to accompany a singer.

segments.chapter: Ma Rainey and the Palace Theater
segments.title: Rainey's fame, kindness and small band
segments.summary: She knew Rainey from records, found her kind to work with, and describes the four or five piece band behind her.

segments.chapter: Ma Rainey and the Palace Theater
segments.title: Not realizing what the Ma Rainey job meant
segments.summary: She says she only recently grasped the significance and recounts a rumor that Rainey was still alive.

segments.chapter: Ma Rainey and the Palace Theater
segments.title: Step 'n Fetchit offers her a job
segments.summary: Step 'n Fetchit, scouting talent, used her as pianist in Lake Charles and offered $65 a week, but her parents refused.

segments.chapter: Ma Rainey and the Palace Theater
segments.title: Checking Ma Rainey's dates in Chilton
segments.summary: Willard reads Chilton's biography of Rainey, who died in 1939; Nellie notes the Rainey and Bunk Johnson jobs mattered for her career.

segments.chapter: Ma Rainey and the Palace Theater
segments.title: Ida Cox, the Whitman Sisters and Peg Leg Bates at the Palace Theater
segments.summary: She recalls the touring revues that passed through Lake Charles as a child.

segments.title: Coming to Los Angeles in 1935 to her aunt Lucille Avery
segments.summary: She lived with her aunt near Central Avenue and cousin Irving Jordan introduced her around.

segments.title: Club Alabam, Rochester and Lillian Randolph
segments.summary: Everyone went to Central Avenue's Club Alabam; she remembers Eddie Anderson's mop act with Johnnie Taylor and her friend Lillian Randolph.

segments.title: Clubs on and around Central Avenue
segments.summary: She and Willard sort out the Cotton Club, Bell Tavern, Apex, Club Alabam and Curtis Mosby's role.

segments.title: The Club Alabam band of Lorenzo Flennoy
segments.summary: Lorenzo Flennoy led the house band with Buddy Harper, Red Mack and Oscar Bradley.

segments.title: The breakfast club above the Club Alabam
segments.summary: After 2 a.m. entertainers went upstairs to the breakfast club with Sylvester Scott at piano, making money from tips.

segments.title: After hours jam spots and working two jobs a night
segments.summary: She and Willard list after-hours places such as Lovejoy's, Backstage and the Brown House, and describe musicians working two jobs a night.

segments.title: Jam sessions at her house with Lloyd Wilson
segments.summary: Lloyd Wilson brought visiting musicians to her home near Central Avenue, where Eddie Barefield, Panama Francis and Benny Carter jammed.

segments.title: Nat King Cole's big band rehearses at her house
segments.summary: Lloyd Wilson brought Nat Cole's band to rehearse and jam at her home; she recalls Nat's show, wife Nadine and brother Eddie.

segments.title: Earl Hines as her idol on the radio and Nat Cole's resemblance to him
segments.summary: She listened to Hines from the Grand Terrace on a neighbor's radio, recalls Ray Nance and Walter Fuller, and says Nat Cole at the piano sounded like Hines before he began to sing.

segments.title: The little piano Nat Cole played
segments.summary: She bought a piano on installments as soon as she got the Dunbar job; Nat Cole played it and she still has it.

segments.title: Art Tatum, Earl Hines and piano influences
segments.summary: She names Art Tatum, whom she knew in Los Angeles, as one of the greatest jazz pianists, alongside Hines.

segments.title: Mary McKay and the May Company record department
segments.summary: Mary McKay, who ran the May Company jazz record department, inspired Nellie to collect records, including 12-inch 78s.

segments.title: Timeless records, reissues and fairness to creative artists
segments.summary: She says the older music is timeless, welcomes reissues, and complains record companies shelve records that will not sell a million.

segments.title: Always owing the record company and signing without advice
segments.summary: She says artists never get out of debt to record companies and she, like others, signed without managers or lawyers.

segments.title: Her first Capitol contract: flat fee and promised royalty
segments.summary: Her first Capitol contract was non-royalty, a flat fee per record with a promised royalty if it hit, before Carlos Gastel became her manager.

segments.title: Artists dropped when the next hot act comes and who owns the masters
segments.summary: She says labels move on to the next hot artist and some masters may revert to the artist; she credits the union and Paul Howard.

segments.title: Leon René, songwriter, and her aunt Augusta Glover
segments.summary: She describes Leon and Otis René as successful songwriters and her aunt Augusta Glover wanting her to meet Leon.

segments.title: Reel Three: meeting Leon René and his lukewarm response
segments.summary: After the reel change, René listened to her songs and vocal arrangements at his home but had no calls for her work.

segments.title: Her son and aunt urge her to join the March of Dimes show
segments.summary: Her small son and aunt Augusta urged her to appear at the Hollywood High School March of Dimes show, as Betty Hall Jones had.

segments.title: The telegram to Frank Bull of KFWB
segments.summary: She telegraphed disc jockey Frank Bull, who read it on air and invited her onto his hour.

segments.title: Where and when the show was held
segments.summary: She and Willard work out that the show was on an outdoor platform at Hollywood High in 1947.

segments.title: One number heard on the radio by Dave Dexter
segments.summary: She sang one song unaccompanied, The One I Love Belongs to Somebody Else; Capitol's Dave Dexter heard the broadcast and sent word through Joe Alexander.

segments.title: Phoning Dexter and her home recordings
segments.summary: After hesitating she called Dexter, met him, mentioned her home records made on a Packard Bell, and learned her brother Joe had played him some without telling her.

segments.title: The test recordings she made for Capitol
segments.summary: She recorded demos of material she had long performed, including Hurry On Down, The Lady's in Love, and You'd Better Watch Yourself, Bub.

segments.title: Feeling taken advantage of; publishing and ASCAP
segments.summary: She feels Capitol took her creative material under a poor contract; she still owns part of the Hurry On Down copyright and praises ASCAP.

segments.title: Why Dexter noticed her among the stars
segments.summary: She did only one number on a bill with Betty Hutton and Bob Hope and calls herself lucky to be heard.

segments.chapter: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
segments.title: The Four Chocolate Drops with Dootsie Williams
segments.summary: Before recording she worked in a four-piece vocal group with Dootsie Williams, George Reed and Joe Lewis.

segments.chapter: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
segments.title: Lena Horne, Curran's Merry-Go-Round and Vine Street radio row
segments.summary: The group played intermissions with Lena Horne at the Little Troc and at Curran's Merry-Go-Round, with Willard and Nellie placing the Radio Room on Vine Street.

segments.chapter: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
segments.title: San Diego engagement and December 7, 1941
segments.summary: The group dated to early 1941 and worked in San Diego, where she was when Pearl Harbor was attacked.

segments.chapter: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
segments.title: Joining the Daniel Brothers at the Club Royal
segments.summary: After the group dispersed she subbed at the Club Royal for the ill pianist Pickens with the Daniel Brothers and stayed when he died.

segments.chapter: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
segments.title: Doug Daniel's seizures and the owner hires Nellie's own group
segments.summary: The Daniel brothers fought and Doug had epileptic seizures on the job, so owner Leonard Castille asked Nellie to lead her own group.

segments.chapter: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
segments.title: Musicians in her Club Royal groups
segments.summary: She names guitarist Tiny Mitchell, Herschel Coleman, Norman Bowden, bassist George Mason and guests like Monk McVeal, Lee Young and Dexter Gordon; the job ran to about 1945-46.

segments.chapter: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
segments.title: Commuting to San Diego and the Pearl Harbor blackout drive
segments.summary: She worked six days a week in San Diego, visiting her young son, and drove home in the blackout after refusing the owner's offer to stay.

segments.chapter: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
segments.title: The Little Troc job and Lena Horne's accompanists
segments.summary: Her group played intermission at the Little Troc on the Sunset Strip while Lena Horne worked six weeks; she recalls Phil Moore, Eddie Beal and Arthur Twine accompanying Lena.

segments.chapter: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
segments.title: Lena Horne's kindness and the dressing room
segments.summary: Lena Horne let Nellie sit in her dressing room during intermissions and always brought her refreshments, insisting on first names.

segments.chapter: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
segments.title: The infected tooth and hospital stay that cost her the Lena Horne job
segments.summary: A tooth her dentist had only packed became a severe jaw and throat infection, forcing a hospital stay and ending the Little Troc engagement after two and a half weeks.

segments.title: The Dunbar Hotel lounge and the plan to restore it
segments.summary: She confirms she worked in the Dunbar lounge and gives her doubts about restoring the hotel because the neighborhood has changed.

segments.title: Dunbar and Clarke hotels and the old Local 767
segments.summary: She and Willard work out the Dunbar's origins and the Clarke Hotel, near Local 767, the black musicians' local used for rehearsals before amalgamation.

segments.title: Paul Howard recruits her into the union
segments.summary: Paul Howard persuaded her to join with a $25 fee paid in installments; her pay rose from $2 to $3 a night.

segments.title: Union benefits and the officers of the old local
segments.summary: Howard explained life membership and protection of pay; she names officers including Florence Cadrez, Ed Bailey and Leo Davis.

segments.title: Her seat on the Board of Local 47
segments.summary: Harvey Brooks's death opened a trial board seat for her; Marl Young and John Tranchitella urged her to serve, and she is now on her third term on the Board.

segments.title: What the trial board and Board of Directors do
segments.summary: She explains the trial board hears claims, the Board of Directors makes policy and hears appeals, and the International Executive Board is the final appeal.

segments.title: Reel 4, February 23, 1979
segments.summary: New session header and Willard's opening remarks on the date and Nellie's cold.

segments.title: Her sister Dina's Coreal Actors group and Janice Johnson
segments.summary: Sister Eugenia (Dina) runs a spoken-and-musical black history group with her children, with sister Florida designing costumes; bassist Janice Johnson began in it.

segments.title: Joe Lutcher takes a tape to Dave Dexter
segments.summary: Joe, trying to get started, took a home tape to Dave Dexter, who liked the voice but never passed the message on.

segments.title: Joe Lutcher's turn to religion; when he came to California
segments.summary: Joe moved into religious work as a Seventh Day Adventist and came to California in the early 1940s after Nellie's 1935 arrival.

segments.title: Joe's music career: saxophones and his Capitol records
segments.summary: Joe began after she left home, played mainly alto, recorded Rocking Boogie and Mardi Gras for Capitol, and was a fine arranger.

segments.title: Her view of Joe's religious music and his illness
segments.summary: She regrets that Joe left jazz and calls his religious commitment fanatical but sincere, and mentions a past serious illness.

segments.title: Her father's birth year
segments.summary: Her father died in 1961 at 80, so he was born in about 1881.

segments.title: Pianist Al Freeman and the actor Al Freeman Jr.
segments.summary: Al Freeman, the Imperial Orchestra pianist, was the father of the actor Al Freeman Jr.

segments.title: Arranger influences and Mary Lou Williams
segments.summary: No single arranger influenced her; she learned from Al Wilson and Paul Barnes and respected Mary Lou Williams.

segments.title: Women musicians with bands
segments.summary: She recalls little about women instrumentalists beyond a Baton Rouge woman and says it was hard for women to travel.

segments.title: Who made the kitties
segments.summary: She cannot recall the piano player who made kitties in Los Angeles.

segments.title: Cleo Brown's records and the demand for women pianist-singers
segments.summary: Cleo Brown's boogie records and Hollywood booking made women pianist-singers in demand, which she says helped her.

segments.title: Joe Wynn's nickname and her second husband
segments.summary: Joe Wynn was nicknamed Windy; her second husband was Leonel Lewis, called Buddy.

segments.title: Working at Stillwell's Hotel while pregnant and going into early labor
segments.summary: Working six nights a week at downtown Stillwell's Hotel with Ben Borders's group, she shopped for the baby and began labor two and a half months early.

segments.title: Giving birth alone to her premature son
segments.summary: Her neighbor Mrs. Garland went to phone the clinic while Nellie delivered the baby alone and kept him alive by spanking him.

segments.title: The homemade oven incubator
segments.summary: The clinic doctor and nurse built an incubator on the stove for the 2-1/4 pound baby, who stayed in hospital six weeks while she supplied her milk.

segments.title: Telling her husband, sister and Jim Wynn
segments.summary: Her husband learned he was a father from bandleader Jim Wynn, who then saw the baby in the homemade incubator.

segments.title: Talmadge's piano and drum lessons
segments.summary: Talmadge started on piano, then drums with Lenny Rosenthal, but lost interest when his teacher changed.

segments.title: Talmadge grows up: school, Air Force and work
segments.summary: He finished school in North Carolina, joined the Air Force, married twice and works in oil exploration in San Francisco.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
segments.title: The Lincoln Theater stage shows and Harry Levette
segments.summary: She recalls the Lincoln Theater's stage shows produced by Bardu Ali and local talent nights run by Harry Levette in 1947.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
segments.title: Pigmeat Markham, Dusty Fletcher and other comedians
segments.summary: Comedians such as Pigmeat Markham and Dusty Fletcher were brought from New York for the shows.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
segments.title: Ralph Cooper's black revue at the Burbank Theater
segments.summary: The downtown Burbank burlesque theater also had a black revue produced by Ralph Cooper, with Alma Travis and Lillian Randolph.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
segments.title: Bandleaders in Los Angeles in 1935
segments.summary: She lists the Club Alabam band, C. L. Burke, Les Hite, Lloyd Reese and George Orendorff as the local bands when she arrived.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
segments.title: Solo pianists Fred Skinner and Harold Brown
segments.summary: Fred Skinner played solo at the Ambassador, and Harold Brown, Lawrence Brown's brother, held long solo engagements with loyal followings.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
segments.title: Elmer Fain, bandleader turned union agent
segments.summary: Saxophonist Elmer Fain led a band before becoming business agent of Local 767 and later 47.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
segments.title: Early women singers: Roberta Hyson, Lottie Gozier and the Breakfast Club singers
segments.summary: She names Roberta Hyson, Lottie Gozier, Ruth Lee, Betty Treadwell and others, intimate table-to-table singers who died young.

segments.chapter: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
segments.title: Clarifying who led the Club Royal and San Diego groups
segments.summary: The Club Royal group was the Daniel Brothers Trio, with Pickens replaced by Nellie, and the San Diego group was Dootsie Williams and the Chocolate Drops.

segments.chapter: Hurry On Down, Capitol and New York
segments.title: Hurry On Down as a flat-fee hit
segments.summary: Hurry On Down was recorded for a flat fee with a promised better contract, which manager Carlos Gastel later arranged.

segments.chapter: Hurry On Down, Capitol and New York
segments.title: Reel 5: composer royalties and The Lady's in Love
segments.summary: After the reel change she confirms writer royalties on Hurry On Down and that The Lady's in Love, a Frank Loesser tune, was its B side.

segments.chapter: Hurry On Down, Capitol and New York
segments.title: Barney Josephson of Cafe Society hears the record
segments.summary: The record was released in New York first; Barney Josephson, a friend of Frank Loesser, sought her for Cafe Society, and Dexter called her in Reno.

segments.chapter: Hurry On Down, Capitol and New York
segments.title: Deciding to go to New York and Carlos Gastel becomes manager
segments.summary: After twelve years working for little, she worried about her son, agreed to eight weeks at Cafe Society, and Dexter got Carlos Gastel and GAC to manage her.

segments.chapter: Hurry On Down, Capitol and New York
segments.title: Carlos Gastel as manager
segments.summary: She and Willard recall Gastel's loud shirts and warmth and how he got her recognition and good pay.

segments.chapter: Hurry On Down, Capitol and New York
segments.title: Correcting Maria Cole's account of the Beaux Cards club
segments.summary: She disputes a passage in the Nat King Cole autobiography saying Gastel fired her at the Beaux Cards club; he in fact booked her there in 1947.

segments.chapter: Hurry On Down, Capitol and New York
segments.title: Nat King Cole as a person and Natalie Cole's style
segments.summary: She praises Nat as a beloved man and artist and comments that Natalie Cole once sounded like Aretha Franklin.

segments.title: Who played at the jam sessions at her house
segments.summary: She names Eddie Cole, Panama Francis, Al Morgan, Lloyd Wilson, Forest Powell and Marshall Royal among those at her house sessions.

segments.title: Playing with Marshall Royal in San Pedro
segments.summary: In the late 1930s she played piano in a trio at a San Pedro club with Alton Red and saxophonist Marshall Royal.

segments.title: Lawrence Welk, her mother, and Marshall Royal's appearance
segments.summary: She and her mother watched Lawrence Welk weekly; she praises Marshall Royal's feature on the show and Welk's long-lasting family entertainment.

segments.title: Sid Catlett as friend and melodic drummer
segments.summary: Sid Catlett played on one of her record sessions and she admires his melodic, listenable drumming.

segments.title: Working with Charles Mingus at the Downbeat Club
segments.summary: She played a couple of nights with Mingus and the Jacquet brothers and found him a bass player who dictated chords to the pianist.

segments.title: Seeing Mingus in New York in 1973 and Willard's Mingus interviews
segments.summary: At the 1973 Newport festival time she thought Mingus seemed distressed and unwell; Willard describes interviewing him in Los Angeles.

segments.title: Mingus on the red car and his bossing of pianists
segments.summary: Buddy Collette's story of Mingus playing on the streetcar leads her to repeat that he bugged piano players.

segments.title: Paul Howard, the early Local 767 and its building on Central Avenue
segments.summary: The early black local was nearly nothing until Paul Howard's membership drive and the purchase of an old house on Central Avenue.

segments.title: Union benefits, scale and refusing low pay
segments.summary: Early benefits were a $250 death payment; scale meant turning down work, but as membership grew musicians gained bargaining power.

segments.title: Rents and living costs in the 1930s
segments.summary: Her aunt's five-room house cost $18 a month and her own one-bedroom flat $16.

segments.title: Joining in 1937 and the amalgamation of Local 767 into 47
segments.summary: She joined around 1937; on amalgamation in the 1950s members kept seniority, received a $1,000 death benefit and the old assets passed to 47.

segments.title: Opposition to amalgamation and working mostly in white clubs
segments.summary: Some older members opposed merging, and she says she always worked in white establishments rather than black spots.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
segments.title: The Swanee Inn: Ivy Anderson, Margaret Bonds and Calvin Jackson
segments.summary: She recalls the Swanee Inn on Vernon where Nat Cole's trio began and where she worked with Ivy Anderson and double-piano Margaret Bonds and Calvin Jackson.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
segments.title: Shep's Playhouse, Bronzeville and Shep Kelly's place
segments.summary: She and Willard discuss the wartime Bronzeville area and Shep's Playhouse, and she recalls a year as a single at Shep Kelly's on Ivar.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
segments.title: The Club Bali with Burrows Fletcher
segments.summary: At the elegant curry-serving Club Bali on Sunset she worked as atmosphere pianist for $5 a night, a job Lillian Randolph recommended.

segments.chapter: This Is Your Life and film work
segments.title: Her Universal short with Ina Ray Hutton
segments.summary: She made a short film with Ina Ray Hutton's all-girl band, singing Real Gone Guy, around 1953-54.

segments.chapter: This Is Your Life and film work
segments.title: Being the subject of This Is Your Life
segments.summary: She says she was the subject of This Is Your Life in about 1951 and recalls always going home for Christmas.

segments.chapter: This Is Your Life and film work
segments.title: How her family set up the surprise
segments.summary: Friends and family in Lake Charles, with her manager, arranged the show and told her she would only sing Let's Start the New Year Right.

segments.chapter: This Is Your Life and film work
segments.title: The surprise voices: nurse Maude Reid and her late teacher
segments.summary: The show brought out her school nurse and her teacher's widowed husband, and she recalls her teacher's death by drowning.

segments.chapter: This Is Your Life and film work
segments.title: Her son appears and Charlotte Hawkins Brown's school
segments.summary: Her son surprised her on stage; he attended the Palmer school founded by Maria Cole's aunt Charlotte Hawkins.

segments.chapter: This Is Your Life and film work
segments.title: Dave Dexter and Alan Prade on the show
segments.summary: Dexter and Southern Rhythm Boys manager Alan Prade were brought on, and Prade recalled her father's summer troupe.

segments.chapter: This Is Your Life and film work
segments.title: Restoring her film of the show
segments.summary: She treasures the film of the broadcast and Willard urges her to have it restored.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Reel Six, February 23, 1979
segments.summary: Header for the last reel.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Why English audiences knew her and her decision to tour Britain
segments.summary: Her records reached England via a German forces radio disc jockey, and after hesitating she accepted Gastel's bookings for two tours.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: British tour: sidemen, Jack Jackson and the Scottish response
segments.summary: She took Earl Hyde and George Duvivier, toured with Jack Jackson and found fans in Scotland who knew all her songs.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Variety houses, Lew Grade's circle and fan Alan Hobbs
segments.summary: She played a week at a time plus Sunday variety shows in London, met the Grade brothers and agent Mumford, and a young fan Alan Hobbs followed her tour.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Later record labels and her string and orchestral albums
segments.summary: Besides Capitol she recorded for Decca, Columbia, Imperial and Liberty, including sung-only albums with Russ Garcia and Harold Mooney and some Billy May sessions.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Regret that her records are out of print
segments.summary: None of her records are being released, which costs her income; she had never planned to be a singer.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Songs she wrote
segments.summary: She lists her compositions including Hurry On Down, He's a Real Gone Guy, Do You or Don't You Love Me, The Pig Latin Song and My Little Boy.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Her discography from a European collector and the lack of availability
segments.summary: A collector friend gave her a European discography of her recordings, though none of her records are available except at auctions.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Thanks to the Smithsonian; disco, rock and jazz's neglect
segments.summary: Willard says little is written about her; Nellie expresses gratitude, then regrets disco and rock taking work from musicians while jazz goes unrecognized.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Foreign offers, the cost of touring and working by feeling
segments.summary: She would tour Europe again only with records out, prefers her own sympathetic musicians such as Morris Edwards and George Duvivier, and plays by feeling.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Her usual Los Angeles sidemen
segments.summary: She names regular bassists Billy Hadnott and Benny Booker, drummers Gene Washington and Al Bartee, and Lee Young on her first session.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Staying home, real estate and the hope for a market
segments.summary: She now rarely travels, owns a six-unit apartment house, serves on the union board, and believes recognition once earned is not lost.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Her South American fan Emilio
segments.summary: A Brazilian poet and director who has all her records befriended her when his group visited, and urges her to tour South America.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Jazz versus rock and roll, and her first airplane flight
segments.summary: Jazz takes years of work unlike quick rock success, and she describes her first flight to Sacramento last May.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Trains and the Queen Mary
segments.summary: She recalls four-day train trips to New York and crossing to Europe on the Queen Mary.

segments.chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
segments.title: Honolulu by ship, closing thanks
segments.summary: She mentions going to Honolulu by ship, says she would choose music again, and thanks the Smithsonian; Willard closes.
